artigo.texto: In the U.S. energy storage system (ESS) market, traditionally dominated by lithium-iron-phosphate (LFP) batteries, Samsung SDI has successfully secured a large-scale supply contract utilizing ternary batteries. Samsung SDI announced on October 26 that its Americas subsidiary (SDIA) has signed an ESS solution supply contract with the U.S. energy firm Alpha Omega Power (AOP) for a capacity of 1 gigawatt-hour (GWh). Combined with a previous phase-one contract late last year, the total volume reaches 1.5 GWh. The supply will be delivered within the year, and AOP plans to deploy it in a large-scale power project breaking ground in Texas next year. While the contract amount is private, industry observers estimate the price of ESS solutions at roughly $160 to $200 per kilowatt-hour (kWh). For 1 GWh, this translates to $160 million to $200 million, or approximately 210 billion to 260 billion Korean won. Batteries are classified into types like prismatic and pouch depending on how the cell is encased. The batteries supplied by Samsung SDI this time are prismatic batteries. Prismatic cells are enclosed in a hard metal can, offering greater impact resistance and higher fire safety compared to pouch types housed in thin film pouches. Among non-Chinese battery manufacturers with North American production facilities, Samsung SDI is the only one producing prismatic batteries for ESS applications. The product being supplied is not just a standalone cell, but a solution called ‘SBB (Samsung Battery Box) 1.7’. It packs not only prismatic battery cells but also cooling and fire-suppression systems, along with battery management software, into a container approximately 6 meters long. Unlike the method of delivering only battery cells, this integrated approach minimizes the need for clients to assemble multiple devices separately, making installation much simpler. The battery chemistry relies on nickel-cobalt-aluminum (NCA) ternary cells. ESS applications with fewer spatial constraints typically utilize LFP batteries, which are cheaper and have longer lifespans. However, although ternary batteries are more expensive, they pack more electricity into the same space and deliver instant high power. Power grids must maintain a stable frequency (60Hz) by balancing supply and demand; when imbalances occur due to power plant failures, ESS systems instantly discharge or absorb electricity to correct it. Company officials explain that ternary batteries are advantageous for projects requiring massive power output in short bursts. Production will be handled by StarPlus Energy (SPE), an Indiana-based joint venture factory between Samsung SDI and Stellantis. Although originally an electric vehicle battery plant, some lines have been repurposed for ESS production since October of last year to navigate a temporary slowdown in U.S. EV demand. Fabrice Hudry, head of the SDIA ESS team and vice president, stated, “We will continue to expand our business foundation in the North American ESS market through differentiated technological competitiveness and local production.”

artigo.texto: GM has partnered with Peak Energy to develop next-generation sodium-ion battery cells, but they’re not going into EVs – they’re for grid-scale energy storage projects. GM Ventures is making a strategic investment in Peak Energy. June 10, 2026: Under the partnership, GM will develop the sodium-ion cells in its Michigan battery labs and retain exclusive manufacturing rights. Peak Energy will integrate the cells into its battery storage systems as it ramps up US manufacturing. The companies are targeting a market that’s growing rapidly as utilities add battery storage to support renewable energy, rising electricity demand, and the buildout of data centers and AI infrastructure. Today’s stationary storage market is dominated by lithium-iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. But Peak Energy believes sodium-ion batteries can deliver a lower-cost alternative for grid applications, where energy density is less important than cost, reliability, and safety. A key part of Peak’s pitch is its passively cooled battery storage platform. Conventional LFP battery systems require active cooling equipment to maintain safe operating temperatures, adding cost and complexity. Peak says its system eliminates those cooling systems entirely. According to the company, its sodium-ion platform can reduce energy storage costs by 20% compared with conventional systems while delivering more than 99% uptime. Peak also argues that its design wastes less energy. It estimates that replacing conventional LFP storage systems with its passively cooled technology could reduce annual battery-storage energy waste in the US by up to 2 terawatt-hours. That’s enough electricity to power a mid-sized city for a year. GM’s vice president of battery and sustainability, Kurt Kelty, said sodium-ion is a strong fit for stationary storage. “At GM, we know that the application should determine the battery, and for grid-scale stationary storage, sodium-ion is the right solution,” Kelty said. “Peak is already demonstrating the value of sodium-ion through their innovative energy storage platform, and together we’re working to push those benefits even further with our next-generation cell – helping deliver more reliable, lower-cost energy storage at scale for the US grid.” Sodium-ion batteries still account for a small share of the global battery market, but interest is growing because they can be made from more abundant, lower-cost materials than lithium-based batteries. GM and Peak are betting those advantages could make sodium-ion an increasingly attractive option for large-scale energy storage. But don’t expect GM to develop sodium-ion battery cells for EVs, because the energy density is too low. October 23, 2026, update: Peak Energy has raised $108 million in an oversubscribed Series B funding round led by GM Ventures, with backing from LG Technology Ventures and other investors. Trains don't worry about aerodynamics - or really even weight. Daisy chain 2 or 3 cars worth of these behind an electric engine or two and do full swap outs for recharge/refuel stops. The sodium-ion battery startup plans to use the money to expand US manufacturing, fulfill more than $1 billion in existing customer orders, and bring its passively cooled energy storage systems to the power-hungry data center market. artigo.texto: Itaipu financia data centers de IA, mas no Paraguai Paraguai atrai megaprojeto americano de infraestrutura para inteligência artificial usando energia de Itaipu. O Brasil bancou US$ 89,8 bilhões da usina e pode ficar para trás na corrida. O vice-secretário de Estado dos EUA, Christopher Landau, visitou a usina de Itaipu nesta semana e anunciou uma parceria estratégica entre a americana Crusoe e a paraguaia Araico para construir um megaprojeto de infraestrutura voltado à inteligência artificial. A eletricidade que vai alimentar os servidores é a mesma de Itaipu, empreendimento quase inteiramente financiado por empréstimos garantidos pelo Tesouro Nacional brasileiro. A ironia é difícil de ignorar. O Brasil pagou US$ 89,8 bilhões em custos líquidos desde o início das operações da usina, segundo dados do Instituto Acende Brasil. O Paraguai obteve receitas de US$ 5,9 bilhões no mesmo período. E agora é o país vizinho que sai na frente para capturar o maior ciclo de investimentos em infraestrutura tecnológica da década. O projeto de IA que pode mudar o Paraguai O Departamento de Estado americano classificou a parceria Crusoe-Araico como “potencialmente um dos maiores investimentos privados na história do Paraguai”. A primeira fase do projeto deve entrar em operação em meados de 2027, oferecendo serviços de cloud computing para consumidores nos Estados Unidos e na América Latina. A Araico planeja construir o Iguazi AI City, um campus de data centers com meta de atingir até 1,3 GW de capacidade total no longo prazo. Para se ter ideia da escala, isso equivale a mais da metade da capacidade contratada de toda a usina de Itaipu pelo lado paraguaio. Além do acordo de IA, a Uranium Energy Corp anunciou um investimento de US$ 12 milhões para desenvolver concessões de exploração de urânio em solo paraguaio. A visita de Landau foi acompanhada por uma delegação comercial focada em tecnologia, minerais críticos, infraestrutura fluvial e logística. O presidente paraguaio Santiago Peña acompanhou pessoalmente o tour pela hidrelétrica. Por que o Paraguai tem vantagem sobre o Brasil A equação é simples: energia barata, abundante e disponível. O Paraguai tem direito a 50% da geração de Itaipu e 50% da geração de Yaciretá, usina em sociedade com a Argentina. Mas o consumo interno paraguaio é uma fração dessa capacidade. Em 2025, o país usou apenas 36% da sua fatia de Itaipu. Marcos Peigo, CEO da Scala Data Centers, uma das maiores empresas do setor na América Latina, afirmou que o Paraguai tem potencial para atingir 1 GW em data centers antes do Brasil, caso o país não aprove rapidamente incentivos tributários estaduais para a indústria. O governo paraguaio, segundo Peigo, “fez a lição de casa de rodar o mundo com o presidente” e está cumprindo suas promessas ao mercado. O Brasil aprovou recentemente o Redata no Congresso, programa de incentivos fiscais para data centers. Mas a implementação depende de adesão dos estados, e o ritmo da burocracia brasileira pode custar posições numa corrida global que se mede em meses, não em anos. A conta desproporcional de Itaipu para o brasileiro O tratado binacional de Itaipu, assinado em 1973, foi desenhado para permitir que o Paraguai, com economia muito menor, conseguisse arcar com seus compromissos. Claudio Sales, presidente do Acende Brasil, reconhece que “o desenho do tratado é de uma brilhante engenharia diplomática”, mas afirma que negociações desfavoráveis ao Brasil nas últimas duas décadas distorceram os números além do razoável. Em 2009, um acordo entre os presidentes Lula e Fernando Lugo aumentou os pagamentos brasileiros pela fatia de energia não utilizada pelos paraguaios. Hoje, o Paraguai recebe 59% dos repasses financeiros da usina, enquanto 89% dos custos ficam com o lado brasileiro. As despesas socioambientais da usina ilustram o problema. Até 2016, essas despesas ficavam em torno de US$ 100 milhões por ano. Em 2022, saltaram para US$ 505 milhões. Em 2025, atingiram US$ 1,2 bilhão. Parte desses recursos foi direcionada para fins desconectados da operação da usina, como obras para a COP-30 no Pará e apoio à Universidade Federal de Integração Latino-Americana. “Essas despesas viraram um verdadeiro orçamento paralelo que, por Itaipu ser fruto de um tratado binacional, não se sujeita aos controles do Tribunal de Contas da União e do Congresso”, afirmou Sales. Tudo isso é repassado à tarifa de energia e bancado pelo consumidor brasileiro na conta de luz. O que está em jogo para o Brasil na corrida dos data centers A demanda global por infraestrutura de IA está redefinindo a geopolítica energética. Países com energia barata e regulação ágil estão atraindo bilhões em investimentos. A corrida por data centers se tornou um dos vetores mais relevantes de desenvolvimento econômico no mundo. O Brasil tem a maior matriz elétrica renovável entre as grandes economias, com capacidade instalada superior a 200 GW. Mas enfrenta gargalos regulatórios, tributários e de transmissão que dificultam a conversão dessa vantagem em projetos concretos. Enquanto isso, o Paraguai oferece ao mercado americano exatamente o que ele procura: energia limpa, preço competitivo e velocidade de implementação. A situação cria um paradoxo incômodo. O contribuinte brasileiro financiou a construção e a operação de Itaipu por décadas. O custo aparece na conta de luz de cada residência e empresa do país. E agora, a energia excedente dessa mesma usina pode se tornar a base da infraestrutura de inteligência artificial da América Latina, gerando empregos, receita fiscal e posicionamento estratégico para o Paraguai. Para o investidor brasileiro, o recado é claro: a vantagem energética do país não se traduz automaticamente em vantagem competitiva. Sem agilidade regulatória e incentivos claros, o Brasil corre o risco de assistir seus vizinhos colherem os frutos de uma infraestrutura que ele mesmo ajudou a construir. Este conteúdo é informativo e educacional e não constitui recomendação de investimento. Renta

artigo.texto: Often hailed as a ‘dream battery’ due to its near-zero explosion risk and vastly expanded electric vehicle driving range, the solid-state battery is facing a shifting industry perspective. As commercialization draws closer, skepticism regarding profitability is mounting due to high costs and mass-production limitations. According to the battery industry, South Korea’s top three battery makers are all racing toward solid-state commercialization, but with varying degrees of urgency. Samsung SDI is currently pushing the hardest, targeting mass production by the second half of 2027. On the 6th of this month, the company signed a joint development agreement with battery material firm Ecopro BM for solid-state cathodes and solid electrolytes. A Samsung SDI official stated, “We are already supplying prototypes to clients and verifying performance. There are no changes in the demand from clients currently in discussions.” However, large-scale mass production will not begin immediately next year. The initial target markets are humanoid robots requiring fewer batteries and ultra-luxury electric vehicles capable of absorbing high battery costs. Yet, whether meaningful profits can be generated solely from supplying small quantities of batteries for robots and EVs remains uncertain. Industry watchers believe that given Samsung SDI’s long-standing dedication to solid-state development domestically, the move is intended to preempt a new market that even China has yet to dominate. In contrast, LG Energy Solution and SK On are adopting a more measured pace. LG Energy Solution has set its mass-production target for EV solid-state batteries in early 2029 and humanoid applications by 2030. A company official remarked, “We view solid-state batteries more as a ‘market extender’ that expands the market rather than an immediate ‘game changer’ that will replace it overnight.” This represents a more cautious stance compared to its self-published report last year, which heavily promoted solid-state technology as a future game-changer. Similarly, while SK On continues development after completing a solid-state pilot production line last year, it has scheduled commercialization for 2029 or later. Recently, the global EV market has seen low-cost Chinese LFP (lithium iron phosphate) batteries become mainstream, even with lower performance than ternary batteries. This background fuels concerns that high-priced solid-state batteries could face market rejection. Professor Lee Ho-keun of Daeduk University noted, “The question is how many cars can actually bear the cost of solid-state batteries. This now needs to be approached as an industrial issue rather than just a technological one, which won’t be easy in the short term.” Technological hurdles must also be cleared. Issues such as poor adhesion between solid materials, cracks during charging and discharging, and low production yields persist. An industry insider noted, “Making things in a laboratory and mass-producing them in a factory are entirely different challenges.” Skepticism is also surfacing in China. Ni Jun, Chief Manufacturing Officer (CMO) of CATL, the world’s largest battery company, stated last month, “The possibility of short-term commercialization for solid-state batteries is very low. Large-scale commercialization will take at least five years.” Chinese battery giants like CATL and BYD have likewise targeted commercialization around 2030. Nevertheless, experts emphasize that South Korea must claim the solid-state battery market first. Professor Park Chul-wan of Seojeong University stressed, “We have been talking about solid-state for decades; now is the time to prove the technology with actual products.” Professor Lee Sang-young of Yonsei University added, “Before China establishes solid-state standards and occupies the market, South Korea must create the benchmarks first and secure an early lead.” This implies finding a breakthrough in the solid-state sector through an “upgrading” strategy powered by technological prowess, escaping China’s onslaught of cheap battery supplies. Professor Kim Pil-soo of Daelim University pointed out, “Mass production is difficult, but the directional path of solid-state technology is correct. Domestic batteries struggling with price competition ultimately have no choice but to compete with high-value-added products.”

artigo.texto: PEMBROKE — Oct. 20, 2026 — Pembroke’s Special Town Meeting adopted a zoning bylaw for battery energy storage systems Tuesday night after voters amended the Planning Board’s proposal, doubling from 150 to 300 feet the setback required where a medium- or large-scale battery facility’s parcel directly abuts an active residential use or a Residence A district lot line, despite town counsel’s warning that the change could draw attorney general disapproval. The Full Story What voters changed Planning Board Vice Chair Alysha Siciliano-Perry moved the bylaw as printed in a handout distributed at the meeting, with two oral corrections: the Tier 2 heading in its permitting table should end at 5 megawatt-hours rather than 10, and electrical substations should be dropped from a sentence encouraging battery systems to locate alongside solar arrays, power generation stations or similar facilities. Susan Bollinger then moved to change the bylaw’s abutting residential lot line buffer from 150 to 300 feet, leaving the rest of that clause unchanged. As printed, the clause requires all battery structures, containers, paved equipment pads and secondary enclosures to keep that distance from the property line wherever a battery parcel directly abuts an active residential use or a Residence A lot line. It falls under setback rules that open by addressing medium-scale Tier 2 and large-scale Tier 3 systems. Siciliano-Perry described Tier 1 as household battery packs, which the bylaw allows by right as an accessory use in every district. After a resident moved the question, voters ended debate and adopted the amendment by majority show of hands. The moderator then declared the amended bylaw passed, saying it required a two-thirds vote. The setback debate Bollinger said the original draft carried 300 feet before the Planning Board reduced it, and that her amendment would not change which properties qualify. I think that residents in Pembroke should reasonably be able to expect that a large-scale industrial size battery yard would not go on the residential property next to them — Susan Bollinger 40:58 She noted the bylaw already sets 300 feet next to schools and similar facilities, where staff help people evacuate, and argued that people at home may be unable to evacuate quickly. She later said she was not opposed to battery storage and that, in reviewing past attorney general decisions, she found rulings in which the office struck specific language while letting the rest of a bylaw stand. Siciliano-Perry said 150 feet mirrors the town’s existing industrial setback from residential properties and cited the state Department of Energy Resources model bylaw as using 50 feet, warning the state would refuse a setback that makes projects impractical. The August 2026 state model first defers to district setbacks; its 50- to 75-foot figures for lots abutting residential districts appear as optional examples, alongside a caution against setbacks so large they amount to a de facto prohibition. Siciliano-Perry added that the fire chief, who served on the drafting committee, proposed the bylaw’s 300-foot distance for schools, hospitals and nursing homes. Town Counsel Michelle Randazzo said it is untested whether the attorney general would view 300 feet as effectively prohibiting battery facilities. if they view a 300-foot setback as effectively prohibiting the siting of any BESS facility then they may end up disapproving the bylaw in its entirety — Michelle Randazzo, Town Counsel 54:22 Asked by Kathleen Keegan whether the state could replace 300 feet with 50, Randazzo said she had not seen the attorney general substitute a number that way and thought the office might instead disapprove the language, sending it back to Town Meeting. Alan Peterson, who described himself as a retired public facilities director, said 300 feet would create an economic barrier to most battery projects, citing time-of-use electricity pricing and schools elsewhere with battery stations within 50 feet. Another speaker, who said they had sat on a past battery storage appeal, backed 300 feet.

artigo.texto: O senador e candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) prometeu ampliar o saneamento básico no Pará, melhorar as condições de tráfego na Transamazônica e atrair investimentos em data centers para o Amazonas. As propostas foram apresentadas nesta sexta-feira (23), durante o debate presidencial da TV Globo, em confronto com o presidente Lula (PT). Ao falar sobre a falta de água tratada e de coleta e tratamento de esgoto, Flávio afirmou que pretende trabalhar em parceria com o governador eleito do Pará, Daniel, para ampliar a infraestrutura de Belém. “Eu me comprometo a ajudar Belém a fazer o maior programa de saneamento básico da cidade”, declarou. O senador relatou ter visto esgoto a céu aberto na capital paraense e criticou as condições enfrentadas por moradores que convivem com mau cheiro e falta de infraestrutura. Ele também prometeu atuar para melhorar o acesso a serviços básicos na Região Norte. Candidato critica situação da Transamazônica Flávio afirmou que pretende garantir o asfaltamento de trechos da Transamazônica e responsabilizou entraves ambientais do governo federal pelas dificuldades para executar as obras. Segundo o candidato, a falta de pavimentação prejudica o deslocamento de moradores e o transporte de cargas, sobretudo durante o período de chuvas, quando caminhões ficam atolados e comunidades podem enfrentar dificuldades de conexão com outras regiões. “Eu vou garantir o que você mais pediu, o direito de trabalhar”, afirmou, ao direcionar o discurso aos eleitores do Pará. A proposta integra o discurso do candidato em defesa da ampliação da infraestrutura e da redução de obstáculos ambientais e burocráticos a projetos de desenvolvimento. Zona Franca e data centers Para o Amazonas, Flávio prometeu manter a Zona Franca de Manaus e ampliar sua capacidade de atrair investimentos. O senador citou a instalação de data centers como uma oportunidade econômica e defendeu aproveitar recursos de gás natural para produzir fertilizantes no Brasil. A proposta busca associar a estrutura industrial da região a novos investimentos em tecnologia e energia. Flávio também afirmou que pretende reduzir a dependência brasileira de fertilizantes importados, utilizando matéria-prima disponível no país. O candidato ainda declarou que pretende garantir autonomia aos povos indígenas para decidir sobre atividades em suas terras, tema que provocou reação de Lula durante o debate. Saneamento tem meta legal para 2033 Ao criticar a situação do saneamento, Flávio afirmou que, por causa do atual governo, a meta de universalização teria sido empurrada para depois de 2050. A declaração, porém, exige uma distinção: o Marco Legal do Saneamento, instituído pela Lei nº 14.026/2020, estabelece como metas o atendimento de 99% da população com água potável e de 90% com coleta e tratamento de esgoto até o fim de 2033. . A existência de metas legais não significa que elas serão necessariamente cumpridas. Em julho de 2026, apesar do aumento dos investimentos desde a aprovação do marco legal, o ritmo de aplicação dos recursos ainda estava abaixo do necessário para universalizar os serviços até 2033. . Lula rebate propostas e defende preservação ambiental Na resposta, Lula acusou o grupo político de Flávio de defender medidas que, segundo ele, enfraqueceriam a proteção ambiental. O presidente citou a gestão do ex-ministro do Meio Ambiente Ricardo Salles e afirmou que a Amazônia pode gerar mais recursos com a floresta preservada do que com sua derrubada. Lula também defendeu a economia verde e o Fundo Amazônia, cuja retomada atribuiu ao atual governo. “Ele não conhece a Amazônia”, afirmou o presidente, ao contestar as propostas do adversário. Sua opinião sobre esta matéria importa.

artigo.texto: Unveiled in Beijing, the system features a standardised, chassis-mounted main battery alongside a 77kWh range-extension battery positioned behind the cab. The secondary battery supports 3C charging and provides backup power. CATL Aims to Improve Battery Utilisation CATL said conventional battery-swapping trucks typically return to stations with around 30% charge remaining to avoid running out of power. This leaves some leased battery capacity unused. The additional battery allows the main battery’s depth of discharge to increase from approximately 70% to more than 95%, enabling vehicles to reach swapping stations with less than 5% charge remaining in the main unit. The system can transfer power delivery to the range-extension battery within milliseconds, providing continuous power and redundancy in demanding operating conditions. CATL’s “1+X” architecture keeps the main battery standardised for compatibility with the Qiji network, while the secondary unit can be adapted for low-temperature performance, high energy density or high power. Both batteries can be upgraded independently, and fleets can lease main batteries according to seasonal demand. Qiji Network Adds Higher-Capacity Batteries The latest Qiji offering includes the 260# and 300# standardised swappable batteries, with capacities of 432kWh and 513kWh respectively, complementing the existing 75# battery. CATL said its new-generation swapping station completes battery replacement in five minutes, reduces construction costs by 10% and requires no excavation pit. Deployment can take as little as five days. Changes to its battery-as-a-service (BaaS) billing model mean customers pay for net energy charged rather than energy discharged. CATL said this could reduce per-kWh rental costs by up to 20% for customers on basic plans, while allowing them to retain the benefits of regenerative braking. Expansion Plans Reflect Growing Demand CATL aims to operate 900 heavy-duty truck swapping stations by the end of 2026, rising to 2,000 by 2027, with a long-term target of 10,000 stations across China. Agreements covering 13,000 vehicles were signed at the launch, including orders from SF Holding and China Postal Express & Logistics. The announcement comes as new energy heavy-duty trucks accounted for 50% of China’s market in September, up from 29% a year earlier, according to China Passenger Car Association analysis of compulsory traffic insurance data. artigo.texto: - The second-generation Seal 07 grows to 5,080 mm in length and will feature the DiSus-M intelligent magnetorheological body control system. - Reservation holders will receive priority production and delivery, with deposits fully refundable before orders are locked in. BYD (HKEX: 1211) has opened reservations for the second-generation Seal 07, a larger electric sedan equipped with its second-generation Blade Battery and flash charging technology. Zhang Zhuo, general manager of BYD's Ocean lineup sales division, announced the opening of reservations on Weibo on Monday, without disclosing pre-sales prices — a practice known as blind reservations. An official poster shows that reservation holders will receive priority production and delivery, with deposits fully refundable before orders are locked in. The reservations serve only as expressions of purchase intent, allowing customers to change colors and configurations after the launch. BYD is also offering exclusive gifts to customers who place reservations and take delivery. The move follows a series of previews. Zhang first unveiled the exterior on September 28 and shared cabin details on October 23. The second-generation Seal 07 will feature the second-generation Blade Battery and flash charging, with BYD promoting its charging capability as "ready in 5 minutes, full in 9 minutes." The car will also feature the DiSus-M intelligent magnetorheological body control system, front double-wishbone and reinforced rear 5-link suspension, and BYD's Smart Ecosystem 2.0. The second-generation Seal 07 adopts the Ocean Aesthetics 2.0 design language, with styling consistent with the Seal 08. It offers 6 exterior colors and 3 interior color schemes. The car measures 5,080 mm in length, 1,960 mm in width and 1,495 mm in height, with a wheelbase of 2,960 mm. It is 85 mm longer than the Seal 07 EV launched in March, with a 60 mm longer wheelbase. The cabin features front zero-gravity seats with massage, ventilation and heating functions, along with a 20-speaker Devialet audio system. BYD lists trunk and front-trunk capacities of 618 liters and 160 liters, respectively. The vehicle shown is equipped with roof-mounted LiDAR, though BYD has yet to detail its driver-assistance capabilities or how equipment will vary across trims. Earlier filings with China's Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) showed that the second-generation Seal 07's battery-electric version offers peak motor outputs of 245 kW (329 hp) and 300 kW, both above the 240 kW of the model launched in March. Alongside the battery-electric model shown in the poster, the filings included a plug-in hybrid retaining the Seal 07 DM-i name, with a 1.5-liter turbocharged engine and a 160 kW electric motor. The plug-in hybrid has a 38.029-kWh battery and a WLTC electric range of 245 km (152 miles). The latest official poster did not specify reservation arrangements for that version. For reference, the Seal 07 EV launched on March 5 was offered in 2 variants priced at 169,900 yuan ($25,300) and 189,900 yuan. The redesign comes as the Seal lineup faces sales pressure. Data compiled by CnEVPost shows that the series sold 46,718 vehicles in September, down 9.04% year-on-year and 1.57% from August. In the first 9 months of the year, Seal-series sales totaled 304,723 vehicles, down 14.11% year-on-year. The lineup includes the Seal 07 and several other battery-electric and plug-in hybrid models. ($1 = 6.7162 yuan)

artigo.texto: BAIC Group and CATL signed an expanded battery-swapping agreement on October 22, 2026, to connect compatible models from multiple BAIC brands to CATL’s Choco-Swap network. The partners’ reported ambition is a mature Chinese ecosystem serving vehicles at the million-vehicle scale, with BAIC dealerships helping support station locations. How the agreement is meant to work CnEVPost reported, citing a BAIC statement, that the cooperation covers vehicle and battery development, swap-station network construction, battery-energy services and new business models. BAIC is to connect compatible vehicles from several of its brands to Choco-Swap. Its dealership network is to help identify station sites, and the companies are exploring joint development and operation of stations with dealers. The partners also aim to consolidate swap assets under specialized management and promote unified standards and interoperable networks. For drivers, compatibility depends on the vehicle and battery system: a CATL-supplied battery alone does not establish that a vehicle can use a CATL swap station. A million-vehicle ambition, alongside CATL’s existing network The million-vehicle figure describes the scale of the partners’ ambition, not a dated deployment target. CATL’s network was reported at 2,520 battery-swap stations across 200 Chinese cities as of September 29, 2026, before the agreement was signed. Battery swapping replaces a depleted pack with a charged one at a station. The agreement sets out cooperation on vehicles, stations and related services, while its stated goal describes the scale the partners hope the Chinese ecosystem will reach. BAIC and CATL had already worked on swap-compatible vehicles The October agreement builds on earlier BAIC-CATL cooperation signed in June 2024, which covered swap-compatible vehicles, battery-block development and battery-data management, according to CnEVPost. CnEVPost reported that the Arcfox Beta S3 swap version, using CATL’s Choco-SEB system, launched on May 22, 2026. A swap version of the Arcfox Beta T1 appeared in an August 2026 filing with China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology.

artigo.texto: - CATL confirms Firefly uses its Qilin Battery, with the 60-kWh version offering a CLTC range of 560 km. - The original 42-kWh battery is supplied by Sunwoda and offers a CLTC range of 420 km. Nio Inc's (NYSE: NIO) Firefly brand uses CATL's (HKEX: 3750) Qilin Battery in its newly launched 60-kWh pack, adding a longer-range option for the small electric vehicle. CATL said on Weibo on Saturday that Firefly uses its Qilin Battery, delivering a CLTC range of 560 km (348 miles). Firefly officially launched the larger-capacity battery a day earlier. Firefly's original 42-kWh standard-range battery is supplied by Sunwoda (SZSE: 300207) and uses lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells, offering a CLTC range of 420 km. Sunwoda is among China's major second-tier battery makers and is also a major partner of Li Auto (NASDAQ: LI). Firefly's new 60-kWh battery uses nickel-cobalt-manganese (NCM) cells, increasing range by 140 km, or about 33%. Battery dimensions and vehicle curb weight remain unchanged, according to Firefly. Qilin is a battery product line CATL introduced in 2022, with its third generation unveiled in April this year. The Weibo post did not specify which generation Firefly uses or its charging rate. For owners, however, these details may matter less, as Firefly vehicles, like other models from Nio Inc, can replenish their batteries through a 3-minute battery swap. For new buyers, Firefly EV equipped with the 60-kWh battery starts at 136,800 yuan ($20,360), including the battery. Under the BaaS (battery as a service) subscription plan, the car starts at 79,800 yuan, with a monthly battery rental fee of 599 yuan. The new battery is also available to existing owners. Under Firefly's announced plan, customers who purchased their vehicles with the battery included can apply for a permanent upgrade once at least 1 year has passed since their purchase invoice date. The upgrade costs 17,000 yuan. Existing BaaS users pay a permanent upgrade service fee of 3,000 yuan, with monthly battery rent rising to 599 yuan from 399 yuan for the 42-kWh version. Firefly said the 2 battery capacities use compatible standardized module designs, with identical casing dimensions, mounting points and locking mechanisms. This allows existing vehicles to receive the upgrade through battery swapping without replacing the car. The brand first gained access to Nio's fifth-generation battery swap stations on August 7. Previously, Firefly's shorter body and wheelbase prevented it from using Nio's fourth-generation stations. The use of Qilin batteries in Firefly extends Nio's cooperation with CATL. In January, the companies announced a 5-year agreement to deepen their strategic partnership, focusing on areas including joint development of long-life batteries and battery swap compatibility technologies. Firefly's first model, which shares the brand's name, launched in China in April 2025, targeting the small electric vehicle market and competing with brands including Mini and Smart. The brand announced on October 16 that cumulative deliveries had reached 90,000 vehicles. Firefly delivered a record 7,327 vehicles in September, bringing its total for the first 9 months of this year to 48,122, according to data compiled by CnEVPost. ($1 = 6.7180 yuan)

artigo.texto: What’s It Like Inside a Data Center? Northern Virginia is laden with structures that house data for Fortune 500 companies. I went inside just one of those monstrosities that bothers its neighbors. What’s It Like Inside a Data Center? Northern Virginia is laden with structures that house data for Fortune 500 companies. I went inside just one of those monstrosities that bothers its neighbors. The sun was beating down as I made my way through a quiet community in Ashburn, Virginia. The roads were wide and lined with cars; there was a nice central playground with no one playing in it; the houses seemed monstrously large; and there were ample trees dotting the clean-cut lawns of the neighborhood. In so many ways, it felt like your typical US suburb, until you looked past the thick wall of trees that defined its boundaries. The white walls of a large facility peeked out from above the deep green foliage. It ran on in the distance, the large houses making it impossible to see its full extent. Towering above it a little farther away were the high-voltage transmission lines that fed it with electricity. The trees acted like a shield, allowing those who lived in the community not to think about what stood on their doorstep and the growing demands that came from the surrounding industrial expansion. I’m talking, of course, about hyperscale data centers. No location on the entire planet has more data centers than Virginia. The state holds more than 13 percent of global hyperscale capacity—double that of Beijing, which comes in second. There were nearly 600 data centers within the state’s boundaries in 2025, about 150 of which were hyperscale—the monstrously large variety that have become much more common since the advent of generative AI—and most of them were clustered in an area in the north of the state around Ashburn, which has since been dubbed “Data Center Alley.” Data centers are unavoidable in Northern Virginia. When I sat on a bench next to a neighborhood lake, a hyperscale data center owned by Microsoft stared back at me from the opposite bank. As I drove through industrial parks, they were dotted throughout. When I pulled into a shopping area to grab a bite to eat, facilities that powered Amazon Web Services loomed behind the strip mall. I could even feel their influence in the street names: Cloud Plaza, Performance Circle, and, worst of all, Growth Mindset Lane. We can thank Microsoft for that one. In short, they were everywhere when I visited in 2025, and following them wherever they set down were the high-voltage power lines needed to keep them running. Data centers were remaking the fabric of a whole region; there seemed to be no end in sight for their expansion. They had become a major industry, and neither worries over local resource demands nor growing concern from residents seemed able to stop the ambitions of some of the most powerful companies on the planet. It’s hard to generalize about the data centers themselves. They come in many shapes and sizes, operate at various scales—from rooms in a nondescript building to entire parks of warehouse-sized facilities crammed with thousands of servers apiece—and seem to be getting bigger with every passing year. Some of them exist to serve the companies operating them; others exist as places where many different groups can rent space for servers of their own. Certain facilities are cooled with air-conditioning, while others depend more on water-based cooling, and even the way those systems are implemented can differ. I guess what I’m trying to say is that one description of a data center will never cover the gamut: There is some standardization, but there is also a lot of room for operators to put their own stamp on how their facility or network of locations is going to work. The interiors of some Google data centers have clusters of brightly colored tubes running throughout them—echoing the primary colors present in the company’s branding—while the average Microsoft or Amazon facility might appear more utilitarian. Digital Realty is one of the largest data-center operators in the world. The company has two major lines of business: It builds entire facilities that then get leased to other companies, including the major cloud providers, but it also offers colocation services. Those are facilities where Digital Realty runs the data center, renting space in racks to other companies that they can then fill with their own servers. I stopped to walk the length of one of its facilities in Northern Virginia. The simplest way to describe it is to say that it looks like a massive box. The company’s logo was visible near the upper portion of the building, and it had some different shades of gray and blue across its exterior. The data center seemed quiet that weekend afternoon, though even on a weekday there weren’t likely to be many people there. Data centers don’t need many employees to keep them clean, secure, and running; the bulk of the jobs they provide are created in the construction phase and mostly disappear once that’s over. The parking lot at the front of the building was surrounded by a large black fence that went around the entire property. I wasn’t trying to get in, but I did wonder if there was a security officer behind a desk somewhere inside the building peering at me through the video feed of one of the facility’s many security cameras. Data centers are notoriously well-guarded, to keep their data safe and to assuage the worries of their clients. There wasn’t much to see as I walked along the fence, the spikes at the top of each pole warning me not to try anything rash. It took nearly five minutes to walk from one end of the building to the other, and this wasn’t even one of the bigger ones I’d seen that day. At the far end, a little beyond the fence, I walked onto a wooden platform where I could make out a serene pond obscured by tall trees and plants. The chirps and trills of birds and insects were just barely audible over the buzz

artigo.texto: Local officials in many parts of Connecticut are not waiting for the national data center boom to come to them. Earlier this month, for example, the East Lyme Zoning Commission voted unanimously to adopt an indefinite ban on all data center development, one of the first such blanket prohibitions in Connecticut. The ban, which went into effect on Saturday, came before anyone had announced even the faintest plan to construct a data center in the coastal town. “It seems like all over the country, they’re trying to figure out the effects of pollution, energy consumption, chemical runoffs,” Anne Thurlow, the chairwoman of East Lyme’s Zoning Commission, said during an August meeting. “I think it’s a good thing to ban them until we know more about them,” Thurlow added. “It could always be reversed if the town wanted to.” East Lyme is one of around half a dozen municipalities that have taken preemptive action to block data center development, either through temporary moratoriums or a complete ban, according to a review of public meetings and records by The Connecticut Mirror. Moratoriums have been passed in communities big and small, suburban and rural. New Haven passed a one-year moratorium in September, with an exemption for the city’s existing quantum computing hub. Morris, a town in the Litchfield Hills with fewer than 3,000 residents, has a two-year ban. “The Connecticut case is quite interesting because many other places in the country, when we see these protests and opposition, either something has started or something is already there,” said Subodha Kumar, a professor of statistics, operations and data science at Temple University’s Fox School of Business. But in Connecticut, he said, political pushback has formed well ahead of actual plans for development. “Connecticut has never been that attractive, frankly speaking, for data centers,” Kumar said. The development of large “hyperscale” data centers in Connecticut, and to a greater extent in New England, has been stymied by the high cost of electricity, along with the need to access to utility infrastructure and large plots of land to house thousands of servers, which can easily cover several football fields. In 2021, Connecticut lawmakers fast-tracked legislation to lure data center developers by promising to waive sales and use taxes for projects that invest at least $200 million in the state (or $50 million for projects located within certain state-designated enterprise zones). To date, the only project to take advantage of that exemption: Cigna’s $386 million renovation of an existing data center in Windsor. Thurlow said the effort in East Lyme was driven, in part, as a reaction to a proposal to erect a massive new data center facility next door in Waterford, which is home to the Millstone Nuclear Power Station. The planned facility would have drawn its power directly from Millstone, a setup known as co-location. But local pushback and years of delays ended up killing that project, according to Waterford First Selectman Robert Brule, who told CT Mirror last month that he and the town were no longer interested in hosting data centers. “We’d rather produce the energy now than produce a project that sucks up the energy,” Brule said. The Department of Economic and Community Development, which oversees the data center tax incentive program, said it has reviewed only two applications under the program since it began and none this year. The credit has become an issue in the gubernatorial election, with Republican candidate Sen. Ryan Fazio arguing the tax incentive should be ended. A spokesperson for Gov. Ned Lamont said the governor was open to discussing changing or eliminating the credit, adding that the tax incentive was never intended for large AI data centers and “should be clarified to ensure it is never used by a hyperscale data center and that data centers bring their own power.” The law also exempted qualified projects from local property taxes but requires developers to enter into a host fee agreement with any municipality in which a data center is located. Randy Collins, a lobbyist at the Connecticut Conference of Municipalities, said developers argued it would be “economically unfeasible” to invest millions of dollars into the necessary equipment for data centers without offsetting some of the taxes. But despite a handful of towns successfully negotiating host fee agreements, Collins said developers have been slow to actually take advantage of the tax breaks. “If you look at the resources and requirements going in, they’re not just going to be popping up everywhere,” Collins said. Still, the issue has drawn considerable attention. Democrats in the state Senate say the moment requires new policy, with Senate Majority Leader Bob Duff announcing this week that he intends to introduce legislation next session that would create a statewide moratorium on new data centers. The proposal was initially outlined in a CT Mirror op-ed in September. “We think there should be rules of the road. We think there should be a moratorium,” Duff told reporters during a Thursday morning press conference in Groton. “We think we should better understand what electric and water and other types of problems are.” The public concern around data centers, he added, is something worth listening to. “We’re seeing people across our state and across our country who are really upset over the proliferation of data centers coming in, literally in people’s neighborhoods,” Duff said. “We should not have these in people’s neighborhoods.” Duff said there is a clear partisan divide over data centers. artigo.texto: General Motors is backing a sodium-ion battery push aimed at making electricity storage cheaper for utilities and data centers. Peak Energy, a sodium-ion battery startup backed by General Motors through its investment arm GM Ventures, announced on October 23 that it had raised $108 million in an oversubscribed Series B funding round. GM Ventures led the round, with participation from LG Technology Ventures and other investors, to support the company’s expansion into grid and data center energy storage. The startup plans to expand manufacturing, fulfill more than $1 billion in existing customer orders, and bring its passively cooled battery storage systems to the data center market. Its platform eliminates active cooling equipment, which the company says can reduce storage costs and energy waste. The funding builds on a partnership announced June 10. GM will develop next-generation sodium-ion cells at its Michigan battery laboratories and retain exclusive manufacturing rights, while Peak Energy will integrate the cells into its stationary storage systems. A battery built for the grid The partnership focuses on grid storage rather than electric vehicles. Stationary batteries have different requirements from vehicle batteries, making cost, reliability, and safety more important than packing maximum energy into a small, lightweight package. Lithium-iron phosphate, or LFP, batteries currently dominate stationary storage. Peak Energy is pursuing sodium-ion as an alternative that uses more abundant, potentially lower-cost materials. More from Energy See All GM’s vice president of battery and sustainability, Kurt Kelty, said the chemistry suits the application. “At GM, we know that the application should determine the battery, and for grid-scale stationary storage, sodium-ion is the right solution,” Kelty said. “Peak is already demonstrating the value of sodium-ion through their innovative energy storage platform, and together we’re working to push those benefits even further with our next-generation cell – helping deliver more reliable, lower-cost energy storage at scale for the US grid,” he added. Removing active cooling equipment Peak Energy’s approach extends beyond battery chemistry to the equipment surrounding the cells. Conventional LFP storage systems use active cooling to manage operating temperatures. That equipment adds components, consumes electricity, and increases system complexity. The company says its sodium-ion platform operates with passive cooling, eliminating the need for those systems. According to the company, the platform can lower energy storage costs by 20 percent compared with conventional systems while delivering more than 99 percent uptime. These figures are company-reported and have not been independently verified. Peak Energy also estimates that replacing conventional LFP storage with its technology could reduce annual battery-storage energy waste across the US by up to two terawatt-hours. That projection concerns potential savings from broader deployment, rather than energy already saved by installed systems. Manufacturing for rising electricity demand The new funding will support Peak’s manufacturing expansion as utilities add storage alongside renewable generation and electricity demand grows. Data centers represent another target, particularly as AI infrastructure increases power demand. Peak Energy plans to bring its passively cooled storage platform to that market while working through its existing customer orders.

Increasing vehicle assembly alone will not be enough to support long-term domestic EV production; battery technology, raw material availability, energy storage and advanced manufacturing capabilities must also be strengthened. Industry leaders focused on these priorities at the Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo and The Battery Show India (TBSI) 2026. Discussions on October 23 highlighted opportunities to combine India’s manufacturing strengths with international technology expertise and mineral resources. This development has direct relevance to the automotive sector, as battery supply chain strength can influence EV production, technology development, and long-term manufacturing competitiveness. Also Read: Ursaa Energyworx Launches Ursaa Hybrid for EV Fleet Tracking & Battery Intelligence Why Is India EV Battery Manufacturing Important for India’s EV Industry? With the growth of electric vehicles, the importance of battery technology and its raw materials is also increasing. EV manufacturers need reliable material supplies, advanced battery technologies, and efficient manufacturing infrastructure to develop competitive products. India is working towards expanding its domestic manufacturing capabilities. However, access to raw materials, technology development, and investment in manufacturing infrastructure will remain significant challenges in this process. Discussions at the REI Expo and TBSI indicated that international partnerships could play a role in strengthening India’s clean energy and EV supply chains. This has potential benefits for the automotive ecosystem, although no new investments or agreements with individual EV manufacturers were announced at the event. Australia’s Lithium and Cobalt Resources Relevant to India Australia highlighted battery manufacturing and electric mobility as important areas of cooperation with India. According to Australia’s High Commissioner to India, Philip Green, the two countries can combine Australia’s engineering expertise and mineral resources with India’s manufacturing strength and global supply chain integration. Green said that Australia produces more than 50 percent of global lithium production, while the country has the world’s second-largest cobalt reserves. He also highlighted Australia’s strong global position in rare earth resources. Lithium, cobalt, and rare earth materials are critical to battery technology and a broader clean energy ecosystem. Collaboration between these resources and Indian manufacturing capabilities could provide opportunities to develop battery-related supply chains. Twenty Australian companies and 32 exhibitors participated in the Expo. Their technologies covered areas such as energy storage, grid infrastructure, green hydrogen, and renewable energy integration. Its importance for the automotive industry lies in future battery supply chains and technology access. However, mineral availability does not automatically guarantee affordable EV batteries or lower vehicle prices. Actual impact will depend on partnerships, processing capabilities, investment, and commercial execution. Also Read: When Does Switching to an EV Make Financial Sense in India? Running Cost Explained India-Germany Collaboration Can Support Battery Research In addition to Australia, technology collaboration with Germany was also an important part of the discussions. Anandi Iyer, Director of the Fraunhofer Office in India, highlighted opportunities for India-Germany cooperation in battery research, power electronics, advanced engineering, and industrial automation. Iyer also shared figures for global renewable energy capacity additions and battery storage deployment. According to her, approximately 800 GW of renewable energy capacity additions will be achieved globally in 2025, while battery storage deployment will reach 108 GW, a 40 percent increase from the previous year. These figures reflect the growth of the broader clean energy sector. Areas such as battery research and power electronics are important in the context of the EV industry, as these technologies can be applied in both electric mobility and energy systems. Iyer also highlighted that technological self-reliance is not exclusive to international partnerships. Trusted partnerships and supply chains can help transform research into commercially viable solutions. The challenge for India will be to leverage global expertise while building domestic capabilities. For automotive manufacturers, such collaborations can support future technology development and supply chain resilience. The Connection Between the Battery Storage Market and Renewable Energy Yogesh Mudras, Managing Director of Informa Markets in India, highlighted the importance of expanding renewable energy generation and grid storage simultaneously. According to Mudras, India’s renewable energy market is projected to reach 486 GW by 2030, with an expected compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15 percent. He also shared a projection for India’s battery storage sector to exceed USD 8.5 billion by 2031, with a CAGR of 33 percent. These projections relate to broader renewable energy and storage markets, not exclusively to EV batteries. Nevertheless, the expanding storage ecosystem could create relevant opportunities for battery-related manufacturing and technology capabilities. artigo.texto: O Departamento de Estado dos Estados Unidos anunciou, nesta semana, um acordo entre as companhias Crusoe (EUA) e Araico (Paraguai) para a instalação de um data center de inteligência artificial no Paraguai, alimentado com energia de Itaipu. Conforme os detalhes tornados públicos, o contrato prevê que a Administração Nacional de Eletricidade (Ande), dona da metade paraguaia de Itaipu, forneça energia a US$ 48 o megawatt. O documento também estipula reajuste anual atrelado à inflação dos Estados Unidos, bem como cláusula de revisão tarifária especial a cada dois anos. Para garantir a confiabilidade do fornecimento, 24 horas por dia, a estrutura será erguida “adjacente à subestação de Itaipu”. Leia também: Trump quer energia de Itaipu para empresas de IA no Paraguai Tal descrição pode significar, por exemplo, a cidade fronteiriça de Hernandarias, vizinha a Ciudad del Este. Hernandarias reúne requisitos como proximidade da fonte geradora e grande disponibilidade de água, insumo essencial para o resfriamento das máquinas. Além disso, Hernandarias já abriga locais como o Parque Tecnológico Itaipu, o que a torna forte candidata. A Crusoe entrará com a capacidade computacional e operacional, enquanto a Araico fornecerá a infraestrutura para a operação. Na primeira etapa, prevista para 2027, o centro de processamento de inteligência artificial poderá alcançar 106 megawatts de capacidade de tecnologia da informação. Quando concluído, prevê chegar a 280 megawatts. Itaipu tem capacidade instalada para produção de 14 mil megawatts de energia. O Paraguai possui metade desse total, com cada uma de suas turbinas podendo produzir 700 megawatts. Atualmente, o país vizinho não utiliza toda energia a qual tem direito na hidrelétrica binacional. De acordo com o estabelecido pelo Tratado de Itaipu, o Brasil adquire o excedente. Em visita ao Paraguai, Christopher Landau, vice-secretário de Estado dos Estados Unidos, comemorou o acordo: Exploração de urânio no Paraguai Ademais da parceria que envolve o uso de energia de Itaipu para inteligência artificial, a Uranium Energy Corp (UEC), dos Estados Unidos, pretende explorar urânio no Paraguai. Para tanto, anunciou investimento de US$ 12 milhões para mineração na pequena cidade de Yuty, departamento (estado) de Caazapá. O local, situado a cerca de 290 quilômetros da fronteira com o Brasil, possui reservas comprovadas de urânio.

artigo.texto: 23/10/2026 - 15:23 Os investimentos globais em data centers devem atingir US$ 1 trilhão em 2026, estima a BofA Global Research. Para 2028, a projeção é de US$ 2,1 trilhões, mais que o dobro do valor previsto para este ano. A estimativa foi divulgada nesta sexta-feira, 23 de outubro, e aponta a inteligência artificial (IA) como principal motor da expansão. A demanda por serviços de IA impulsiona a construção de infraestrutura, beneficiando fabricantes de chips e desenvolvedores de servidores, particularmente nos Estados Unidos. Inteligência artificial sustenta expansão dos data centers O levantamento do BofA projeta crescimento do mercado até 2030. A expansão acompanha o desenvolvimento de serviços de inteligência artificial e a necessidade de ampliar a capacidade de processamento. Os fornecedores de semicondutores e servidores estão entre os maiores beneficiários desse movimento. Esses equipamentos concentram parte relevante dos recursos destinados aos empreendimentos. Construção custa US$ 49 milhões por megawatt O custo médio de construção de um data center é estimado em US$ 49 milhões por megawatt, de acordo com o banco. As despesas relacionadas à tecnologia da informação representam a maior parcela do investimento total. Os servidores são o componente mais caro. A infraestrutura de rede aparece como o segundo maior item de investimento. O orçamento inclui sistemas de distribuição de energia e geradores. Equipamentos de alimentação de reserva e refrigeração completam a estrutura necessária à operação. Data centers focados em IA têm custo maior As instalações voltadas à inteligência artificial, chamadas de neoclouds no levantamento, apresentam custo por megawatt superior à média estimada para o setor. Esses projetos, porém, exigem menos espaço que os equivalentes tradicionais. A diferença combina maior concentração de investimento em equipamentos com menor necessidade de área física. artigo.texto: BYD Lifts on Sector Tailwind as Battery Roadmap, Seagull Launch and Brazil Permits Set Up October 30 Test Published on 10/25/2026 at 09:10 | Editorial boerse-global.de BYD shares climbed 4.4% in Hong Kong on Friday, riding a broad rebound across auto and lithium-battery names rather than any company-specific catalyst. The advance followed losses in the prior session and reflected a friendlier market backdrop for the whole sector — a distinction that matters when weighing what actually drove the stock. Europe Sales Offer an Operating Anchor Reuters reported Thursday that BYD's European sales rose in September, with Chinese automakers collectively gaining market share on the continent. That gives investors an operating reference point beyond the short-term sector bounce. Still, a sales increase on its own says nothing about the profitability of the European business. Trade policy belongs in the same frame. Reuters also reported a provisional agreement between the EU and China to limit Chinese hybrid and plug-in hybrid exports. For shareholders, volume growth and potential export restrictions now sit side by side. The deal is preliminary and should not be read as a final settlement. Technology Priorities Confirmed, Not Delivered On an investor platform today, BYD said it is prioritizing megawatt fast charging, a next-generation Blade Battery and integrated body-battery technology. The distinction is critical: the company is confirming its technological direction, not reporting a completed development milestone or a concrete launch date. Should investors sell immediately? Or is it worth buying BYD? No performance figures for the announced programs were disclosed. BYD said it will formally update the market once applicable disclosure obligations kick in, so no near-term product launch can be inferred from the statement. The message underscores how central battery and charging technology are to the development plan, yet it offers no basis for quantifying added revenue or earnings. Separating technological potential from commercially proven success remains the key task for valuation. Seagull Refresh Puts Charging Tech on the Road Already-launched products are a separate matter. On Tuesday, BYD began selling the second-generation Seagull in China at an entry price of CNY 65,900, with Flash Charging versions starting at CNY 75,900. That puts fast-charging hardware into more affordable segments rather than reserving it for premium classes. The caveat is infrastructure: advertised charging power depends on compatible stations, so the vehicle's technical capability alone does not guarantee the same charging speed at every plug. For equipped variants, BYD quotes a 10% to 70% charge in 5 minutes — figures that describe the Seagull on sale, not the next-generation development steps discussed today. A European launch of the new Seagull has not been confirmed, so the Chinese sales start implies no European volume contribution; execution in the home market is the near-term focus. Brazil Doubles Down as Analysts Split on Margins Fitting the international growth story, Reuters reported Friday that BYD is seeking approvals to double the annual capacity of its Brazilian plant to 600,000 vehicles. Alexandre Baldy said investments have already exceeded 5.5 billion reais, and BYD is targeting a local component share above 50% by the start of 2027. Both figures are goals, not current production capacity or achieved localization. BYD at a turning point? This analysis reveals what investors need to know now. The expansion push meets a more cautious read on the business from parts of the analyst community, which cite weak domestic demand, higher input costs and policy uncertainty. Barclays, by contrast, keeps an "Overweight" rating and points to global expansion, while flagging softer domestic volumes after subsidy cuts and amid tougher competition. The divergence makes clear that growth opportunities alone do not answer the question of future profitability — the economic proof behind the development strategy remains the central yardstick. The next scheduled disclosure is October 30, when BYD is due to report third-quarter 2026 results. That date offers the first real opportunity to weigh the model offensive and international expansion in financial terms. Until then, Friday's gain looks chiefly like a recovery within the sector. artigo.texto: Asia-Pacific is becoming a bigger force in the global carbon market, but not in the way many might expect. The region’s share of global carbon credit issuance and retirements has fallen since 2021. At the same time, its companies are becoming a major source of new buyers, while governments are shaping how credits are produced, traded and used. These are key findings from AlliedOffsets’ APAC Carbon Market Report 2026, published in October. The report examines carbon credit supply, buyer demand, pricing, Article 6 cooperation and aviation’s carbon offsetting system across the region. The data reveal a market in transition. New demand is emerging, but supply is uneven. Some countries are opening new routes for international carbon trading, while others are building pipelines of credits that could qualify for use under foreign carbon market rules. APAC’s Share of Global Carbon Credit Supply Shrinks Asia-Pacific’s share of global carbon credit issuance fell from about 50% in 2021 to around 30% in 2025, according to AlliedOffsets. Its share of global credit retirements also declined, from 42% to 33% over the same period. Retirement happens when a carbon credit is permanently removed from circulation. This often occurs after a company uses it to support a climate claim or meet a requirement. Issuance, by contrast, refers to credits created after a project completes the required process under a carbon crediting program. The decline in APAC’s global share is notable because issuance and retirements grew in regions outside APAC over the same period. This suggests that the region’s carbon market has not kept pace with growth elsewhere. However, the report identifies one area of stronger activity: offtake agreements. These contracts allow buyers to purchase credits that a project expects to deliver in the future. APAC accounted for about one-fifth of global offtake volume in 2025 and more than one-third of global volume recorded through October 19, 2026. The report cautions that it is too early to know whether this increase marks a lasting trend. Still, offtake activity could help project developers secure revenue and financing before their credits are delivered. APAC Companies Become a Major Source of New Buyers While the region’s share of credit supply has weakened, demand from APAC-based companies is growing. In 2025, companies headquartered in APAC overtook European companies as the largest source of new carbon credit buyers. APAC-based businesses accounted for about one-third of new buyers in 2025, up from around one-fifth in 2020. The momentum continued in 2026. AlliedOffsets counted 954 new APAC buyers through October 19, already approaching the record 1,056 recorded for all of 2025. This shift matters because more buyers can create new demand for projects that deliver credible emissions reductions or remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. Buyer numbers alone don’t reveal how much credit each company will buy. They also don’t show if the announced interest will result in completed deals. The report also finds that APAC nature-based removal supply remains concentrated among a relatively small group of developers. Projects in the region issued about 13.2 million nature-based removal credits in 2025. Nepal’s Ministry of Forests and Environment accounted for 20% of this total, while Terra Carbon supplied 14%. Permian Global contributed another 12%, and Woodside Burrup accounted for 7%. Smaller developers made up the remaining 38%. This concentration highlights the role of a few major project developers in regional carbon removal supply. Carbon Credit Prices Vary by Project Type The report’s pricing data show that APAC credits do not always trade at a discount to those from other regions. Prices depend heavily on the type of project. AlliedOffsets estimated that in 2025, APAC biochar credits cost an average of $135 per tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent. This is about 10% lower than similar offers from other regions. Enhanced rock weathering credits averaged $168 per tonne, around 13% lower than offers elsewhere. Biochar is produced by heating organic material, such as agricultural waste, with little or no oxygen. Enhanced rock weathering uses crushed minerals to speed up natural processes that remove carbon dioxide from the atmosphere. The pattern was different for some other project categories. APAC energy-efficiency and waste-disposal credits had estimated offer prices more than twice those of comparable credits from other regions. These figures are estimated offer prices, not confirmed transaction prices. They also apply to specific project types and credit vintages, so they should not be treated as a single market-wide price for APAC credits. The differences show why buyers need to assess credit type, quality, and project details rather than relying only on regional averages. Article 6 Could Open New Routes for Regional Carbon Trading International cooperation under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement is another major development in APAC. It helps countries work together to cut emissions. This includes transferring internationally transferred mitigation outcomes, or ITMOs, based on the rules. AlliedOffsets estimates that APAC countries could supply 38.7 million ITMOs in 2030 under their updated nationally determined contributions. This is potential supply, not a forecast of credits that will definitely be approved or transferred. Papua New Guinea accounts for a potential 12.9 million tonnes, followed by Cambodia at 10.5 million and Jordan at 7.9 million. The Philippines might provide 6 million tonnes. Bangladesh contributes 1.4 million, and the Marshall Islands adds about 23,300 tonnes. The report also tracks projects listed under Singapore’s eligible carbon credit arrangements. These published lists could provide 27.2 million credits from APAC projects with 2021–2030 vintages. Mongolian grassland and agricultural land projects account for about 19 million, or almost 70% of the total. Philip

artigo.texto: The European Union is moving toward a major change in how it gives free carbon permits to industry. The European Parliament’s environment committee has backed a plan that could provide around 99 million additional free emissions allowances to certain industrial installations from 2026 to 2030. The proposal aims to help European businesses manage carbon costs and compete with companies in countries with weaker climate rules. But it also raises a key question: how can the EU protect its industries while keeping pressure on them to cut emissions? The committee’s position differs from the plan backed by EU member states, which would provide around 121 million allowances. Neither proposal should be treated as final law. The two sides must still agree on the rules. EU Committee Backs 99 Million Free Allowances The European Parliament’s Committee on the Environment, Climate and Food Safety (ENVI) backed changes to the EU Emissions Trading System (EU ETS). The vote was 64 in favor, 11 against, and two abstentions. The plan covers industrial installations whose free allowances are calculated using heat and fuel benchmarks. These benchmarks apply when a specific product benchmark is not available. Under the committee’s approach, around 88 million allowances available for free allocation would be used. It would add another 11 million allowances linked to existing conditions that some installations failed to meet. Together, these would bring the total to about 99 million allowances for the period through 2030. Each EU ETS allowance permits its holder to emit one metric tonne of carbon dioxide equivalent (CO₂e). Companies that receive more free allowances may need to buy fewer permits to cover their emissions, depending on their actual emissions and allocation. The proposal does not give every industrial company the same benefit. It concerns installations covered by the relevant heat and fuel benchmarks and remains subject to the final rules. Why the EU Wants to Ease Carbon Costs for Industry The EU ETS puts a price on greenhouse gas emissions from power generation, industry, aviation and other covered activities. Companies must surrender enough allowances to match their reported emissions. They can buy allowances at auction or trade them with other market participants. The system is designed to make pollution more costly and encourage businesses to reduce emissions. However, some industries receive free allowances to limit the risk of carbon leakage. This happens when companies move production to countries with weaker climate rules, potentially shifting emissions rather than reducing them. Free allocation is based on common benchmarks that reflect the emissions performance of the 10% most efficient installations in each sector. The EU has been tightening its carbon market rules as it pursues deeper emissions cuts. The new proposal responds to concerns that updated heat and fuel benchmarks could raise costs for some industrial businesses. These rules are especially relevant to sectors that use large amounts of heat or fuel and do not have a specific product benchmark. The European Commission’s original July proposal estimated that around 80 million allowances could be used for additional free allocation. Later estimates put the available amount at around 88 million. The committee’s position adds a further 11 million allowances to that pool. EU Member States Want an Even Larger Allocation The European Parliament committee and EU member states have taken different approaches to the available allowances. In September, the Council of the European Union backed a plan to combine around 88 million available allowances with a pool of roughly 33 million allowances linked to existing allocation conditions. That would bring the total to about 121 million allowances for industry over 2026–2030. Reuters estimated that the Council approach could save affected companies around €8.25 billion in carbon costs. The Parliament committee proposes a different split. It would direct about 11 million of the 33 million pool to industry, with one-third going to the Modernisation Fund and another third to the Innovation Fund. These funds support energy-system upgrades and low-carbon technologies. The disagreement is not only about the number of permits. It is also about how much support should go directly to industrial companies and how much should help finance the wider energy transition. The Commission has separately estimated that the roughly 88 million available allowances could avoid around €6 billion in costs for the affected sectors. That estimate relates to the available pool, not the full 121 million allowance option. The European Parliament’s legislative tracker still lists the file as awaiting Parliament’s position at first reading. The committee vote therefore marks progress, but it does not make the proposed allocation rules law. EU Emissions Are Falling as Climate Rules Tighten The debate comes as the EU ETS continues to drive emissions reductions. The European Commission reported that verified emissions covered by the system fell by 1.3% in 2025 compared with 2024. Since the system began in 2005, emissions in covered sectors have fallen by about half. The EU ETS remains on track to meet its target of cutting covered emissions by 62% by 2030 compared with 2005 levels. Separately, the EU aims to reduce its net greenhouse gas emissions by at least 55% by 2030 compared with 1990 and reach climate neutrality by 2050. These targets create a challenge for policymakers. European industries face pressure to lower emissions while managing energy and production costs. Free permits can offer short-term relief, but too much free allocation may weaken the financial incentive to invest in cleaner processes. The EU has also been changing its wider carbon market rules.
