artigo.texto: Greenvolt Group, through Greenvolt Power, has agreed to sell two standalone battery energy storage system (BESS) projects in Poland to A&R Investments. The projects are located in Ełk and Turośń Kościelna in north-eastern Poland, and have a total installed capacity of 400 MW/1,600 MWh. Both projects were completed in the third quarter of 2026 and have received the required permits for use. The transaction is expected to close by the end of 2026, subject to the fulfillment of the applicable conditions. Furthermore, both Ełk and Turośń have secured 17-year capacity market contracts starting in 2028. Under these contracts, each project will receive a fixed payment for making 85 per cent of its capacity available to the system. The projects are also covered by 10-year tolling agreements, under which the batteries will be optimised and their flexibility traded in the power markets. Earlier, in October 2026, Greenvolt Power raised € 284 million in project financing for its 253.1 MW wind project in Gurbănești, located east of Bucharest, Romania. The project is currently under construction and is expected to begin commercial operations by the end of 2027.

artigo.texto: Aluminum-air batteries generate electricity by reacting aluminum plates with oxygen from the air in a water-based electrolyte. Aluminum has a very high theoretical energy density, and instead of being recharged from a socket, spent plates are swapped for fresh ones while the aluminum hydroxide produced is recycled into new aluminum. The technology is still in early commercial use, mainly as backup power for telecom towers and data centres and as a range extender for electric vehicles. The global aluminum-air EV battery market was valued at about USD 96 million in 2025 and is projected to grow at nearly 14% a year to 2034. India's aluminum industry, EV ambitions, and pilots by Indian Oil, Phinergy, and Hindalco make Aluminum Air EV Battery Manufacturing Plant Setup in India an emerging opportunity for investors willing to take on technology risk. Investment depends mainly on scale, technology access, in-house cathode and plate production, and testing capability. The Aluminum Air EV Battery Manufacturing Plant Cost ranges from about INR 15–30 crore for a pilot line of 500 to 1,000 systems a year to INR 80–150 crore for a commercial plant of about 5,000 systems a year with cathode, plate, and stack lines, and INR 400–700 crore for a large integrated facility of 25,000 systems a year or more with plate production and recycling partnerships. Raw materials make up 50 to 60% of operating cost and utilities 15 to 25%. IMARC's analysis points to a gross margin of 35 to 50% and a net margin of 15 to 30%, but these depend on reaching commercial volumes, which few producers have yet achieved. This guide is written for investors exploring how to start an Aluminum Air EV Battery manufacturing plant in India. It focuses on a commercial plant of about 5,000 systems a year producing aluminum-air power modules for telecom and data centre backup and EV range extenders, together with a recurring business in replacement aluminum plates and recycling, and also explains pilot lines and large integrated facilities. It covers technology and markets, process flow, machinery, location, costs, approvals, and how a DPR and financial model turn this into a bankable plan. The snapshot shows a small but fast-growing market at an early stage of commercial use. Most current deployments are stationary backup systems replacing diesel generators, while EV applications remain in trials. The wide investment range reflects a real choice between a pilot line, a commercial plant, and a large integrated facility, with technology access and customer pilots mattering as much as capital. The sections below work through that choice. Indicative Project Cost in India (2026) These ranges should be read with caution. Actual returns depend on access to proven technology, the cost of aluminum fuel per kilowatt-hour, cathode life, recycling logistics, customer adoption beyond pilots, competition from lithium-ion and sodium-ion batteries, and the pace of regulatory approvals for vehicle use. A site-specific Aluminum Air EV Battery Feasibility Report tests each of these assumptions against your chosen technology route, applications, capacity, location, and customers. Table of Contents An aluminum-air cell has three main parts: an anode made of a specially alloyed aluminum plate, an air cathode that lets oxygen from the air in while keeping liquid electrolyte from leaking out, and an alkaline or saline electrolyte between them. As the cell works, the aluminum is gradually converted to aluminum hydroxide, releasing electrons that power the load. Small amounts of alloying elements such as tin, indium, or gallium reduce unwanted corrosion that would otherwise waste aluminum and release hydrogen. Cells are stacked into modules with pumps to circulate electrolyte, scrubbers to remove carbon dioxide from incoming air, heat management, and power electronics to deliver steady output. Because the aluminum is consumed, these systems behave more like a fuel-based generator than a rechargeable battery. Customers buy or lease the system and then pay for replacement aluminum plates, while spent electrolyte and aluminum hydroxide are collected for recycling into new aluminum. An Aluminum Air EV Battery Manufacturing Plant therefore earns revenue from both system sales and a recurring fuel and recycling service. Buyers value long run time, low weight, zero on-site emissions, fast refuelling, reliable operation, and a total cost competitive with diesel generators or lithium-ion batteries. The Main Applications and Product Types Choosing the application is the most important commercial decision, because it determines system design, certifications, partners, and the speed of adoption: These choices shape the whole plant. Stationary backup systems are the most commercially advanced, with simpler safety approvals and customers who value replacing diesel, while vehicle range extenders need compact designs, crash and safety testing, and vehicle homologation. Most new entrants therefore start with telecom and data centre backup modules and a plate supply service, and move into EV range extenders as vehicle trials, approvals, and refuelling networks mature. Key Growth Drivers in India and Export Markets Interest is supported by decarbonisation goals, the search for alternatives to diesel and imported lithium, and India's aluminum base: India-Specific Market Opportunity The strongest near-term opportunity lies in replacing diesel generators at telecom towers and data centres, where pilots are already under way, and in building the aluminum plate supply and recycling chain with smelters. EV range extenders are a longer-term opportunity that depends on vehicle trials and refuelling infrastructure. Producers that secure proven technology, strong aluminum partners, and early anchor customers will be best placed to grow. artigo.texto: Uma das grandes vantagens de notebooks com chips Arm é a autonomia prolongada de bateria. Essa é uma característica muito bem explorada pela Qualcomm na linha Snapdragon X, que no início de 2025 ganhou uma linha voltada para dispositivos mais acessíveis. Essa aposta tem ganhado mais adeptos. A Lenovo, parceira direta da Qualcomm, trouxe para o mercado o IdeaPad Slim 3x no início de 2026 com isso em mente: tornar possível uma máquina acessível em preço, mas com bateria prolongada. E o foco dessa máquina é justamente atender quem quer um aparelho para trabalhar ou estudar. É aí que está o limite desse notebook. Para quem busca uma máquina para fazer trabalhos simples, levar para a faculdade e não ficar dependente do carregador, o Slim 3x é ótimo; para quem busca ir além em desempenho, por outro lado, ela pode deixar a desejar. Design e teclado O IdeaPad Slim 3x é o clássico notebook feito para trabalhar e estudar, ou seja, para quem precisa de uma certa discrição e portabilidade. Ele não exagera no design, possui cantos e detalhes suaves e aposta mais na praticidade. Por exemplo, o seu corpo inteiro possui esse tom cinza escuro com apenas o logo da Lenovo na tampa superior. Ele aposta em um corpo quase todo em peça única, formato que já é bem popular na indústria — e visto mais em modelos de ponta. Aqui, nós vemos o plástico predominando, já que o alumínio fica somente na tampa. Mas esse ainda é um notebook muito bem construído e que não deixa a desejar para essa faixa. Vale notar que esse é o tipo de decisão que ajuda a reduzir o preço final do produto. O Slim 3x é robusto e não dá sinais de ser “barato”, apesar de ser econômico. Não notei áreas flexíveis e até a tampa superior tem certa dureza, o que é importante. Ainda sobre a tampa, ela pode ser inclinada em até 180°, mas não permite ao usuário abrir o notebook só com uma mão sem levantar a parte inferior também. Esse modelo é portátil, são cerca de 1,6 kg e 16,9 mm de espessura. Para o tamanho, esses são números confortáveis. O aparelho cabe tranquilamente na mochila e dificilmente será de grande incômodo ao levá-lo por aí — a minha experiência foi bem tranquila e eu costumo usar mochilas mais compactas. A Lenovo ainda destaca o certificado MIL-STD 810H de resistência como uma das vantagens. E como sendo um notebook voltado para o trabalho, existem algumas escolhas um tanto peculiares que máquinas do tipo carregam: - O botão de energia, por exemplo, fica na lateral do IdeaPad Slim 3x; - Já o leitor de digitais fica no cantinho do palm rest, logo abaixo do teclado numérico; - O touchpad, mais simples também, não é muito grande — ele cumpre o seu papel. Mas está bem alinhado à esquerda, já esbarrei nele algumas vezes sem querer enquanto digitava; - E por falar em digitação, o teclado não possui luz de fundo. Esse é um ponto negativo do aparelho. A digitação no Slim 3x fornece aquela experiência típica de notebooks mais econômicos, ou seja, ele equilibra as coisas para que tudo funcione bem, mas sem alavancar as expectativas. As teclas têm altura confortável e o clique é silencioso, mas não exatamente muito macio. Esse é um teclado no padrão ABNT2, então você possui atalhos mais práticos para o nosso idioma e o “Ç”. Além disso, existem as teclas numéricas no canto direito. Mas eu sinto que as teclas “F” são muito fininhas — não é algo impossível de acostumar, mas definitivamente não achei tão confortável para apertá-las sem precisar olhar. Sobre as entradas, nós temos o adaptador de energia, duas USB-A (5 Gbps), uma USB-C (5 Gbps) com Thunderbolt 3.0 e DisplayPort 1.4, um conector HDMI 1.4 (até 4K com 30 Hz), fone de ouvido/microfone, leitor de cartões SD. É uma quantidade bem confortável — senti falta apenas da porta RJ-45. Tela e multimídia Sabendo que este é um modelo mais “direto ao ponto” e sem tantas características avançadas, o IdeaPad Slim 3x que testei também possui uma tela mais comum. O painel IPS tem 15,3 polegadas de tamanho e resolução um pouco acima do Full HD (1920 x 1200 pixels). O pico de brilho é de apenas 300 nits, mas o acabamento antirreflexo ajuda a usá-lo em ambientes externos ou próximo a janelas sem ser incomodado. Além disso, outras características indicam que esse se trata de um notebook mais voltado para o trabalho, estudos e navegação simples. A taxa de atualização é fixa em 60 Hz, enquanto a proporção é de 16:10. Esse é um padrão que ajuda na multitarefa, principalmente ao usar dois apps ao mesmo tempo sem deixá-los “espremidos”. Já a cobertura de cores é de apenas 45% do padrão NTSC. Não espere por cores vibrantes, nem profundidade impressionante — é o suficiente para assistir e fazer coisas básicas, mas não fornece uma experiência que surpreende. Por outro lado, eu gostei das saídas de som (estéreo, cada uma com 2W de potência) do IdeaPad Slim 3x. Elas não possuem graves definidos e o som não é exatamente muito envolvente, mas o volume é suficiente para ter uma experiência confortável sem apelar para os fones de ouvido no dia a dia. Mas a webcam desse modelo é uma das mais básicas que eu já testei até hoje. Ela tem resolução de somente 720p e certamente não entrega boa qualidade, nem mesmo se apoiando em funções de IA do Windows que prometem melhorar a qualidade. Ao menos há a trava física para trazer um pouco mais de segurança ao usuário. Desempenho e bateria: onde o Snapdragon brilha O IdeaPad Slim 3x é um notebook ajustado para duas coisas específicas: desempenho constante para trabalho e autonomia de bateria. Nisso, o chipset da Qualcomm é o componente que traz um pouco mais de brilho ao projeto. - A máquina que eu testei possui o Snapdragon X (X1-26-100) com clock de 2,97 GHz; - Esse é um processador Arm de entrada, feito justamente para máquinas mais acessíveis; - A CPU deste modelo tem 8 núcleos com cache de 30 MB. Já a GPU integrada (Adreno X1-45) possui 1,25 GHz. Na NPU, são até 45 TOPS; - A ficha técnica ainda inclui 16 GB de RAM LPDDR5 (8.448 MT/s) e 512 GB de armazenamento em SSD (M.2 2242 PCI

artigo.texto: Texas' rapidly growing data center industry could reverse much of the state's progress on air quality by the end of the decade, according to a new report released Tuesday. The air emissions report published by the Houston Advanced Research Center revealed that the industry's impact on air quality depends heavily on how data centers are powered. The outlook is far worse if the facilities rely on natural gas plants. "What we are showcasing here is that there is a significant increase in different pollutant emissions that needs to be addressed because otherwise this could have strong implications for the population and environment," said Carlos Gamarra, vice president for energy, air and IT for HARC, whose team produced the air quality impact scenarios. Between 2002 and 2024, Texas sharply cut its major air pollutants -- particularly from transportation, industry and the power generation sectors -- even as the state's population grew by millions and its economy roughly doubled, according to the report, which used federal and state agencies' data on air emissions. At least 288 data center projects are planned across the state, according to a recent Texas Tribune analysis. The scale of the projected data center build-out means that the sector's future emissions trajectory now depends heavily on how electricity is supplied. According to the report's modeling, emissions could plausibly range from a marginal increase to a reversal of two decades of progress in reducing air emissions. By 2031, the report projects that statewide nitrogen oxide emissions could rise 35% -- even under a cleaner "net zero" scenario where data centers connect to the grid and deploy wind and solar on site. Under a different scenario where data centers choose traditional on-site natural-gas power sources, those emissions could increase nearly 400%. Such emissions can damage the human respiratory system with long-term exposure, causing chronic lung disease. "We need to treat data centers as the industrial facilities they are ... to hold them accountable to the same industrial and power generation emissions standards that produced Texas progress," Gamarra said. The report's researchers argue that it's not too late to stop this outcome. Instead of relying on the cheapest, fastest power options, Gamarra said, Texas lawmakers and industry leaders have the opportunity to shape the state's air quality by choosing cleaner choices like renewable and wind and implementing regulation that could help reduce the impact. HOW DO DATA CENTERS IMPACT AIR QUALITY? Data centers need electricity to keep their servers running. Those servers also need cooling systems to avoid overheating, and some of the most water-efficient technologies use the most electricity to operate. As AI computing chips get more powerful and run at hotter temperatures, the need for cooling increases -- and that means more energy. Data centers can get that electricity in a number of ways. Historically, the most common method has been connecting to the Texas power grid. But there's a wait to get connected. The Electric Reliability Council of Texas, the grid operator, in the last two years received over 500 requests to connect large electricity users, many of which are data centers, compared to two dozen such requests the year before that, according to state records from this summer. Proposed data centers in Texas range from five to 11,000 megawatts in planned capacity, which reflects the maximum power an individual facility could use in any given moment. The estimated electricity that large projects could need from the grid added up to 439 gigawatts -- which would equal roughly a third of all the power generation in America. Gov. Greg Abbott has temporarily halted new data centers from connecting to the state's power grid pending an audit examining each facility's power demand, water and cooling use, public financial assistance and community impacts. Data center developers and operators that can't wait for a grid connection look for alternatives. "The challenge right now is for these data centers when they try to connect to the grid, they have long timelines, like three to five years, and they cannot wait," Gamarra said. "So they start deploying their own on-site energy systems, and they don't always pick the cleanest version of on-site generation because of timelines." He also notes that cleaner, more renewable technologies cannot always provide continuous energy to the data centers. Operators that choose cleaner technologies pay a higher price. GOING BACK ON TEXAS AIR QUALITY PROGRESS Researchers modeled how four power supply scenarios could affect air pollutant levels over the next five years, based on projections of data center energy demand. The report studied a number of scenarios, comparing pollution from data centers connected to the grid versus combinations of on-site generation, including natural gas, solar and wind. Gamarra attributed Texas's declining emissions over the past two decades to changes in the electricity mix, especially the growth of wind and solar, pollution controls across power generation for industry and transportation, and the retirement of coal-fired generation. That progress could be reversed if natural gas plants are the primary power sources for data centers. Levels of nitrogen oxides would increase 136% by 2031 and approach the level they were at in 2004. Volatile organic compounds would exceed their 2002 level by 32%. Levels of particulate matter, microscopic particles that can penetrate deep into the lungs and enter the bloodstream, would increase to levels not seen since 2006. Some scientists call particulate matter the deadliest form of air pollution because it can trigger health problems such as asthma attacks, irregular heartbeat and respiratory diseases. The report also found that the power sources of data centers can drive enormous swings in air pollution. On-site natural gas engines emit about four times as much nitrogen oxide

artigo.texto: O senador e candidato à Presidência da República Flávio Bolsonaro (PL-RJ) prometeu ampliar o saneamento básico no Pará, melhorar as condições de tráfego na Transamazônica e atrair investimentos em data centers para o Amazonas. As propostas foram apresentadas nesta sexta-feira (23), durante o debate presidencial da TV Globo, em confronto com o presidente Lula (PT). ✅ Siga o canal do Claudio Dantas no WhatsApp Ao falar sobre a falta de água tratada e de coleta e tratamento de esgoto, Flávio afirmou que pretende trabalhar em parceria com o governador eleito do Pará, Daniel, para ampliar a infraestrutura de Belém. “Eu me comprometo a ajudar Belém a fazer o maior programa de saneamento básico da cidade”, declarou. O senador relatou ter visto esgoto a céu aberto na capital paraense e criticou as condições enfrentadas por moradores que convivem com mau cheiro e falta de infraestrutura. Ele também prometeu atuar para melhorar o acesso a serviços básicos na Região Norte. Candidato critica situação da Transamazônica Flávio afirmou que pretende garantir o asfaltamento de trechos da Transamazônica e responsabilizou entraves ambientais do governo federal pelas dificuldades para executar as obras. Segundo o candidato, a falta de pavimentação prejudica o deslocamento de moradores e o transporte de cargas, sobretudo durante o período de chuvas, quando caminhões ficam atolados e comunidades podem enfrentar dificuldades de conexão com outras regiões. “Eu vou garantir o que você mais pediu, o direito de trabalhar”, afirmou, ao direcionar o discurso aos eleitores do Pará. A proposta integra o discurso do candidato em defesa da ampliação da infraestrutura e da redução de obstáculos ambientais e burocráticos a projetos de desenvolvimento. Zona Franca e data centers Para o Amazonas, Flávio prometeu manter a Zona Franca de Manaus e ampliar sua capacidade de atrair investimentos. O senador citou a instalação de data centers como uma oportunidade econômica e defendeu aproveitar recursos de gás natural para produzir fertilizantes no Brasil. A proposta busca associar a estrutura industrial da região a novos investimentos em tecnologia e energia. Flávio também afirmou que pretende reduzir a dependência brasileira de fertilizantes importados, utilizando matéria-prima disponível no país. O candidato ainda declarou que pretende garantir autonomia aos povos indígenas para decidir sobre atividades em suas terras, tema que provocou reação de Lula durante o debate. Saneamento tem meta legal para 2033 Ao criticar a situação do saneamento, Flávio afirmou que, por causa do atual governo, a meta de universalização teria sido empurrada para depois de 2050. A declaração, porém, exige uma distinção: o Marco Legal do Saneamento, instituído pela Lei nº 14.026/2020, estabelece como metas o atendimento de 99% da população com água potável e de 90% com coleta e tratamento de esgoto até o fim de 2033. . A existência de metas legais não significa que elas serão necessariamente cumpridas. Em julho de 2026, apesar do aumento dos investimentos desde a aprovação do marco legal, o ritmo de aplicação dos recursos ainda estava abaixo do necessário para universalizar os serviços até 2033. . Lula rebate propostas e defende preservação ambiental Na resposta, Lula acusou o grupo político de Flávio de defender medidas que, segundo ele, enfraqueceriam a proteção ambiental. O presidente citou a gestão do ex-ministro do Meio Ambiente Ricardo Salles e afirmou que a Amazônia pode gerar mais recursos com a floresta preservada do que com sua derrubada. Lula também defendeu a economia verde e o Fundo Amazônia, cuja retomada atribuiu ao atual governo. “Ele não conhece a Amazônia”, afirmou o presidente, ao contestar as propostas do adversário.

artigo.texto: Resumo - Google firma parceria com a Voltus para gerenciar sobras de energia dos data centers - Residências e empresas serão recompensadas por reduzir consumo da rede elétrica - Capacidade liberada chega a 1.070 megawatts, o equivalente a um reator nuclear - O sistema recebe o nome de VPP, abreviação em inglês para usina elétrica virtual - Participantes recebem economia na conta e pagamentos diretos quando acionados - Valores a serem pagos ainda não foram divulgados Quem diminuir o uso de eletricidade poderá receber pagamento e, de quebra, contribuir para alimentar os data centers do Google: é o que prevê um acordo fechado com a Voltus, companhia do setor de recursos energéticos distribuídos. O combinado prevê que, quando for preciso, a Voltus coloque à disposição do Google até 1.070 megawatts de capacidade elétrica. Esse montante equivale ao gerado por um reator nuclear, conforme noticiou o The New York Times. A lógica por trás do acordo tem nome: usina elétrica virtual, conhecida pela sigla em inglês VPP. Trata-se de um sistema que, no lugar de recorrer a uma única central geradora, articula recursos distribuídos por diversos locais. Residências e empresas entram na conta reduzindo o que consomem da rede ou aproveitando a energia que elas mesmas produzem. Como o consumidor ganha com a conta Acionados esses participantes, surgem os incentivos financeiros. Segundo a Voltus, os ganhos se dividem em duas frentes: redução nas faturas de luz e pagamentos feitos diretamente aos clientes. Dessa forma, quem colabora transforma em retorno econômico a necessidade do Google por capacidade elétrica. Entre as recomendações da empresa está adotar termostatos inteligentes, que permitem definir, por exemplo, a duração em que um aparelho de ar-condicionado permanece funcionando. Nesses casos, a redução no consumo é feita automaticamente, dispensando qualquer ação do usuário. Quanto será pago a quem participar, no entanto, segue sem divulgação.

artigo.texto: Paris Marx’s new book couldn’t have landed at a better time. The longtime critic of Big Tech and host of the Tech Won’t Save Us podcast has been thinking about data centers for years, and Hyperscale: The Ambition and Excess of Big Tech's Data Empires comes out right as opposition hits a fever pitch. “I certainly didn't predict that it was all going to kind of come to a head as my book was coming out,” he says with a laugh. While data centers are playing a role in shaping US elections—they’re one of the issues that could decide key midterm races in less than two weeks—there’s a history of struggle around the world. Marx’s book takes the reader on a tour of the tech industry’s quest for power and its opposition, from antiwar protests targeting American computers during the Vietnam War, to more recent resistance in Ireland and Chile, and an alternative vision for the future of data centers in New Zealand. I caught up with him this week to talk about what he’s seen, and what could happen if the AI bubble pops. This interview has been edited and condensed for clarity. MOLLY TAFT: When did you decide to write a book about data centers? PARIS MARX: In the Netherlands and Singapore, they had moratoriums going back to 2019. But in 2022, there was a growing recognition of the demands of data centers in Ireland, on the energy grid in particular. There were huge quantities of electricity that data centers were starting to consume over there. The other story that really got on my radar was what happened with Google in The Dalles, Oregon. Google was really trying to hide its water use figures, to the degree that it got the city council to try to keep its water use figures secret. They kept that going for the better part of a year before the community finally got the actual numbers and found out that Google was using 29 percent of the water in the community. ChatGPT came out at the end of 2022. It became apparent that there's going to need to be a lot more data centers for generative AI. These places were already feeling the effects of significant data center construction, and it felt like that was going to start coming to a lot more communities very soon. I feel like a lot of Americans think data centers just came out of the blue in the US over the past year or two, just in time to be this huge midterms issue. One thing I like about your book is that it shows us how other countries and communities served as early warning signs. Ireland was a real example of what can happen. Dublin had a moratorium passed back in 2021. It was actually the grid operator that said, “Hey, there are too many data centers. We do not have the grid capacity to connect any more of them.” In response to that, you had the industry moving to make sure it can still build data centers in Ireland. They can't get grid connections in Dublin, so they start looking at building in other parts of Ireland. They also looked at starting to tap into the gas network so they can use generators. Eventually, they start building dedicated gas power plants to power their data centers instead of connecting to the grid. The Irish energy grid is a public grid—only the public utility can build electricity lines. And data center companies actually lobbied for legislation that essentially allows private companies to build electricity cables. That obviously concerns a lot of people and presents questions about equity in the system. The gas stuff looks so prescient with what’s happening in the US now, where companies are racing to build these massive private gas power plants for data centers. [Data center operators] were getting these emission licenses from the Irish Environmental Protection Agency to be able to burn all these fossil fuels. The agency was warning that climate targets are going to be a lot harder to achieve now. When I started to see that happen in the US, I wasn’t surprised. I’d already seen the story play out before. But the scale of it is staggering, and how quickly it’s escalated. What happens to the physical infrastructure—from the gas plants to the data centers themselves—that's getting built out if this industry falls apart? Is there historic precedent for that? I think we're in an AI bubble. But what does the collapse of that bubble look like? They're planning to add all these data centers and all of these gas power plants in order to power the data centers. But there are issues with getting turbines, with getting chips, with getting different kinds of pieces of the puzzle for the data center itself. Are these even going to get built out before there’s a reassessment of the demand for AI? We often talk about the excess build-out of fiber capacity back in the dotcom boom and bust. But there was also a build-out of data centers—obviously a much earlier stage than what we're at now. A lot of data center companies went under. Companies like Equinix, which did survive, bought up a ton of data centers to be ready for when that capacity returned. But the issue we have now is that if data centers are being planned for AI use, and we’re operating under the assumption that the chips are going to have to be cycled out within a few years. Even if the data center is there, what makes it most valuable is potentially not going to be useful by the time that demand returns. Inevitably, even if the data centers don't come, then those gas plants will exist. They will be looking for new customers to justify their existence. I'm sure that people are not building them with the intention to just shut them down. artigo.texto: Technology competition among manufacturers is intensifying as makers of power banks, electric bicycles and electric scooters work to lower fire risks in products that consumers use every day. Manufacturers of battery-powered goods are rolling out products designed either to suppress heat buildup or to limit the damage from thermal runaway, industry officials said on the 25th, following a string of incidents in which power banks overheated or emitted smoke on aircraft and subways. Anker, a power bank maker, recently launched the MagGo Power Bank 2 Pro, which carries a smart cooling fan to address overheating. The device automatically detects charging and heat conditions and adjusts the fan's rotation speed to cut the heat generated during wireless charging. "Consumers have become sensitive to overheating recently, so we applied a cooling fan to improve it," an Anker official said. "It can reduce heat generation compared with conventional wireless charging, which tends to run hot." Personal mobility companies are also developing technology to strengthen battery safety. Alton applied lithium manganese iron phosphate (LMFP) batteries, which offer improved thermal stability, to its electric bicycles early this year. The company said LMFP batteries lower the risk of thermal runaway while improving range and charging life compared with conventional lithium iron phosphate (LFP) batteries. Electric bicycles using the battery have accounted for 19% of Alton's total bicycle sales since their release, and the company's overall second-quarter revenue rose 29.1% from a year earlier. Electric scooter maker Gcoo unveiled the Upgrade Gcoo, a new model designed to vent internal gas to the outside when thermal runaway occurs, reducing the risk of explosion. Rather than suppressing battery overheating, the product focuses on minimizing damage once thermal runaway begins. Gcoo also operates a battery subscription service for electric bicycles that uses external battery swap stations instead of indoor charging. Users of the safety-focused service rose 391% in the first half of this year from a year earlier. As battery use spreads across daily life, safety technology to prevent fires is growing more important. Battery-related fires in South Korea, including those involving general batteries and capacitors, rose to 706 in 2025 from 543 in 2024 and 359 in 2023, roughly doubling in two years, according to the National Fire Agency. "Companies are developing technology to reduce the risk of thermal runaway, but lithium-ion batteries structurally carry risks of heat buildup and thermal runaway," said Chae Jin, a professor of fire and disaster prevention at Mokwon University. "Along with technology development, safety measures must be put in place so that thermal runaway can be dealt with quickly if it occurs in actual use."

artigo.texto: Jason Padgett is convinced mathematics can reduce the need for data centers. Data centers are facilities that house computer systems, servers and related IT infrastructure to store, process and distribute large amounts of data. Padgett, a Carmel resident, was diagnosed with acquired savant syndrome after suffering a traumatic brain injury during a mugging in Tacoma, Wash. The aftermath allowed him to develop exceptional math and geometric visualization, which he applied to come up with his data center theory. It all comes down to black holes. “Black holes actually store data, and then they project what’s called probability waves, which are like waves in the ocean,” Padgett said. “When a bunch of waves overlap, they make a new wave inside a black hole.” Those waves create patterns, which he said can be linked through a process that looks like connecting the dots. Padgett said brains – and AI – process data in a similar way. “In the model I have been developing, many possible quantum paths interfere, some cancel out, and the strongest coherent path becomes the route to the readable result,” he said. “I began asking whether a computer could copy that basic idea: eliminate what does not fit early and follow the most efficient path to the answer.” He said finding ways for AI to process information in fewer steps could make a big difference. “Fewer unnecessary calculations can mean less work for computer chips,” he said. “At large scale, less work could mean less electricity, less heat to remove and less water needed for cooling. We believe we have an early proof of concept showing that some internal AI work can be reused and some repeated computation can be skipped. But this is still early, and the next step is much bigger than one person.” Padgett said a team is needed. “That means software engineers, AI and machine-learning specialists, mathematicians, physicists, hardware and data-center experts, researchers, business leaders, investors and people who know how to turn an early technical idea into something that can be tested at real scale,” he said. Padgett primarily works independently, but he has spoken at Science of Consciousness conference organized by Dr. Stuart Hameroff, an anesthesiologist and quantum consciousness theorist and researcher at the University of Arizona.

artigo.texto: Créditos de carbono florestal e a lacuna da voz das mulheres na governança. O processo de alteração e complementação de diversos artigos da Lei de Proteção Ambiental está atraindo considerável atenção pública, especialmente as normas destinadas a aperfeiçoar o arcabouço institucional do mercado de carbono. No contexto geral da transição verde, a comercialização dos serviços de absorção e armazenamento de carbono prestados pelas florestas é vista como uma etapa estratégica, criando um recurso financeiro sustentável para a proteção florestal e, ao mesmo tempo, abrindo oportunidades para melhorar a qualidade de vida das populações locais. No entanto, por trás dos números relativos à área ou às despesas, surge uma questão profunda de governança: o estatuto e a voz das mulheres no processo de alocação e decisão sobre como utilizar esses fundos. Créditos de carbono florestal: da pegada do trabalho à realidade dos benefícios. Essencialmente, os créditos de carbono florestal são certificados que representam uma tonelada de CO2 (ou equivalente em CO2) absorvida e armazenada por meio de atividades de proteção, reflorestamento ou restauração florestal. Quando países ou empresas precisam compensar emissões, compram esses créditos. Os recursos do mercado de carbono, portanto, se tornam um fluxo de financiamento verde para regiões florestais. A relação entre créditos de carbono florestal e mulheres não se resume à distribuição de benefícios sociais, mas decorre de suas contribuições diretas para a criação de "bens" de carbono. Os créditos são calculados com base na quantidade de CO2 reduzida ou absorvida devido à melhor proteção florestal, vegetação mais densa e expansão da área florestal. Nessa série de atividades, as mulheres em áreas rurais e montanhosas são a força de trabalho silenciosa, porém direta, que mantém essa "fonte de absorção". Desde o plantio de sementes e o cuidado com as árvores recém-plantadas até a colheita controlada de produtos florestais não madeireiros para evitar a degradação do ecossistema, as mulheres participam de quase todas as etapas da conservação da biodiversidade. Um exemplo vívido disso é a história da Sra. Le Thi Thinh, uma mulher Pa Co da aldeia de A Nieng, comuna de Le Trieng 1, distrito de A Luoi 1, cidade de Hue . Ao se tornar membro do Conselho de Gestão Florestal Comunitária, superando estereótipos de gênero como "mulheres não podem ficar na floresta o dia todo" ou barreiras relacionadas ao cuidado infantil, a Sra. Thinh lidera com confiança patrulhas que gerenciam quase 1.500 hectares de floresta natural, utilizando habilmente a tecnologia SMART Mobile para coletar dados para a proteção florestal. Ao proteger diretamente as florestas e prevenir a exploração madeireira ilegal, os esforços e o conhecimento indígena de mulheres como a Sra. Thinh contribuem para o valor agregado gerado por cada crédito de carbono florestal. Enfatizando esse papel fundamental, a especialista independente em gênero, Nguyen Thi Lan, afirmou: "As mulheres podem ser grupos impactados negativamente pelas mudanças ambientais e pelos processos de transição, e ao mesmo tempo possuir o conhecimento, a capacidade e a habilidade para impulsionar a mudança." Você também pode gostar A implementação piloto do Pagamento por Créditos de Carbono Florestal (ERPA, na sigla em inglês) em seis províncias do centro-norte do Vietnã demonstrou que os créditos de carbono realmente chegaram à população, proporcionando uma fonte prática de financiamento complementar para a proteção florestal e a melhoria dos meios de subsistência. No entanto, o processo de pagamento em nível familiar também revelou uma lacuna de governança relacionada ao gênero. Devido às práticas legais e normas sociais vigentes, a pessoa designada como chefe de família que recebe os pagamentos geralmente é um homem. Quando a receita é transferida diretamente para uma conta ou entregue ao chefe de família do sexo masculino, permanece questionável se as mulheres – as trabalhadoras diretamente envolvidas na floresta – têm o direito de discutir, propor ou participar das decisões sobre como esse dinheiro será gasto. Quando as contribuições das mulheres geram diretamente receita de carbono, elas têm todo o direito e precisam ser reconhecidas como partes interessadas em igualdade de condições, com voz decisiva na governança e na alocação desse benefício econômico . O mecanismo de pagamento chega às famílias, mas ainda há pouca cobertura da mídia. A promulgação do Decreto 180/2026/ND-CP, em meados de julho de 2026, estabeleceu uma base legal unificada para os serviços de sequestro e armazenamento de carbono florestal no Vietnã. Este documento regulamenta de forma abrangente tudo, desde o planejamento do projeto e a determinação dos resultados de redução de emissões até os métodos de pagamento. Os fundos arrecadados podem ser transferidos diretamente ou confiados ao Fundo de Proteção e Desenvolvimento Florestal, ampliando os beneficiários para incluir famílias, indivíduos e comunidades. Para os proprietários florestais que sejam famílias ou comunidades, o valor total recebido será reinvestido na gestão florestal e na melhoria de seus meios de subsistência. A política aproximou o financiamento verde das comunidades locais. No entanto, quando os fundos chegam às aldeias ou famílias individuais, surge uma realidade: a "família" ou a "comunidade" é considerada uma unidade coletiva. O fato de uma comunidade receber benefícios ou uma família receber pagamentos não reflete a estrutura de governança interna: quem participa diretamente das discussões e as mulheres têm o direito de decidir como essa renda será gasta? A especialista Nguyen Thi Lan enfatizou: "Uma abordagem neutra em termos de gênero, que trata todos igualmente, às vezes cria inadvertidamente desigualdades de gênero indiretas. A questão a ser considerada não é apenas se as mulheres participam, mas qual o papel que desempenham, se têm poder de decisão e se se beneficiam de forma justa." Embora

artigo.texto: A fábrica localizada em Darque e Vila Nova de Anha projeta produzir 450 equipamentos por ano e faturar 650 milhões de euros. A fábrica da Nordic Epod, instalada entre as freguesias de Darque e Vila Nova de Anha, no concelho de Viana do Castelo, assinalou a saída da sua primeira unidade industrial com destino à exportação. A empresa, que iniciou a atividade operacional no passado mês de agosto de 2026, é especializada no fabrico de EPODs (Electrical Power Optimization Devices), equipamentos para receção, transformação, distribuição e estabilização de energia para centros de dados (data centers). O presidente da Câmara Municipal de Viana do Castelo, Luís Nobre, destacou o feito como um marco de relevo para a dinamização económica e atração de investimento tecnológico para o concelho. Com uma área total de 110 mil metros quadrados — dos quais 21 mil metros quadrados de área construída e 12 mil metros quadrados afetos à linha de montagem —, a unidade é única do género em Portugal. Faturação de 650 Milhões e Foco na Europa e Médio Oriente A fábrica vianense prevê atingir uma capacidade de produção anual de cerca de 450 EPODs, estimando um volume de negócios de 650 milhões de euros por ano. Cerca de 90% da produção será canalizada para os mercados externos, assumindo a Europa e o Médio Oriente a prioridade na estratégia de expansão internacional da empresa. Os módulos produzidos em Viana do Castelo não utilizam baterias, mas sim sistemas de continuidade e estabilização energética. As boas acessibilidades marítimas através do Porto de Viana do Castelo, a rede rodoviária e a proximidade aos eixos aeroportuários do Noroeste Peninsular foram determinantes para a fixação do investimento industrial no concelho.

artigo.texto: Forest carbon credits and the women's voice gap in governance. The process of amending and supplementing several articles of the Law on Environmental Protection is attracting significant public attention, especially the regulations aimed at perfecting the institutional framework for the carbon market. In the overall picture of green transition, the commercialization of carbon absorption and storage services provided by forests is seen as a strategic step, creating a sustainable financial resource for forest protection while also opening up opportunities to improve the livelihoods of local people. However, behind the figures regarding area or expenditure, a profound governance issue arises: the status and voice of women in the process of allocating and deciding how to use these funds. Forest carbon credits: From the imprint of labor to the reality of benefit. Essentially, forest carbon credits are certificates representing one ton of CO2 (or CO2 equivalent) absorbed and stored through forest protection, reforestation, or restoration activities. When countries or businesses need to offset emissions, they buy these credits. The funds from the carbon market thus become a green financing flow into forestry regions. The link between forest carbon credits and women is not simply a matter of welfare allocation, but stems from their direct contributions to the creation of carbon "goods." Credits are measured based on the amount of CO2 reduced or absorbed due to better forest protection, denser vegetation, and expanded forest area. In this series of activities, women in rural and mountainous areas are the silent but direct workforce maintaining this "absorption source." From sowing seeds and caring for newly planted forest trees to harvesting non-timber forest products in a controlled manner to avoid ecosystem degradation, women participate in almost all stages of biodiversity conservation. A vivid example of this is the story of Ms. Le Thi Thinh, a Pa Co woman in A Nieng village, Le Trieng 1 commune, A Luoi 1 district, Hue city. Becoming a member of the Community Forest Management Board, overcoming gender stereotypes such as "women cannot stay in the forest all day" or barriers related to childcare, Ms. Thinh confidently leads patrols managing nearly 1,500 hectares of natural forest, skillfully using SMART Mobile technology to record data for forest protection. By directly protecting forests and preventing illegal logging, the efforts and indigenous knowledge of women like Ms. Thinh contribute to the added value generated by each forest carbon credit. Emphasizing this key role, independent gender expert Nguyen Thi Lan stated: "Women can both be groups negatively impacted by environmental change and transition processes, and possess the knowledge, capacity, and ability to drive change." You may also like The pilot implementation of Payment for Forest Carbon Settlements (ERPA) in six provinces of North Central Vietnam has shown that the carbon credits have truly reached the people, providing a practical source of supplementary funding for forest protection and improving livelihoods. However, the payment process at the household level has also revealed a gender-related governance gap. Due to prevailing legal practices and social norms, the person named as the head of the household receiving the payments is usually a man. When the revenue is transferred directly into an account or given to the male head of the household, it remains questionable whether women – the laborers directly involved in the forest – have the right to discuss, propose, or participate in decisions regarding how that money is spent. When women's contributions directly generate carbon revenue, they have every right and need to be recognized as equal stakeholders with a decisive voice in the governance and allocation of this economic benefit. The payment mechanism reaches households, but there is still a lack of media coverage. The promulgation of Decree 180/2026/ND-CP in mid-July 2026 has laid a unified legal foundation for forest carbon sequestration and storage services in Vietnam. This document comprehensively regulates everything from project planning and determining emission reduction results to payment methods. The funds collected can be transferred directly or entrusted to the Forest Protection and Development Fund, expanding the beneficiaries to include households, individuals, and communities. For forest owners who are households or communities, the entire amount received will be reinvested in forest management and improving their livelihoods. The policy has brought green finance closer to the grassroots level. However, when the funds reach villages or individual households, a reality arises: the "household" or "community" is considered a collective unit. Whether a community receives benefits or a family receives payments doesn't reflect the internal governance structure: Who directly participates in discussions, and do women have the right to decide how that income is spent? Expert Nguyen Thi Lan emphasized: "A gender-neutral approach, treating everyone equally, sometimes inadvertently creates indirect gender inequalities. The issue to consider is not just whether women participate, but what role they play, whether they have decision-making power, and whether they benefit fairly." Although current regulations require community consultation and ensuring a fair benefit-sharing mechanism, the guiding documents do not yet set separate reporting targets by gender. Financial planning forms only record the number of households, area, and total cost, leaving management agencies without sufficient real-world data to accurately assess women's participation. artigo.texto: Sumitomo Corp. is studying how battery energy storage systems operate alongside electricity trading in Leicester, England, to prepare for expanding the technology across Japan. The Japanese trading house gained operational insights from a site storing enough power for 160,000 homes for two hours. Sumitomo studies UK battery storage model as Japan eyes wider adoption Japanese trading house Sumitomo Corp. is studying how battery energy storage systems operate alongside electricity markets in Leicester, England. The project offers lessons the company will apply as it pushes for wider deployment of the technology across Japan. A facility outside Leicester houses 30 shipping containers packed with batteries and inverters. Together, the units can store enough energy to power 160,000 homes for two hours. The site demonstrates what large-scale battery storage looks like in practice. Sumitomo gained insight into how the system functions as part of an electricity grid and how that relationship shapes trading activity. The company is learning how stored energy flows back into the market and how pricing signals drive demand for storage operations. Japan has been accelerating its own battery storage ambitions. The country's power sector faces growing pressure to integrate renewable energy sources while maintaining grid reliability. Battery systems offer a way to store surplus generation and release it when demand peaks, smoothing supply without relying on gas-fired backup plants. Sumitomo's move reflects broader momentum in Japan toward commercializing battery storage at scale. Trading companies have been positioning themselves as operators of the technology, leveraging their existing networks and relationships with utilities and industrial customers. The Leicester project gives them a concrete reference point for planning similar deployments domestically. The company did not immediately disclose specific timelines or investment figures for its domestic plans. Industry observers expect Sumitomo to use the Leicester experience to shape proposals for utilities and large industrial consumers who want storage assets on their sites. The East Midlands facility represents one of several battery storage projects being developed by UK firms as the country navigates its own energy transition. Japan's experience operating such systems at commercial scale could prove instructive as the technology moves from demonstration to widespread adoption. Sumitomo's exploration of the Leicester site underscores how international knowledge transfer is becoming a practical tool for energy companies seeking to accelerate deployment in markets where regulatory frameworks and market structures still are being defined. For Japan, the lesson is straightforward: build the capability, study the operations, then scale. Sources: Nikkei Asia reporting, Oct. 26, 2026 Source:asia.nikkei.com

artigo.texto: By Devyn Lyon, FOX23 News TULSA, Okla. — Oklahoma regulators have moved a hearing on OG&E’s proposed rules for large electricity users to January, extending a case that could help determine how the costs of powering data centers are divided and whether other customers could be left paying more. The hearing, previously scheduled for November 3, is now set for January 12, 2027. The central question for households and small businesses is straightforward: as large customers connect to the electric grid, who pays for the power plants, lines and other equipment needed to serve them? OG&E filed the case to seek approval of a proposed “large-load tariff.” A tariff establishes the rates, and service requirements customers must follow. In this case, OG&E wants special payment requirements for very large electricity users, including data centers. Google is participating in the proceeding and advocating for changes to how those customers can obtain power. In emailed responses to FOX23, OG&E said its proposal is intended to protect existing customers from costs associated with bringing large users onto the grid. “Current customers should never pay for the impact of bringing large-load customers onto the electric grid,” the company said. Simply put, OG&E wants large customers to make financial commitments, so the utility’s other customers are not left covering costs if a project uses less electricity than expected cuts back or closes. The company said its proposal would require large customers to: - Pay for infrastructure built to serve them - Sign long-term, binding contracts - Pay substantial minimum bills, even if they use less power than expected - Pay fees if they reduce their commitments of leave early - Provide financial security to back up those obligations OG&E also argues those customers should contribute toward the costs of its existing power plants. There are proposed requirements, regulators must determine what rules to approve. Google wants large customers to have the option to buy electricity from independent generators while continuing to use OG&E’s grid to receive it. Google argues that approach could reduce the need for OG&E to build expensive new power plants. OG&E argues those arrangements could leave large customers paying less toward its existing plants while continuing to depend on the utility’s system. The company also says it must maintain reliable service when a customer’s outside power source is unavailable. Its concern is that costs could fall to other customers if the large user does not adequately pay for that backup. Buying electricity from another supplier would still involve using power lines and other grid infrastructure. The dispute is over which costs those customers would remain responsible for, and whether state law permits the arrangements being proposed. The hearing delay itself does not approve a rate of increase or decide how those costs will be divided. The potential impact comes from the rules regulators ultimately adopt. If large customers do not cover the costs assigned to serving them, other customers could face pressure to cover more. But, if outside power purchases reduce the need for costly new utility construction, that could also affect future costs. Those competing arguments are part of what the commission must evaluate. Neither side’s position establishes what will happen to an individual customer’s bill. OG&E said other parties’ proposals raised legal questions that should be addressed before the commission hears the evidence. The company said it wants those parties to explain what law allows large customers to buy electricity from third-party generators while relying on OG&E’s grid. OG&E said the additional time would allow those arguments to be considered before the hearing. FOX23 also asked whether the requested date was connected to Commissioner Todd Hiett’s term ending January 11, one day before the rescheduled hearing. The company said it was not, saying its request was driven by proposals introduced by parties. The proceeding is Oklahoma Corporation Commission Case No. PUD2026-000046. Customers can search for that number in the commission’s Electronic Case Filing system to review filings, testimony, and orders. The commission’s October 21 scheduling order is available here. The January hearing is the next opportunity to examine the proposals and evidence. Moving that hearing does not resolve the underlying dispute over who should pay.

artigo.texto: Data center construction to require many more workers SCOTT TRUXELL/independent editor Original estimates had approximately 1,500 construction workers needed to build Van Wert’s $10 billion QTS data center but those figures have been revised. The number is now larger – a lot larger. During Sunday’s “Commissioner’s Corner/Mayor’s Conference” program on radio stations 99.7FM WKSD and 1220AM/104.3FM, Van Wert Area Economic Development Director Brent Stevens said Stevens said ground was recently broken on Phase I of the project, which will include four buildings at the Mega Site on Van Wert’s east side. “Each building is roughly 650,000 square feet apiece and they’re all being built at once, so that has shifted their numbers up quite a bit,” Stevens said. “There’s going to be a couple of hundred people on this massive ground excavation over the next six months, then they’ll start to go vertical. For the first 12 months, we’re going to be in that 2,000 (construction worker) range, then all the subcontracters are coming in.” That when the number of construction workers is expected to climb to as many as 5,500 per day. “5,500 people in town per day, I would say after March of 2028,” he stated. With several thousand workers coming to the area, the question is – where will they stay? “I’ve been in the process of going to everybody that can facilitate new housing and going ‘we need to work on getting this done,” Stevens stated on the show. “We’ve been talking about housing for the last year and a half or two years, it’s just sinking in to everybody. I’m talking with several different developers – I’ve been talking to developers in Fort Wayne about building over there as well.” “Of the 5,550 that are going to come here, how many are actually going to be moving to Van Wert because we need to prepare the schools too,” he added. Stevens did say some of the workers will be local. As far as rest of the workers and where they will come from, Stevens quipped it’s like a “traveling road show” “They’ll go to this data center and build it,” he said. “They have these certain groups that will fly in, do all the things they need to do but for example, for this particular project, the head Suffolk guy (Suffolk Construction Company, the contractor in charge), is actually moving to Van Wert and will be here for 6-7 years.” The topic of an adequate number of local restuarants and bars was also discussed during the program and he mentioned the old Marsh hotel could and other storefronts downtown could be put to use, along with available space in the Towne Center Blvd area. Stevens mentioned that for every job that’s created at the data center, 3.5 ancillary jobs follow. “Even our surrounding communities – Ohio City, Convoy – people are looking at doing things over there because of this particular project,” Stevens said. Stevens noted that a temporary off-ramp will be built of off U.S. 30 directly into the construction site and a 6,000 spot parking lot. As far as dollars to the local community, Stevens stated QTS is going to take “zero incentives.” “None,” he said. “They’re going to give back to the community in an unbelievable fashion and I’m hoping we’ll be able to announce that (soon).” Stevens said there have been ongoing discussions about how to manage the money coming into the community and how to do things in a fiscally responsible way. “What we have decided in talking with the commissioners and the mayor, is there’s going to be funding coming in that will be city money and funding coming in that will be county money,” he explained. “We will create two boards – a board for the city and a board for the county.” The full program can be heard below. artigo.texto: As supostas baterias do Galaxy S27 Ultra e do Galaxy S27 Pro vazaram após passarem por uma certificação sul-coreana. Os componentes foram encontrados no Safety Korea, que funciona como um órgão regulador. Essas baterias podem trazer uma capacidade elevada em comparação à atual geração. A listagem aponta para os modelos com código de série EB-BS958DBY e EB-BS957CBY, certificados pelos números YU10899-26034 e YU10899-26036, respectivamente. Essas baterias foram confeccionadas pela Jinwan, uma subsidiária da Zhuhai CosMX Power na China. Informações sobre a autonomia dos componentes são escassos através desse vazamento, mas rumores anteriores indicavam que o S27 Ultra teria capacidade de 5.534 mAh e o S27 Pro ficaria com 5.087 mAh. Geralmente, esses valores nominais correspondem à capacidade típica de 5.700 mAh e 5.200 mAh, respectivamente. Vale notar que esses 5.700 mAh do S27 Ultra representam uma evolução interessante frente aos 5.000 mAh do S26 Ultra. O aumento na capacidade da variante Ultra se tornou uma tônica entre os pedidos dos usuários e pouco a pouco a Samsung tenta resolver isso. Na atual geração, todos os modelos já usam baterias de silício-carbono. Como serão os Galaxy S27? Diversos rumores apontam para o lançamento dos Galaxy S27 com algumas melhorias interessantes para toda a linha. Esses aparelhos devem receber os novos chips Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6, incluindo a versão Extreme, e também o Exynos 2700 de fabricação própria da Samsung. - Esses aparelhos apareceram com seus supostos designs vazados na internet e devem ganhar novidades no módulo de câmeras; - Há certos rumores de que toda a linha de aparelhos poderia receber a Tela de Privacidade, inclusive o modelo base; - Essa versão mais parruda da linha pode ter uma das lentes teleobjetivas removidas; - Um modelo “Pro” deve ser lançado e ficar posicionado entre a versão Plus e Ultra, inclusive com uma câmera de 200 MP; - Os Galaxy S27 devem ser oficialmente anunciados a partir de janeiro de 2027. Por falar em celulares, a Apple iniciou nesta sexta-feira (23) as vendas do iPhone Duo com preços altos e estoques com pouco volume. artigo.texto: The debate over data centers has found its way into Los Angeles County’s election season, where for months, even the mention of data center in public forums in some local cities has drawn keen attention in the run-up to November. In cities such as Alhambra and Monterey Park, the local fate of centers — the giant warehouses, built to power the nation’s artificial intelligence boom, and their kin, battery energy storage systems (BESS) — has manifested itself in ballot measures and candidate talking points, as towns debate whether such hubs should be built. In most cases, the centers don’t exist at all, and in a handful they’ve been proposed. But in L.A. County, like the rest of the nation, they’ve often become a symbol of pushback in a nation grappling with high costs and the relentless drive of technology companies seeking to build an AI infrastructure. Case in point: Alhambra. In July, the City Council voted to place Measure DB on the Nov. 3 ballot, giving residents the chance to codify an existing city ban that has been an ordinance in the city. “While a Data Center ban already exists by ordinance, this measure lets Alhambra voters decide whether to make that ban permanent and subject to voter approval to change” City Manager City Manager Jessica Binnquist said back in September announcement, after the council approved the ballot measure. Many residents had reportedly emailed the city about wanting data center protections, leading to the June 22 ordinance. And, like many cities, the action for the ban came amid a broader discussion on responsible development and long-term investments in schools, infrastructure, public spaces and environmental safety. If the proposed Alhambra measure sounds familiar, it’s because neighboring Monterey Park has become the impetus for voter action on data centers after its voters approved a pioneering ban in June. The momentum has carried over, becoming a template for this November’s ballot action on the centers, proponents said. In Monterey Park, developer HMC StratCap had proposed a center before a months-long grassroots campaign and various city ordinances brought the project to a halt, first with a city council moratorium and then a vote of the people. In the wake of the win, an array of local community organizers and leaders involved in supporting the measure are running for office this November, not just in Monterey Park but in neighboring cities. - Also see: In Monterey Park, 2 candidates vie for a seat in aftermath of trailblazing data center ban In Monterey Park and Alhambra, the anti-data center movement led Steven Kung and Amy J. Wong – organizers from No Data Center Monterey Park and SGV Progressive Action – to run for their respective city council seats. Leveraging their Monterey Park success, Wong and others from SGV Progressive Action have advocated for other cities to follow suit: promote a voter-ballot based ban, which is harder to overturn than a council ordinance banning the facilities city-wide. Beyond advocating for ordinances in Montebello, El Monte and Baldwin Park, Wong’s advocacy could lead to Alhambra being the second city in the county to ban data centers city-wide through public vote with its Measure DB. Wong, who is running against Ron Sahu for an Alhambra seat, co-founded SGV Progressive Action, helped establish Monterey Park’s data center ballot initiative and campaigned for the same action in other San Gabriel Valley cities, including Alhambra. It’s become part of her pitch as she battles it out with Sahu over quality-of-life and development issues. Sahu also supports the ban. It’s not just them. Leslie Garcia, an air quality instrument specialist with the South Coast Air Quality Management District running for West Covina City Council District 2, became involved with the No Data Center San Gabriel Valley coalition, which has fueled her run for office. “I started becoming more involved with the No Data Center coalition, and as we’re continuing to do our work against the City of Industry, that’s when people who were running for positions in Covina started to speak up about the battery energy storage system,” Garcia said. In June, the Covina Planning Commission rejected energy developer RWE’s controversial Covina Reliability Project, a BESS facility, citing several inconsistencies in the project. And, in September, West Covina Council unanimously approved a resolution opposing large-scale data centers and BESS facilities from being built in the city. Locally, many see BESS facilities — which harness electrical energy — as a precursor to data centers. In February, the City of Industry’s City Council unanimously approved energy utility developer AYPA Power’s application to begin developing the Marici Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Facility along Gale Avenue. The project’s approval followed previous concerns at a Jan. 27 planning commission meeting that the proposed facility would lead to a future data center, which AYPA and the city have denied. Stefanie Leilua decided to run for council in Walnut because “when one city gets an approval, it’s gonna affect two to three cities, no matter what, because of how we’re lined up.” “Look at the La Verne fire that happened,” pointing to the Metropolitan Water District BESS fire that led to a four-day evacuation in late September. The fire involved two 250-kilowatt battery units housed in an indoor-outdoor facility to support a 2-megawatt solar farm. By comparison, the City of Industry’s Marici BESS facility is to be approximately 400 megawatts. “It wasn’t even as big, but everybody had to end up staying indoors because of the chemical pollution that was coming out of the battery center,” Leilua said. Garcia noted the nexus between local cities. “I went to go help them out since they’re our sister city,” Garcia continued. “In the San Gabriel Valley, this feels like the first time we have a really large progressive movement united by the fact that we don’t want data centers … If we get

Start your Independent Membership today. Join today Already a member? Log in BYD has gone from being a name few British buyers had heard of to one of the biggest success stories in the global car industry in just a few short years. The Chinese company started out making rechargeable batteries at its headquarters in Wuhan, before moving into electric cars. Today, it's one of the world's largest manufacturers of electrified vehicles, while it makes pretty much everything in its vehicles – from the batteries and the semiconductors to the electric motors and the steel. It even has its own shipping company to move its cars around the world, although local production is very much on the agenda with a first factory in Europe opening soon. The Sealion 7 is currently the flagship of BYD's UK range, sitting just below the more premium models that will carry the newly introduced Denza badge. A sleek family SUV aimed squarely at the heart of the most competitive sectors of the market, it’s taking on the Tesla Model Y, Hyundai Ioniq 5 and Kia EV6, as well as other Chinese rivals such as the Xpeng G6, with BYD banking on a combination of generous standard equipment, impressive technology and competitive pricing. It's exactly the sort of car we wanted to spend more time with. A first drive can tell you plenty about a new model, but it's only after weeks and months of everyday use that you discover whether an electric car really delivers. Is it as easy to charge as the brochure suggests? Does the technology remain intuitive once the novelty wears off? Can it cope with long journeys, family duties and the day-to-day demands of modern life? We’re now well into our second month of living with the Sealion 7 and it’s proving its worth in more ways than one – and persuading other people of the benefits of electric cars, while helping us all discover more about one of China's biggest automotive success stories. BYD Sealion 7 Comfort - Base price: £46,990 - Options: Polar White metallic paint (£1,100) - Total price: £48,090 - Battery size: 82.5kWh - Maximum claimed range: 300 miles - Maximum charging rate: 150kW - 0-62mph: 6.7 seconds BYD Sealion 7 Comfort – first report It wasn’t the acceleration, the giant touchscreen or even the fact that I was driving a Chinese electric car through deepest Somerset that made me realise the BYD Sealion was something rather different. It was the yawn. Somewhere on a winding country road, bordered by high hedgerows and the sort of villages where everyone notices an unfamiliar number plate, I let out an entirely innocent yawn. Before I’d even finished, the car politely interrupted. “Are you tired? Perhaps you should take a break.” I blinked. My wife has been known to say something similar. I wasn’t expecting it from the car. The Sealion had actually seen me yawn. It wasn’t scolding me so much as looking after me. Slightly unnerving? Yes. Clever? Undoubtedly. It felt like the first of many moments when I realised this wasn’t simply another electric SUV packed with gadgets. It was almost trying to be a travelling companion. Driving a Chinese car is still something of a conversation starter in rural Somerset. The Sealion, in gleaming white and with more than a hint of rock-star swagger, attracted plenty of curious glances in market squares and village car parks. Questions followed almost everywhere I stopped. “How far does it go?” “How quickly does it charge?” And, inevitably… “So…it’s Chinese?” We’ve become entirely comfortable with our phones, laptops, televisions and half the contents of our kitchens coming from China. Cars somehow still surprise people. After only a couple of weeks, I found myself confidently answering technical questions like I’d worked for BYD for years. “Is it more hi-tech?” asked our local mechanic. “I think it probably is,” I replied, sounding far more authoritative than I had any right to. The Blade Battery sounds like marketing jargon until I was told it’s a fundamentally different approach to battery design. It’s engineered for durability, thermal stability and efficient packaging, allowing more of the car’s floor to be devoted to energy storage. You don’t notice any of that while driving, of course. Inside, it certainly feels futuristic. The vast central screen—about the size of a family pizza—makes sat-nav directions blissfully easy to follow. Better still, my phone simply sits on a flat charging pad instead of disappearing into one of those mysterious storage compartments that manufacturers always seem to imagine we’ll fill with pencils, loose change or forgotten receipts. The cabin itself somehow feels lighter than the car’s considerable dimensions suggest. It’s airy, spacious and astonishingly quiet. Even at motorway speeds there’s remarkably little wind noise, leaving only the faintest whisper from the tyres. Conversation becomes effortless and, perhaps more surprisingly, so does thinking. You arrive feeling noticeably less fatigued than after covering the same distance in many conventional SUVs. The dashboard screen can rotate from landscape to portrait at the press of a button – a feature that never quite loses its novelty. It’s one of those gimmicks that initially makes passengers smile before you discover it can actually be rather useful depending on which apps you’re using. One small gripe? The door handles. They protrude when the car is unlocked and only sit flush once it’s locked. It’s not quite as elegant as some rivals. Then again, perhaps that’s simply another way the Sealion is qu

artigo.texto: Dozens gather to discuss concerns on Google data center in Fort Wayne FORT WAYNE, Ind. (WPTA) - With Fort Wayne’s growing data center presence, Protect Allen County held a community gathering Sunday afternoon for residents to voice their opinions. About 50 people packed inside a home near the Google data center on Adams Road. Organizers said the goal was to build a coalition for those who are worried about the negative impacts, whether they relate to air quality or energy costs, and show concerned citizens how they can advocate for each other. The resident of the home everyone was gathered at, Barry Dibble, said traffic spiked near his house. “I want them to check their politicians out to see how they would feel about it. Without their support, this means nothing. Our politicians need to support us and to support what’s going on and stop this nonsense.” He added that he hopes Sunday’s gathering pushes more people to talk to local officials. Protect Allen County plans to hold more community gatherings going forward. View all previous coverage here. artigo.texto: Europe’s carbon market is getting more room to manoeuvre as the EU agrees to raise the threshold for scrapping surplus permits. That should give industry flexibility while keeping a lid on oversupply and price swings. The Council of the EU and the European Parliament have reached a provisional deal to change how the EU’s carbon market handles surplus emissions permits. The mechanism for cancelling excess permits will stay in place. But the threshold will rise from 400 million to 700 million. The new threshold will take effect once the deal is formally adopted. The European Commission had originally proposed scrapping the cancellation mechanism altogether. Higher threshold, bigger buffer Negotiators instead settled on a compromise that preserves a safeguard against oversupply while leaving more room to respond to future market swings. “In response to European leaders’ call for accelerated action, we reached a balanced outcome on the Market Stability Reserve that provides European industry with immediate flexibility, while ensuring price stability and protecting the integrity of the EU carbon market,” said Darragh O’Brien, Ireland’s Minister for Climate, Energy and the Environment. He described the deal as part of the EU’s ‘One Europe, One Market’ roadmap. The Mmarket Stability Reserve (MSR) helps balance supply and demand in the EU emissions trading system (ETS). When too many permits circulate, it removes some from the market. Under the rules, it can also release permits when needed. The mechanism aims to limit imbalances caused by a surplus or shortage of allowances. Three billion permits off the market Since the cancellation mechanism began in 2023, it has removed more than three billion permits from the market. This helped tackle the historic oversupply that had built up in the ETS. Negotiators say the higher threshold will strengthen the market’s long-term stability and provide a larger buffer against future fluctuations. The change could also matter after the mid-2030s, when the ETS emissions cap will continue to fall and the market could face tighter supply. A broader review of the ETS is still under way. It will also consider gradually lowering the cancellation threshold to ensure a consistent approach across the system. The current deal is a standalone change intended to help address high and volatile energy prices, rather than a full reform of the carbon market. The provisional agreement must now be confirmed by the Council and Parliament before both institutions formally adopt it.
