artigo.texto: The debate over data centers has found its way into Los Angeles County’s election season, where for months, even the mention of data center in public forums in some local cities has drawn keen attention in the run-up to November. In cities such as Alhambra and Monterey Park, the local fate of centers — the giant warehouses, built to power the nation’s artificial intelligence boom, and their kin, battery energy storage systems (BESS) — has manifested itself in ballot measures and candidate talking points, as towns debate whether such hubs should be built. In most cases, the centers don’t exist at all, and in a handful they’ve been proposed. But in L.A. County, like the rest of the nation, they’ve often become a symbol of pushback in a nation grappling with high costs and the relentless drive of technology companies seeking to build an AI infrastructure. Case in point: Alhambra. In July, the City Council voted to place Measure DB on the Nov. 3 ballot, giving residents the chance to codify an existing city ban that has been an ordinance in the city. “While a Data Center ban already exists by ordinance, this measure lets Alhambra voters decide whether to make that ban permanent and subject to voter approval to change” City Manager City Manager Jessica Binnquist said back in September announcement, after the council approved the ballot measure. Many residents had reportedly emailed the city about wanting data center protections, leading to the June 22 ordinance. And, like many cities, the action for the ban came amid a broader discussion on responsible development and long-term investments in schools, infrastructure, public spaces and environmental safety. If the proposed Alhambra measure sounds familiar, it’s because neighboring Monterey Park has become the impetus for voter action on data centers after its voters approved a pioneering ban in June. The momentum has carried over, becoming a template for this November’s ballot action on the centers, proponents said. In Monterey Park, developer HMC StratCap had proposed a center before a months-long grassroots campaign and various city ordinances brought the project to a halt, first with a city council moratorium and then a vote of the people. In the wake of the win, an array of local community organizers and leaders involved in supporting the measure are running for office this November, not just in Monterey Park but in neighboring cities. - Also see: In Monterey Park, 2 candidates vie for a seat in aftermath of trailblazing data center ban In Monterey Park and Alhambra, the anti-data center movement led Steven Kung and Amy J. Wong – organizers from No Data Center Monterey Park and SGV Progressive Action – to run for their respective city council seats. Leveraging their Monterey Park success, Wong and others from SGV Progressive Action have advocated for other cities to follow suit: promote a voter-ballot based ban, which is harder to overturn than a council ordinance banning the facilities city-wide. Beyond advocating for ordinances in Montebello, El Monte and Baldwin Park, Wong’s advocacy could lead to Alhambra being the second city in the county to ban data centers city-wide through public vote with its Measure DB. Wong, who is running against Ron Sahu for an Alhambra seat, co-founded SGV Progressive Action, helped establish Monterey Park’s data center ballot initiative and campaigned for the same action in other San Gabriel Valley cities, including Alhambra. It’s become part of her pitch as she battles it out with Sahu over quality-of-life and development issues. Sahu also supports the ban. It’s not just them. Leslie Garcia, an air quality instrument specialist with the South Coast Air Quality Management District running for West Covina City Council District 2, became involved with the No Data Center San Gabriel Valley coalition, which has fueled her run for office. “I started becoming more involved with the No Data Center coalition, and as we’re continuing to do our work against the City of Industry, that’s when people who were running for positions in Covina started to speak up about the battery energy storage system,” Garcia said. In June, the Covina Planning Commission rejected energy developer RWE’s controversial Covina Reliability Project, a BESS facility, citing several inconsistencies in the project. And, in September, West Covina Council unanimously approved a resolution opposing large-scale data centers and BESS facilities from being built in the city. Locally, many see BESS facilities — which harness electrical energy — as a precursor to data centers. In February, the City of Industry’s City Council unanimously approved energy utility developer AYPA Power’s application to begin developing the Marici Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) Facility along Gale Avenue. The project’s approval followed previous concerns at a Jan. 27 planning commission meeting that the proposed facility would lead to a future data center, which AYPA and the city have denied. Stefanie Leilua decided to run for council in Walnut because “when one city gets an approval, it’s gonna affect two to three cities, no matter what, because of how we’re lined up.” “Look at the La Verne fire that happened,” pointing to the Metropolitan Water District BESS fire that led to a four-day evacuation in late September. The fire involved two 250-kilowatt battery units housed in an indoor-outdoor facility to support a 2-megawatt solar farm. By comparison, the City of Industry’s Marici BESS facility is to be approximately 400 megawatts. “It wasn’t even as big, but everybody had to end up staying indoors because of the chemical pollution that was coming out of the battery center,” Leilua said. artigo.texto: EU Carbon Market Proposal Would Reshape Marine Fuel Economics Unevenly Europe’s carbon market may soon begin compensating shipowners for fuel switching, yet the assistance available is anything but uniform. In July, the European Commission put forward a revision of the EU Emissions Trading System that would set aside as many as 110 million allowances from 2028 through 2040 for a new Sustainable Maritime Alternative Propulsion mechanism, designed to bridge part of the cost difference between fossil marine fuels and sustainable substitutes. Read also: IMO Approves New Safety Guidelines for Ammonia as Marine Fuel Rystad Energy’s analysis indicates that, taken together with the EU ETS itself and the FuelEU Maritime regulation, the proposal would alter the cost hierarchy of marine fuels across Europe. BioLNG and renewable e-fuels are positioned to benefit most, whereas biodiesel derived from used cooking oil and animal fats, among the most commonly used marine biofuels today, receives no support. Timing and Compliance Pressure Timing is significant. Starting in 2026, shipping firms must surrender ETS allowances covering 100% of their verified in-scope emissions, which now include methane and nitrous oxide, while FuelEU Maritime mandates a progressively stricter reduction in the greenhouse-gas intensity of onboard energy use. Both frameworks depend on the sustainability criteria of the EU’s revised Renewable Energy Directive. For shipowners, charterers and fuel suppliers, the central question is which fuel pathway the combined rules favor. How the Subsidy Would Work SMAP would bridge 55% of the remaining price gap to fossil fuel for biogas and advanced biofuels, and 90% for renewable fuels of non-biological origin such as e-ammonia and e-methanol, with an extra 10 percentage points when the feedstock originates in the EU. Since support scales with the size of the gap, the costliest fuels receive the most per tonne, and EU-made e-ammonia could have its entire remaining premium covered. Support is cut in half for voyages entering or leaving the EU, and fuels generally must be produced within the EU or in a country with a linked carbon market. Cost Rankings on Intra-EU Routes Combined, the three instruments push several alternative fuels below the cost of very low sulfur fuel oil on intra-EU voyages. At third-quarter 2026 prices, bioLNG costs more than double that of VLSFO before any incentives, yet it ends up at roughly half the cost of VLSFO once FuelEU credits and the proposed subsidy are factored in. Most of that advantage stems from FuelEU Maritime, and bioLNG would already undercut VLSFO without SMAP. Since bioLNG is a drop-in fuel for liquefied natural gas engines, this reinforces the business case for LNG dual-fuel ships trading in Europe. Renewable fuels of non-biological origin receive the most generous treatment of all and, on paper, EU-produced e-ammonia could become the cheapest fuel on intra-EU routes, although very few vessels can burn ammonia today and EU output remains limited. Waste-Based Biofuels Left Out The most obvious losers are liquid biofuels made from waste oils and fats. Used cooking oil and category 1 and 2 animal fats satisfy every EU sustainability test and earn full credit under both the ETS and FuelEU Maritime, but SMAP covers only advanced biofuels made from feedstocks listed in Annex IX Part A of the revised Renewable Energy Directive. Biogas, in contrast, appears eligible irrespective of feedstock. The exclusion matters given the structure of Europe’s biodiesel industry. By 2030, crops and waste lipids such as used cooking oil and other waste fats and oils are projected to make up about 96% of the region’s biodiesel and renewable diesel production capacity, leaving only around 2% clearly eligible for support. Aviation’s sustainable fuel mandate draws on the same waste lipids, meaning shipping is unlikely to secure much eligible liquid biofuel.

artigo.texto: A weekly roundup of public health news Data center boom puts pressure on US water supplies Data centers, which are multiplying across the U.S., are often built where water supplies are already strained, new research finds. About 21% of the nation’s 3,600 data centers are located in areas where demand for water exceeds the supply for at least one month annually, according to a study in the October issue of Environmental Science & Technology. Climate change could increase that share to 35% in coming decades, researchers estimated. The U.S. accounts for nearly 40% of the world’s data centers, with another 1,500 facilities in the works. That expansion could put additional pressure on local water supplies, particularly in communities where communities, farmers and businesses already compete for limited resources. More than half of U.S. data centers are located in areas where public water supplies account for the largest share of water consumption. Another 20% are in areas where agricultural irrigation is the largest water use. Data centers house thousands of heat-generating computer systems that are cooled using water. Unlike electricity, water generally must come from nearby sources, making data centers particularly vulnerable to local droughts and seasonal shortages. While most data centers in the eastern U.S. are located in areas with adequate water supplies, facilities in parts of the West and South face shortages for four to eight months annually, researchers said. Coal miners in high-dust jobs face outsized black lung risk Black lung disease continues to threaten U.S. coal miners, with workers in Appalachia facing particularly high risks, new federal research finds. Despite decades of regulations designed to protect miners, cases of coal workers’ pneumoconiosis, also known as black lung disease, continue to impact the workforce, according to an Oct. 20 study in Frontiers in Public Health. Underground dust may be playing a major role. Researchers from the National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health examined 1991-2024 data collected through a U.S. coal worker health surveillance program, finding mining workers in dusty jobs are more at risk for the deadly disease. Continuous miner operators — workers who rip materials such as coal and stone from mine faces — and roof bolters — who reinforce and secure mine shafts and tunnels — were much more likely to develop black lung disease and progressive massive fibrosis, the disease’s severe, late-stage form, the study found. Both jobs involve heavy machinery that cuts or drills through coal and rock, releasing fine dust that workers can inhale deep into their lungs. The dust often contains coal particles and crystalline silica, which can cause permanent lung damage. Continuous miner operators had nearly twice the prevalence of black lung disease and three times the prevalence of progressive massive fibrosis compared with miners without those jobs. Roof bolters also faced elevated risks. The disparities were particularly severe in Central Appalachia, including Kentucky, Virginia and West Virginia. More than 8% of miners there had black lung disease, compared with less than 2% elsewhere in the U.S. Even after accounting for years of work, Appalachian miners had nearly four times the prevalence of black lung disease and 10 times the prevalence of its most severe form, researchers found. The region’s thinner coal seams often require miners to cut through more silica-containing rock, increasing exposure to dangerous dust. More PFAS may lurk in US drinking water than known Contamination of U.S. drinking water with “forever chemicals” could be much worse than reported. New research published Oct. 23 in Cell Reports Sustainability estimates levels of per- and polyfluoroalkyl substances, also known as PFAS, could be twice as high as current monitoring shows. Researchers examined 1.8 million PFAS measurements that were shared with the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency by public water systems, finding that standard reporting practices can overlook substantial amounts of the chemicals. At issue is the practice of excluding PFAS concentrations from calculations if they fall below certain levels. As a result, reporting may capture only 44% of the average concentration of 25 PFAS in community water systems, the study estimated. For six PFAS covered by federal drinking water standards, concentrations modeled by researchers were twice as high as those calculated using conventional reporting methods. The gap was larger for water systems relying on surface water than those using groundwater. PFAS are used in consumer and industrial products and have been linked to cancer, liver damage and other health issues. The chemicals persist in the environment and can accumulate in the human body, hence the name “forever chemicals.” World on course to blow past climate safety limits New estimates of increasing global temperatures paint a bleaker-than-expected picture for human health. The world is on track to warm by 2.8 degrees Celsius above preindustrial levels this century if current climate policies continue, according to an Oct. 21 report from the U.N. Environment Program. The estimate is higher than last year’s projections and far above international goals for limiting climate change. The additional warming threatens to intensify deadly heat waves, flooding, wildfires and droughts, exposing millions more people to dangerous conditions and significantly increasing risks to health. Even if countries fulfill all their current commitments to reduce greenhouse gas emissions, global temperatures are projected to rise by 2.6 degrees Celsius, the report found. Meeting additional long-term targets would still leave warming increases at about 2.1 degrees. The 2015 Paris Agreement, approved by about 200 nations, set a goal of keeping warming increases below 2 degrees Celsius, while pursuing a more protective limit of 1.5 degrees. artigo.texto: As I write this, the lights are coming back on after a power outage that impacted more than 1,500 Norfolk residences, including my house, where we lost electricity for more than 12 hours. Fortunately, I had made a run to the store earlier that week for a fresh stock of batteries to power all our flashlights. Yet, throughout the night, I couldn’t help wondering what life would be like if we all had home batteries capable of powering our homes? That kind of backup power is no longer a futuristic concept, and it’s no longer something we can wait for. Battery technology is changing how we use and access electricity in our everyday lives. If I were a homeowner with solar panels, I could store my excess energy in a battery system. That way, if there’s an outage, I would still be able to power my home appliances for four to eight hours or longer if needed, depending on the system and energy requirements. Then, once power is restored, the battery can recharge directly from the electric grid at night, when demand is typically lower, but other sources such as offshore wind projects are still generating power. Under the right conditions, electric vehicle owners can even use the batteries in their cars or trucks to power their homes. Home batteries provide flexibility to our lives, and utility-scale batteries can provide flexibility to our electric grid — the infrastructure that carries electricity from power plants to our homes. The same basic principle applies across the board: Batteries can charge when electricity is plentiful and less expensive, then discharge when demand is high. Naturally, your next question might be, aren’t these technologies expensive? But the cost of energy storage has decreased dramatically over the past several years. According to Lazard’s “Levelized Cost of Electricity” study, the gold standard of energy-pricing tools, battery storage paired with solar or wind projects are cost competitive and, in some cases, less expensive than fossil-fuel generation, particularly gas peaker plants. Coal and gas peaker plants remain among the more expensive options for meeting electricity demand. Quite simply, if we’re searching for ways to curb rising energy prices, we should be installing more batteries in more locations. Virginia is already starting to put this idea into practice. Gov. Abigail Spanberger’s 2026 Virginia Energy Plan recognizes that a more flexible grid, including more energy storage and other distributed resources, will be essential as electricity demand grows. In Danville, two battery projects totaling more than 20 megawatts are expected to save customers $70 million over 20 years. Batteries are not a far-off solution. They are part of the grid Virginia is building now. Finally, battery storage devices provide the cleaner option, releasing zero carbon emissions during their operation. We can meet our growing demand for electricity without locking Virginians into decades of fossil fuel dependence. And that matters not only because of climate change, but because the hottest and most demanding days are exactly when our electric system is under the most strain. If we want an electric grid that can keep the lights on as temperatures rise and electricity demand grows, we need solutions that don’t add to the problems we’re already seeing from climate change. And by storing electricity from clean resources and making it available when we need it, batteries can help us get more from the clean energy we’re already building. I spent 12 hours without power, and I don’t want to do it again. The technology is here. Let’s put batteries to work in Virginia. Jim Purekal of Norfolk is a legislative and energy expert and a director at Advanced Energy United.

artigo.texto: BRAZORIA COUNTY, Texas (KTRK) -- A potential data center in Brazoria County is raising concerns among residents, who told ABC13 they're being left in the dark. Landowners in Damon said they noticed a company buying more than 400 acres along the Brazos River, which is when they started asking questions. On Sunday, residents held a community meeting to discuss what they've found out so far. "We got to fight. We got to stop it before it gets here," one resident said. They told ABC13 that the county district attorney's office held a meeting earlier this month and showed them a map of seven parcels of land that included solar panels and batteries. Residents said that infrastructure pointed toward the potential for a data center. "That means a data center which could have gas turbines, and that means 24 hours, seven days a week, 365 days a year, noise, lights, vibration," Christine Clark, a concerned citizen, said. Experts previously told ABC13 that Texas counties have few tools to stop these developments, particularly in unincorporated areas, where regulations and permitting hurdles are limited. SEE ALSO: Permits related to data centers issued after Abbott's halt directive, advocacy groups found Residents said they're concerned about what a potential project like this could mean for a place they say is rich in both wildlife and history. "It concerns the dignity of our ancestors, the preservation of Black family heritage, and our rights to continue caring for our land that has sustained our family for generations," one community member said. Residents said the company buying the land is CleanSpark. In January, CleanSpark announced an agreement to acquire up to 447 acres of land in Brazoria County that was "positioning the Company to develop a large-scale data center project." In its press release, CleanSpark called itself America's Bitcoin Miner, a market-leading data center developer. ABC13 reached out to the company for more information and is awaiting a response. This comes as data centers continue to expand across Texas. ABC13's data team found that, as of February, 429 data centers were in the state. They found 293 were already operating, and the rest are planned or under construction. Brazoria County residents hope the place they call home won't join that growing list. artigo.texto: Bulgaria's grid battery capacity has doubled in a year, from 3 to about 6 gigawatts. Electricity exports this year reached 3.5 terawatt hours, 62% more than last year, according to the Association for Production, Storage and Trade of Electricity (APSTE). The figures came out on Friday, 23 October. The batteries store solar power during the day and feed it back into the grid in the evening, when demand is highest. In July and August, heatwaves strained the grids of neighbouring countries, which struggled to meet demand. Bulgarian exports helped them. How it all started: Bulgaria doubles power storage capacity as exports jump 62% On the busiest days, Bulgaria sent out up to 50,000 megawatt hours a day, said Dimitar Zarchev, head of the Central Dispatch Department at the Electricity System Operator (ESO). By his count, that is about 2,000 megawatts an hour on average, roughly what the Kozloduy nuclear plant in north-west Bulgaria produces. Some of the power went to Romania this summer. In August, Romania shut down a nuclear reactor because of drought and low water in the Danube, whose water cools the reactor's turbines. Power from batteries cut the need for hydropower plants, which usually cover the peak, so reservoirs kept their levels. The European Union gave €700m in grants for batteries in Bulgaria ($783.86m at a rate of 0.8930 euros to the dollar). Together with changes to the rules, the money also drew private investment. Battery storage is now critical, not a luxury but a necessity, said Nikola Gazdov, chairman of APSTE. Energy is costly in Europe, there are worries about supplies, and hotter summers are expected because of climate change. High prices this year fuelled anger that led to social unrest. Storing power for peak hours affects consumers' bills and softens the shocks linked to the US and Israeli war against Iran. Bulgaria has little oil and gas of its own and produces far less electricity than many other EU countries. More batteries will need a bigger grid. Fast growth has already narrowed the gap in power prices between the hour of charging and the hour of discharging. That means owners will earn less, and investors have less reason to put in money. At some point batteries may start to "eat" part of their own revenue, the Energy Ministry said in a statement. For that reason, it says, they should take part not only in trading between cheap and expensive hours, but also in balancing markets and grid services. In winter the days are shorter and solar plants produce less, so batteries will help less. Zarchev said Bulgaria will rely more on conventional plants than on stored renewable energy. Greece's solar capacity grew more than threefold between 2020 and 2025, according to data from the International Renewable Energy Agency (IRENA). Batteries there lag behind, and the evening peak is covered with imported gas. Since 2023, Athens has held three auctions for stand-alone batteries, and the first of them were installed only in April. By the end of the year, total storage in Greece will reach 1 gigawatt, government data show, a small fraction of Bulgaria's capacity. Greek officials say another 5 gigawatts will be added by 2030. In the first half of the year, Greek households paid an average of €0.1967 per kilowatt hour before taxes and charges, against €0.1117 for Bulgarian households, according to Eurostat. The Greek energy ministry said in a presentation last month that it is working to build batteries faster with EU money, to bring down power prices. Manolis Karapidakis, chief executive of the Greek association of energy storage developers, says that with 6 gigawatts of working batteries, Greece's power system would be better balanced today. Consumers would feel that too, he says. The EU has tried for years to expand batteries, because the sun and wind do not supply power all the time. Progress is slow because of long waits for permits and grid connections. Batteries are expected to spread faster, especially in Germany, Britain and Italy.

artigo.texto: In the battleground state of Pennsylvania, data centers have become a kitchen-table issue. This September, nearly two-thirds of likely Pennsylvania voters told The New York Times they either strongly or somewhat oppose the construction of data centers to support artificial intelligence. For Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro, who is seeking reelection in November, the subject has become unavoidable. After proudly announcing Amazon’s $20 billion data center investment in the Commonwealth in June 2025, the governor signed an executive order in August restricting further data center development across the state and requiring local approval for new installations. The reversal, according to his press release, was informed by “many residents who have expressed their concerns to him directly, and to many more who have shared feedback.” Neither political party has “really figured out how to respond to the challenge” of rising voter discontent over the issue, according to Matthew Levendusky, a professor of political science and communications. Levendusky expects the pressure to keep building into the 2028 presidential race. “Data center construction has become a bipartisan issue,” Parrish Bergquist, an assistant professor of political science, said. Any electoral effect, she added, might be “an anti-incumbent effect rather than a partisan effect.” “This is why you see Shapiro coming out against them, because if people are mad about these things, they will vote against whatever incumbent they view as being responsible for building them,” Bergquist added. “At the city council, town council level, I think that could have implications on both parties.” Bergquist thinks the debate over data center construction is largely driven by concerns from residents. “People don’t like the disruption associated with construction, or they don’t like noise or disruption to their sense of place,” she said in an interview. “People are like, ‘this isn’t a thing that's going to benefit us,’” Bergquist said. “Why does it need to be built here?” RELATED: Penn Democrats hosts Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro ahead of Election Day New Penn center aims to tackle AI-backed cybersecurity threats Levendusky — who is also the Stephen and Mary Baran Chair of the Institutions of Democracy division — said that media coverage of data centers and AI as a whole has generally “been framed in a way that generates a sense of grievance.” On one hand, he explained, voters are told the rise of AI will reduce the value of higher education, eliminate white-collar jobs, and might even wipe out humanity. The data centers that power that very technology, he continued, “raise utility bills, pollute, and reduce the quality of life for neighbors.” “Who benefits?” Levendusky continued. “Mostly a few large companies and their billionaire founders. So, you have highly concentrated benefits and much more broadly dispersed costs — a recipe for people to feel aggrieved.” John Quigley, a senior fellow at the Kleinman Center for Energy Policy, said that while corporations have made “promises about the economic benefits of data centers,” those claims “don’t withstand scrutiny.” While data centers create temporary jobs during construction, he said they “hardly employ anybody” once fully operational. According to Levendusky, companies need to “figure out how to structure the benefits of these centers” so that they “outweigh the costs for communities.” State Sen. Anthony Williams (D-8), whose district includes parts of Penn, said he has heard pronounced concerns from constituents regarding larger data centers. Despite that public opposition, he said the facilities did “meet a need that the public may have.” “There’s a lot of ads and literature that’s been generated about who supports a data center, who does not, what data centers would do to a community,” Williams explained. “The actual substantive portion related to policy and bills – I don’t think we’ve spent much time on that at all.” Instead, Williams said that on a statewide level, discussions of data centers and AI were more “political fodder” than substantive policymaking conversations. These concerns could be amplified by a lack of regulation, according to Quigley, who explained that, so far, the data centers proposed in Pennsylvania largely rely on diesel backup generation. “A data center could be running several hundred generators, which, even with the best available technology, are going to be releasing significant amounts of NOx and particulate matter pollution, to say nothing of carbon dioxide pollution,” Quigley said. If inhaled, NOx, or nitrogen oxides, can cause respiratory harm — and even lead to the development of asthma. Professor of Earth and Environmental Sciences Michael Mann wrote in a statement that data centers are “massive sinks of energy and water” that “produce substantial waste and pollution.” Mann, who is also the director of the Penn Center for Science, Sustainability, and the Media, said the environmental impact of data centers had previously been mitigated by using renewable energy. The Trump administration, though, has moved to have data centers run on natural gas, which Mann argued adds to “carbon emissions when we need to be rapidly decreasing them.” According to Bergquist, there has not been a concurrent push for the development of renewable energy sources to support the centers. “We have to figure out how to be able to build clean and renewable energy capacity and distribution in ways that are just and fair and not environmentally detrimental, but that don’t delay things for longer than they need to be delayed,” she explained. Despite rising calls for a pause on construction, Pennsylvania does not currently have a data center moratorium. Philadelphia already houses eight data centers, though none are the hyperscale developments needed for AI. artigo.texto: O mais recente relatório de pesquisa global do Bank of America (BofA) prevê que o gasto total com centros de dados em todo o mundo atingirá US$ 1 trilhão em 2026 e, em seguida, mais que dobrará para US$ 2,1 trilhões em 2028. O principal fator que impulsiona essa onda massiva de investimentos em infraestrutura decorre da crescente demanda e do rápido crescimento de serviços que utilizam inteligência artificial (IA). Segundo o Bank of America, o mercado de data centers deverá atingir US$ 2,93 trilhões até 2030, um aumento significativo em relação aos US$ 275 bilhões de 2022. A crescente demanda por tecnologia de inteligência artificial é vista como um fator-chave para manter uma taxa de crescimento anual composta (CAGR) de 37% entre 2025 e 2030. Essa onda de construções está contribuindo para um aumento significativo na receita de fabricantes de chips semicondutores e empresas de desenvolvimento de servidores (especialmente no mercado americano). Ao mesmo tempo, esses investimentos também estão gerando receita considerável para empresas industriais de apoio que fornecem geradores de energia de reserva, equipamentos de construção, painéis elétricos e sistemas de refrigeração especializados. Analisando detalhadamente a estrutura de custos, o BofA estima que o custo médio de construção seja atualmente de US$ 49 milhões por megawatt (MW) de capacidade de data center, com despesas diretamente relacionadas a hardware de TI representando até 78% do orçamento total. Para centros de dados dedicados à IA (também conhecidos como Neoclouds), os custos de investimento chegam a cerca de US$ 57 milhões por MW. No entanto, essas instalações têm a vantagem de economizar espaço físico em comparação com os modelos tradicionais. Na categoria de hardware, os sistemas de servidores são os itens mais caros, custando até US$ 31,4 milhões por MW de capacidade. Em segundo lugar está o sistema de conectividade de rede, com um custo aproximado de US$ 4,8 milhões. Outros equipamentos técnicos auxiliares – incluindo equipamentos de distribuição de energia, painéis elétricos, geradores de reserva e sistemas de refrigeração – custam entre US$ 100.000 e US$ 1,1 milhão por MW de capacidade.

artigo.texto: Remover obstáculos para localidades com reservas florestais elegíveis para a venda de créditos de carbono. Durante a discussão sobre o projeto de lei que altera e complementa diversos artigos da Lei de Proteção Ambiental no Grupo 4 (composto pelas delegações da Assembleia Nacional da cidade de Dong Nai e das províncias de Quang Tri e Dien Bien), os delegados propuseram que os obstáculos relacionados aos créditos de carbono sejam resolvidos em breve, criando condições para que as localidades com reservas florestais tenham acesso ao mercado de créditos de carbono. Garantir a sustentabilidade e o controle da poluição da água. Dando especial atenção à política de tratamento de águas residuais domésticas, o Deputado da Assembleia Nacional Le Hoang Hai (Cidade de Dong Nai ) elogiou bastante o fato de que, no geral, o projeto de lei trouxe mudanças positivas para sanar as deficiências na gestão de águas residuais domésticas, tais como: o controle rigoroso do lançamento de águas residuais em fontes de água degradadas (Cláusula 2, Artigo 7), proibindo que novos projetos lancem águas residuais diretamente em corpos d'água superficiais que já atingiram sua capacidade de suporte (a menos que 100% sejam reciclados ou tratados para atender aos padrões de qualidade da água superficial); e a adição de mecanismos legais claros (Artigos 72 e 72a) que permitem a reutilização de águas residuais domésticas tratadas (para irrigação de plantas, lavagem de ruas, resfriamento, etc.). Segundo os delegados, a regulamentação pressionará as cidades e os grandes projetos a investirem em tecnologias mais avançadas de tratamento de águas residuais antes de as lançarem no meio ambiente. Ao mesmo tempo, mudará a mentalidade do "tratamento de resíduos" para a "exploração dos recursos hídricos", promovendo uma economia circular para as águas residuais. Contudo, ao analisar o Artigo 40 à luz da gestão efetiva da coleta e do tratamento de águas residuais domésticas e industriais, os delegados apontaram diversas deficiências, tais como: O projeto de lei não diferencia a natureza das águas residuais domésticas das industriais. As águas residuais domésticas (provenientes de escritórios, edifícios e áreas residenciais) apresentam vazão e concentração de poluentes (DBO, DQO, amônia, etc.) que variam significativamente de acordo com o horário do dia e a estação do ano. O licenciamento baseado em "vazão máxima" e "limites fixos de parâmetros", como ocorre com as águas residuais industriais, leva a situações em que o sistema de tratamento biológico de um projeto sofre sobrecarga biológica localizada durante os horários de pico, causando infrações administrativas devido a parâmetros que excedem os padrões, mesmo que a carga total diária de poluentes não ultrapasse o limite permitido. A próxima deficiência reside na identificação da "fonte receptora de águas residuais". Na realidade, muitos empreendimentos e áreas residenciais lançam águas residuais domésticas no sistema de drenagem comum da cidade ou do polo industrial (sem uma estação de tratamento centralizada), em vez de diretamente em rios e lagos. Enquanto isso, o ponto a, inciso 2, do Artigo 40, que exige a especificação da localização e da fonte receptora final de águas superficiais nas licenças ambientais, transfere a responsabilidade pelo controle da fonte receptora (a capacidade de vazão do rio ou lago) para os proprietários de pequenos empreendimentos, quando essa responsabilidade cabe às autoridades locais pela gestão da infraestrutura geral. Com base nas deficiências mencionadas, os delegados propuseram a revisão do regulamento do Artigo 40 (conforme alterado e complementado) para distinguir claramente as normas e os métodos de concessão de licenças de descarga de águas residuais domésticas (com base na carga total/média diária) das águas residuais industriais perigosas. Ainda sobre este assunto, o deputado da Assembleia Nacional Nguyen Minh Tam ( Quang Tri ) sugeriu que a agência responsável pela redação da lei considere a inclusão de regulamentações sobre investimentos em infraestrutura de proteção ambiental para áreas de produção, comércio e serviços concentrados que ainda não concluíram a infraestrutura de tratamento de águas residuais e resíduos. Você também pode gostar Com base na situação atual dos parques industriais e zonas de produção concentrada em operação em todo o país, em geral, e em Quang Tri, em particular (Quag Tri possui atualmente 31 polos industriais estabelecidos e em funcionamento), fica evidente a desigualdade na infraestrutura de proteção ambiental entre essas zonas e polos. Algumas áreas carecem de sistemas centralizados de tratamento de efluentes, enquanto outras instalações, mesmo em uso há algum tempo, apresentam sinais de desgaste e deterioração. Enquanto aguardam a conclusão e modernização da infraestrutura, as unidades de produção ainda precisam tratar os efluentes para atender aos padrões exigidos antes de descartá-los no meio ambiente e cumprir os procedimentos ambientais necessários. Para garantir a sustentabilidade e o controle da poluição a longo prazo, especialmente à medida que a escala de produção aumenta, a infraestrutura continua a se deteriorar ou o volume total de águas residuais excede a capacidade de recepção da fonte de água, os delegados propuseram que a lei seja alterada para definir com mais clareza os requisitos para projetos existentes de produção concentrada, negócios e serviços que ainda não atendem aos padrões necessários. Especificamente, os regulamentos estipulam um prazo obrigatório para a conclusão da infraestrutura de tratamento de águas residuais em zonas e polos industriais em operação que ainda não atendem aos requisitos; eles também especificam as responsabilidades de coordenação entre os investidores em infraestrutura e as instalações de produção quando águas residuais que excedem os padrões prescritos são lançadas no meio ambiente. artigo.texto: Gasgoo Munich- Just recently, Yinwang Intelligent Technology, CATL, and Amperex Technology Service signed a strategic cooperation agreement on an intelligent replenishment ecosystem in Ningde, Fujian. Robin Zeng, chairman of CATL, and Jin Yuzhi, Huawei senior vice president and CEO of Yinwang, both attended the signing. The market sees this as a watershed moment marking the Huawei camp's official entry into the battery swapping race. For years, NIO single-handedly carried the battery swapping torch. But in 2026, the landscape began to shift. Geely partnered with NIO, CATL accelerated its station network rollout, and the Huawei camp made its debut. On October 22, BAIC Group also signed a comprehensive agreement with CATL to deepen their battery swapping cooperation. With multiple players entering the fray, battery swapping has emerged as one of the most closely watched sectors in the energy replenishment space this year. The "2026 Moment" for Battery Swapping First, a look at the latest developments. On September 28 this year, Geely Holding Group and NIO struck a strategic partnership: Geely acquired a 30% stake in NIO Power by contributing 100% of its E-E-Link equity plus 640 million yuan in cash, valuing NIO Power at roughly 16 billion yuan post-investment. In exchange, NIO bought a 10% stake in Geely's Haohan Energy with cash. The two parties will now collaborate extensively on charging and swapping technology, standards, and service networks. Image source: Geely Holding The logic behind the deal is straightforward: Geely's E-E-Link primarily serves commercial vehicles like taxis and ride-hailing cars, while NIO focuses on private passenger vehicles. Their networks are naturally complementary. At the 2026 World Intelligent Connected Vehicles Conference, Geely Holding Chairman Li Shufu put it bluntly: the development of intelligent electrification depends on building and investing in replenishment infrastructure. The core of Geely and NIO's September partnership is open sharing, unified standards, and resource coordination to give users more options. "But we can't have duplicate construction. It makes no sense for Geely to build one system and NIO another, so we merged," he said. NIO's swapping network continues to expand. In February 2026, NIO announced cumulative swapping services had surpassed 100 million. By August, the 4,000th station was completed, and the fifth-generation station officially went into operation, capable of serving NIO, Onvo, and Firefly simultaneously. NIO says it has poured more than 20 billion yuan into charging and swapping, creating a network density and replenishment experience that competitors will struggle to replicate in the short term. CATL is also accelerating its dual-track strategy with "Chocolate Swap" for passenger vehicles and "Qiji Swap" for heavy trucks: On the passenger vehicle front, over 2,500 Chocolate Swap stations have been built across 31 provinces and 200-plus cities, supporting more than 30 models. The plan calls for 4,000 integrated super-swap stations by the end of 2026, covering nearly 190 cities and a highway network spanning 12 vertical and 11 horizontal corridors. By the end of 2028, the goal is to have over 100,000 facilities in place. On the product side, CATL launched the Chocolate No. 26 battery, compatible with 800V high-voltage architectures, extending coverage from A0- to C-segment vehicles. On the network side, it introduced the "Super Swap Shared Network," with initial partners including Changan, Chery, GAC, Seres, and SAIC-GM-Wuling, aiming to push open sharing through an alliance model. For commercial vehicles, CATL plans to build 900 heavy-truck swap stations by the end of this year, 2,000 next year, with an ultimate target of 10,000. Just on October 20, its new "electric-electric range extension" swapping solution secured its first batch of orders for 13,000 units. CATL views the heavy-truck market as a "second growth curve" for swapping. Beyond building its own network, it has partnered with major commercial players like FAW Jiefang, Dongfeng Commercial Vehicle, and Sinotruk to promote standardized battery blocks and flexible leasing policies. Several swapping corridors have already been incorporated into the national zero-carbon freight corridor. Estimates suggest that for a daily transport distance of 400 kilometers, a swapping heavy truck saves about 130,000 yuan annually in replenishment costs compared to a diesel truck—a key reason why commercial vehicle adoption is outpacing passenger vehicles. The Huawei camp is accelerating its layout too. Yinwang's partnership with CATL and Amperex Technology Service focuses on an "intelligent swapping ecosystem." Image source: CATL Qiankun Intelligent Driving integrates deeply with the Chocolate Swap network, connecting the vehicle, station, and cloud at the system level. Vehicles can autonomously locate stations and align themselves, completing a fully automated swap in 99 seconds. The first batch of five swappable models is slated to launch in 2027. At the same event, Huawei Senior Vice President and Yinwang CEO Jin Yuzhi explained the logic behind the move: Qiankun Intelligent Driving had already connected to 1 million charging piles nationwide, and now it is adding swapping capabilities. "We believe this kind of ecosystem is more beneficial for automakers," he said, adding that it also enhances the user experience across different scenarios. An industry report predicts that the battery swapping market will surpass 90 billion yuan in 2026, a year-on-year increase of about 22%, with roughly 45,000 new stations added throughout the year. Battery swapping is shifting from "one man's persistence" to a "hot sector with multiple players." artigo.texto: BYD acelera no Brasil: fábrica quer dobrar produção e virar exportadora regional A fabricante chinesa de carros elétricos BYD deu início aos pedidos de licenças para dobrar a capacidade anual de produção de sua fábrica brasileira para 600.000 veículos, ao mesmo tempo em que entra na fase final de obras e testes de seus galpões de estamparia, soldagem e pintura, disse à Reuters o principal executivo da empresa no país. A unidade da BYD no Brasil deve iniciar 2027 ultrapassando o mínimo exigido de 50% de nacionalização de componentes, o que atenderá às exigências regulatórias e ajudará a empresa a iniciar as exportações regionais, afirmou o vice-presidente sênior Alexandre Baldy em entrevista. A empresa enfrentou reclamações de grupos da indústria local de que dependia muito de importações e de tarifas temporariamente baixas. “A gente trabalha para inaugurar 2027 já ultrapassando essa posição e termos essas etapas em operação para sermos considerados um fabricante local”, disse Baldy. A BYD tem como meta se tornar a maior montadora do Brasil em volume de vendas até 2030 e já vê a demanda superar sua capacidade atual de produção, disse Baldy. Embora a BYD esteja acelerando suas operações e planeje atingir uma produção mensal de 25.000 veículos até o final de 2026, a tendência é de que a demanda continue superando a oferta. “Nossa demanda tem ficado em uma média de cerca de 30.000 carros por mês, o que significa que estamos deixando de faturar cerca de 5.000 a 6.000 vendas adicionais”, disse Baldy. O investimento na nova fábrica da empresa no Brasil já ultrapassou os R$ 5,5 bilhões e as vendas faturadas da unidade brasileira atingirão esta semana a marca de 200.000 carros no acumulado de 2026, afirmou Baldy. Em setembro, a empresa teve um total de 22.209 veículos emplacados no Brasil, o equivalente a uma fatia de mercado de 8,5%, segundo dados da empresa. A BYD já é líder de mercado no Uruguai e suas vendas ocupam posições de destaque na Colômbia e na Argentina, disse o executivo. A montadora no Brasil também recebeu pedidos de 50.000 unidades do México e da Argentina cada, e estará apta a atendê-los a partir do ano que vem graças ao aumento do índice de componentes locais. A BYD inaugurou sua fábrica em Camaçari, Bahia, em 9 de outubro de 2025, em um complexo industrial que pertenceu à Ford Motor Co. A fábrica emprega atualmente cerca de 9.000 pessoas e espera expandir sua força de trabalho para cerca de 10.000 trabalhadores até o final deste ano.

artigo.texto: O Ministério de Minas e Energia (MME) mantém a suspensão do horário de verão com base na segurança energética e nos níveis elevados dos reservatórios das hidrelétricas. O titular da pasta, Alexandre Silveira (PSD), afirmou em entrevista ao programa Bom Dia, Ministro, da Empresa Brasil de Comunicação (EBC), que o planejamento do setor elétrico está concluído e dispensa o adiantamento dos relógios. Em vez de alterar a rotina da população, a estratégia federal prioriza o primeiro leilão de baterias do país, agendado para dezembro de 2026. Suspensa desde 2019 por decreto assinado pelo então presidente Jair Bolsonaro (PL), a mudança anual de fuso horário só voltaria a ser aplicada em caso de necessidade hídrica ou operacional comprovada. A pasta governamental baseia a dispensa nas projeções anuais superadas nos reservatórios e na modernização da rede para absorver fontes renováveis intermitentes. Monitoramento diário do ONS e estabilidade hídrica Os volumes armazenados nas usinas hidrelétricas superam as expectativas técnicas traçadas para o período e asseguram o fornecimento de eletricidade sem intervenções no fuso horário. O Operador Nacional do Sistema Elétrico (ONS), órgão responsável pela coordenação e controle da operação das instalações de geração e transmissão, acompanha diariamente a situação das bacias hidrográficas. Os relatórios técnicos elaborados pelos especialistas do ONS apontam estabilidade no abastecimento em todas as regiões integradas. Qualquer revisão futura sobre a necessidade de medidas adicionais de economia pelo Ministério de Minas e Energia depende diretamente dos indicadores apurados por esse acompanhamento contínuo. Regras do certame de armazenamento em dezembro de 2026 Para reforçar o Sistema Interligado Nacional (SIN), rede que conecta a produção e a transmissão de energia no território nacional, o governo federal estruturou o primeiro certame voltado à contratação de sistemas de baterias. Em 2 de junho de 2026, Alexandre Silveira anunciou a publicação da portaria com as diretrizes oficiais para o dia 3 de junho de 2026, fixando a realização da disputa para dezembro de 2026. Saiba mais: Horário de verão segue suspenso no ciclo 2026 e 2027 após análise do Ministério de Minas e Energia A iniciativa substitui a previsão anterior do ministério, formulada em outubro de 2025, que cogitava lançar o edital naquele mesmo ano. Na ocasião, Silveira havia antecipado durante o Fórum Esfera, em Belém (PA), que a demanda estimada para a contratação alcançaria 2 gigawatts (GW) de capacidade, em articulação com o Tribunal de Contas da União (TCU) e a Controladoria-Geral da União (CGU). - Capacidade de estoque dos equipamentos por até 22 horas para compensar a oscilação da geração eólica e solar. - Participação aberta a empresas nacionais e estrangeiras com tecnologias comprovadas sob regulação da Agência Nacional de Energia Elétrica (Aneel). - Exigência de conteúdo local nas regras do edital para estimular a indústria instalada no país, sem adoção de subsídios públicos. - Despacho controlado de eletricidade para evitar sobrecargas na rede nos horários de pico de consumo. Em 22 de maio de 2026, durante encontro no Guarujá (SP), o ministro explicou que a formulação do modelo exigiu rodadas de discussões técnicas internacionais antes do lançamento. “O armazenamento de energia será central para integrar renováveis, reduzir perdas e modernizar o sistema elétrico do Brasil”, declarou Silveira. Ao confirmar as diretrizes em junho de 2026, o ministro também mencionou a ex-presidente Dilma Rousseff (PT), que em 2015 defendeu o desenvolvimento de tecnologias para estocar a energia dos ventos. Veja também: Horário de verão 2026 é descartado pelo MME e pelo ONS com foco nos leilões de baterias em dezembro Mudança no perfil de consumo desde 1931 Instituído pela primeira vez em 1931, o adiantamento oficial de uma hora nos relógios tinha como objetivo aproveitar a luminosidade natural e aliviar a demanda elétrica no início da noite. Levantamentos técnicos do setor demonstraram que a alteração nos hábitos da população transferiu o pico de consumo para a faixa da tarde. A expansão do uso de aparelhos de ar-condicionado nos horários mais quentes do dia e a substituição de lâmpadas comuns por modelos de tecnologia LED reduziram os ganhos operacionais da medida. Com a confirmação do calendário regulatório da Aneel e do MME, o foco do setor elétrico permanece na execução do leilão de reserva de capacidade em dezembro de 2026.

artigo.texto: Poland calls for ETS2 to be included in emissions trading system review — RMF24 During a meeting of EU member states’ ambassadors, Poland demanded that the ETS2 system be included in the ongoing review of the rules of the European ETS1 emissions trading system. Warsaw seeks either to halt the launch of ETS2 or at least postpone it until 2030, RMF24 reports. Assessment of ETS2’s impact The Polish delegation referred to a provision agreed at the EU summit a week earlier. It obliges the European Commission to update its assessment of the consequences of ETS2 for households and the economy. Poland is seeking the swift preparation of such an assessment, but at this stage has not presented specific proposals for changing the rules. The launch of ETS2 is scheduled for 2028. According to RMF24, its introduction would mean higher prices for fuel and home heating. At the EU summit, Poland demanded that the system’s start be postponed until at least 2030, but no corresponding decision was made then. More current news is available on the UA.News Telegram channel Telegram. Support and objections Poland’s position was supported by nine other states, including Italy, the Visegrád Group countries and Greece. Some of them directly advocated postponing ETS2, while others insisted that the issue be considered in further work on revising the rules. The European Commission confirmed that it was aware of the commitment adopted at the summit and would consider the issue a priority, but did not specify a deadline for completing the assessment. At the same time, Denmark, Sweden and a number of other countries opposed extending the current ETS1 review to ETS2. They believe this could complicate negotiations and delay an agreement. By the end of October, the EU presidency is to submit the first technical draft of the ETS1 revision. After bilateral consultations in early November, a political compromise text is planned to be prepared by the end of the month, while the EU Council’s position is expected to be agreed on December 11.

artigo.texto: Aurora City Council to vote on data center moratorium following community pushback Aurora's mayor made his opinion on pausing the data center discussion clear in writing. The answer is a resounding "no," Mayor Mike Coffman said, responding to a developer's letter to the city council. Vantage said it will evaluate locating the Trident data center on sites farther from residential neighborhoods if the city council agrees to a 90-day pause on any efforts to enact new legislative requirements on development. Mayor Coffman said, "We need to move forward 'NOW' with new guidelines that protect residential areas so that we don't have another Trident situation." The co-presidents of Join Unite, a nonprofit formed just weeks ago to oppose the Trident data center, hope the third time's the charm to finally put firm rules in place around data centers. "We are cautiously hopeful that that actually is what's happening behind the scenes. But we're dealing with billionaires and huge corporations," said Makayla Llanos, one of the organization's leaders. Monday, city council will decide whether to implement a data center moratorium. That follows the city council's rejection of a six-month moratorium earlier this year, with Coffman casting the tie-breaking vote to kill it. After an uproar from the community in mid-October, the council unanimously voted to approve the first reading of an ordinance keeping data centers from being built in areas zoned "mixed-use office/ institutional" near schools, homes and assisted living facilities. City leaders will vote on an indefinite moratorium on new applications. "I hope the city does not agree to those terms, and I hope the city stands up for themselves and for us," said Tara Miller, one of the leaders of Join Unite. A new moratorium would not stop Vantage from moving forward with the Trident data center because it's already been approved. Any moratorium proposed would need seven votes to pass because the effort previously failed and likely wouldn't go into effect until February.

artigo.texto: Trending Champion and Warren township officials plan a public meeting Nov. 4 to discuss what needs to be on the books to handle a data center if one were to locate in either township. Champion Trustee Chairman Doug Emerine said to date, the Champion zoning department has not been approached by anyone about a data center. He said the township zoning board is working on guidelines and has been reviewing what Hubbard Township and other communities have done. Emerine said one property that has been discussed is the former Copperweld Steel property off state Route 45 that straddles both townships. He said the 360-acre site has one-third of the land in Champion and two-thirds in Warren Township. Emerine said of the available properties in Champion, that one would be the one to locate a data center on, and the zoning department needs to be prepared. “Right now we need to get as much information as we can on data centers. I am not sure what Warren Township officials want to do, but we need to get together and discuss this,” Emerine said. He said if a data center or any other large business were to express interest in locating in Champion, there would be public meetings to keep residents informed. “No matter what, there will be a data center located somewhere in Trumbull County,” Emerine said. Warren Township Trustee Ed Anthony said he agrees with Emerine that the Copperweld property would be the one where a data center would possibly locate. “It is prime property because of the available land and being by the river, which would provide water, but we have not received any inquiries,” Anthony said. He said the property does have many cleanup issues and there is litigation still on the property. Anthony said the township’s zoning board has been reviewing what to include in the zoning codes. Anthony said a joint meeting is being planned for 6 p.m. Nov. 4 at the Champion administration building. Also, Champion officials approved providing between $6,000 and $7,000 for the road department to do drainage upgrade work this year on Marshall Road. Emerine said the money will cover the costs for materials and supplies needed for the work. In another matter, Vanessa Teuscher found a bulletin and a service schedule from Dec. 1, 1985, when the township cemetery chapel was dedicated. She had the two items framed and they will be placed inside the chapel.

artigo.texto: A weaker ETS puts €90 billion in green investment at risk The review of the European Union's Emissions Trading System, or ETS, is now underway to bring the mechanism in line with the EU's new climate target: a 90% cut in net greenhouse emission by 2040 compared with 1990 levels. Yet that goal appears far off today. The ETS has helped decarbonize the power sector, but the EU urgently needs to drive investments in hard-to-abate sectors, where fossil fuels still dominate. Europe's carbon market is the very foundation of its climate policy. By putting a price on carbon dioxide, the cap-and-trade system gives industries a steady incentive to invest in alternative production methods, be competitive and reduce emissions. The ETS also generates large revenues that can fund climate and clean energy projects. A proven tool The carbon market cannot transform industry on its own. The right enabling conditions, whether in energy, infrastructure or markets for clean materials and products, are critical. But it is an essential industrial policy, and not a new one. For two decades, it has guided capital across many sectors. Following the price signal, companies are spending tens of billions of euros to switch to low-carbon or even net-zero processes. Where is new money going? Increasingly, into decarbonization. In 2025, large European companies put €313 billion into Taxonomy-aligned activities, and those with credible transition plans added a further €182 billion, according to the latest Report on Monitoring Capital Flows to Sustainable Investments, published by the Platform on Sustainable Finance, an advisory body to the European Commission. Clean power, green steel and net-zero cement: The future is already taking shaped. Mixed signals Despite the carbon market's positive economic and environmental impact, proposals now under negotiation threaten to derail the business models of companies that underpin Europe's long-term competitiveness and jobs. The Commission has tried to navigate pressures from industries and countries still heavily reliant on expensive and polluting fossil fuels while maintaining momentum toward the green transition. The aim is to avoid penalizing front-runners that have already invested in decarbonization. Nonetheless, the proposal includes several technical but far-reaching changes. It lowers the linear reduction factor, the annual rate at which the emissions cap shrinks. It also adds free allowances and creates a role for unproven international credits and carbon removals. On top of this, the European Parliament's draft report would weaken the market even further, potentially injecting more uncertainty into the outlook for the carbon price. A €90 billion shortfall According to a new study by Strategic Perspectives and Veyt, the Commission's proposal would blow a gigantic financial hole in Europe's climate plans. Industries covered by the ETS would spend €90 billion less on decarbonization technologies by 2040 than under current law, a drop of more than a quarter. In absolute terms, the Netherlands would be hit hardest, with its total halving to less than €20 billion. Germany would lose €15 billion and Italy €12.5 billion. The further softening proposed in Parliament's draft report could widen the gap even more. Recent reports by businesses and investors identify predictable price signals and policy coherence as key factors in their decisions. Europe will require hundreds of billions of euros a year, most of it from businesses and investors willing to commit capital at scale. In energy-intensive sectors such as steel, projects must be planned at least 10 to 15 years ahead. The jury is in: Diluting the ETS rewards high-emitting competitors and in the end punishes front-runners. A stable and robust carbon price is non-negotiable for European industrial leadership. Europe needs an agreement on an effective system that drives investment in industry. artigo.texto: Belkin introduced a 10,000mAh USB-C model at 220g and a 5,000mAh MagSafe Qi2 version, both using semi solid-state cells in premium aluminum bodies that weigh less than conventional lithium-ion packs. Belkin has released two new power banks built on semi solid-state battery technology, cutting weight without sacrificing capacity. The 10,000mAh model weighs 220 grams — roughly 20 to 80 grams lighter than comparable lithium-ion packs — while the 5,000mAh MagSafe version prioritizes thinness for direct iPhone attachment. Semi solid-state cells replace part of the liquid electrolyte with a gel-like substance, reducing the need for heavy protective casing. That translates to a denser energy package in a smaller footprint. Both units feature aluminum shells that feel cold to the touch and resist the heat buildup common in plastic-bodied competitors. The 10,000mAh unit delivers up to 60W over USB-C, enough to charge a MacBook Air at near-full speed. A small integrated display shows remaining capacity in real time. Belkin lists it at $89.95 on Amazon. The 5,000mAh MagSafe model supports 15W Qi2 wireless charging and snaps magnetically to the back of any iPhone 12 or newer. At roughly half the thickness of Apple's discontinued MagSafe Battery Pack, it slides into a pocket with the phone attached. The trade-off: no kickstand, no display, and a slight overhang on the new iPhone Duo's bottom edge. Belkin prices it at $69.99. Early hands-on impressions note the weight difference is immediately apparent when picking up either unit. The 10K model fits a jacket pocket without the usual brick sensation; the 5K model disappears against the phone. Both charge via USB-C and support pass-through, so the bank and a connected device can recharge simultaneously. Belkin says the semi solid-state chemistry also improves cycle life, targeting 1,000 full cycles before capacity drops to 80 percent — roughly double the rating of standard lithium-ion packs in this class. The company has not disclosed whether the cells come from a new supplier or an existing partner's updated line. Both power banks are shipping now through Amazon and Belkin's direct store. artigo.texto: Retiree Eileen Castle hasn't been able to enjoy her backyard since a data center moved in next door in Lowell, Massachusetts, bringing noise, fumes, dust and water mist. But a few streets away, contractor Louis Haas is grateful to Markley, the company running the facility, for redeveloping an abandoned site he says was rife with drug use. Dubbed "the Dungeon" by some locals for the imposing black silhouette it casts over a residential neighborhood of this old milling city, those opposing views encapsulate how data centers are polarizing communities across the United States. Republican-governed states, with their looser regulations, host most of the country's current AI build-out. But in liberal-leaning New England, some feel betrayed by their elected representatives, while others fear being left behind if the industry is curbed. Over the din of construction behind a spiked fence, Castle, 82, told Agence France-Presse (AFP) her great-great-grandparents bought the property. But since the data center moved into a disused pasta factory a decade ago, "We have had nothing but noise. We have dust, dirt. We have all kinds of mist" from the adjoining cooling towers, which she fears could carry Legionnaires' disease. Noxious fumes made a long interview outdoors impossible, and she lamented that her grandchildren can no longer swim in her small pool. "I think every once in a while that maybe I should sell my house," she says, but adds her property value has plummeted. "The Markley Group serves more than 600 clients in Massachusetts and connects the digital infrastructure that powers our economy, our schools, and the everyday needs of our community," Markley Group CEO Jeff Markley said in a statement to AFP. The company said its backup diesel generators run only for five-minute tests each week and, thanks to abatement efforts, produce "about 44 decibels of sound, quieter than a soft conversation three feet away." It said it tests its water twice a year for Legionnaires' disease and has planted 2,000 trees. In 2015, the city council gave Markley a 20-year property and personal property tax break estimated at $77 million, the Lowell Sun newspaper reported at the time. Enthusiasm has since cooled. In March, the council unanimously passed a 360-day moratorium on construction and expansion of commercial data centers, though Markley's 352,000-square-foot (32,700-square-meter) site was grandfathered in. Residents represented by the Conservation Law Foundation (CLF) and others have sued to challenge its expansion, which included increasing the number of generators to 27, and won a temporary injunction in August. CLF attorney Adam Reynolds told AFP that it is the "compounding effect of pollution that's really significant" in a historically industrial area. Markley has supporters. Haas, 50, who supplies coffee to a major tech company, said the boom had been good to contractors like him. "I'm a big liberal, I'm a Democrat. But I'm also pro-jobs and pro-economy," he told AFP. Markley said it employs more than 100 full-time staff in Lowell, a third of them local. On top of that, over 100 unionized trades workers work on campus. Another backer, Sarah Bibeau, a 43-year-old single mother of two who works in the defense sector, told AFP the company had been "kind and considerate," fixing roads and offering favors ranging from yard work to free Red Sox tickets. Detractors include Jake Fortes, a 44-year-old travel agent who founded the group "Honest Future for Lowell" and whose property sits on the fence line. "We're getting steamrolled by this company. So some of us have taken it to task," Fortes told AFP. Like Castle, he feels let down by Democrats, including state Gov. Maura Healey, who signed a sales tax break for data centers into law but then paused new applications this year, a reversal that illustrates the party's dilemma. Luz Marte, a 38-year-old lab technician, bought her house a year ago, without realizing the site was a data center. "It sounds very loud, like an airplane is going to take off," she told AFP as her 3-year-old son played. Her home insurer recently moved to triple her premium, which she believes is linked to Markley buying a building even closer to her property. "This is a home I bought for my son, to grow up, feel alive, and have a future," she said. "Now I'm doubting that idea."

artigo.texto: ACME Solar Holdings Limited has commissioned an additional 17.91 MW/74.323 MWh Battery Energy Storage System (BESS) component for its Firm and Dispatchable Renewable Energy (FDRE) project in Rajasthan. The new installation was commissioned on October 23, 2026, with its commercial operation date scheduled for October 25, 2026. The project is being developed through ACME Sigma Urja Private Limited, a wholly owned subsidiary of ACME Solar Holdings Limited. It is located in Village Neemri, Tehsil Rawatbhata, in the Chittorgarh district of Rajasthan. The BESS installation forms part of the project’s planned total discharge capacity of 250 MW/1,069 MWh. With this latest commissioning, ACME Solar Holdings has increased its cumulative commissioned battery energy storage capacity to 71.640 MW/297.292 MWh. The development represents further progress in implementing the energy storage component of its FDRE project. Battery energy storage systems play an important role in supporting renewable energy integration by storing electricity and making it available when required. These systems can help address the variability of solar and wind power generation by enabling electricity generated during periods of high renewable output to be used during periods of lower generation or increased demand. For FDRE projects, energy storage is particularly important because it helps developers deliver electricity according to scheduled requirements. Combining renewable energy generation with battery storage can improve the flexibility and reliability of power supply while supporting the integration of clean energy into the electricity grid. The commissioning of the additional BESS capacity brings ACME Solar Holdings closer to completing the planned storage capacity associated with the project. The company has now commissioned a cumulative 71.640 MW/297.292 MWh of battery storage capacity against the project’s total planned discharge capacity of 250 MW/1,069 MWh. The remaining capacity is expected to be commissioned in phases as project implementation progresses. The expansion of its commissioned storage portfolio reflects the company’s continued efforts to develop renewable energy projects supported by energy storage infrastructure. As India increases its renewable energy capacity, battery storage is expected to become increasingly important in managing fluctuations in generation, improving grid flexibility, and supporting the delivery of reliable electricity. artigo.texto: O secretário do Conselho Supremo de Segurança Nacional do Irã, Mohsen Rezaei, ameaçou nesta sexta-feira (23) atacar petróleo, cabos submarinos e data centers de inteligência artificial em até sete países do Golfo, caso EUA e Israel retomem a ofensiva militar contra o país. A ameaça amplia a que Rezaei fazia desde agosto, quando só prometia bloquear a exportação de petróleo pelo Estreito de Ormuz. Agora o alvo declarado inclui infraestrutura digital. Nesta sexta, o presidente dos EUA, Donald Trump, acusou o Irã de forjar ataques no Golfo para inflar o petróleo antes da eleição legislativa americana de 3 de novembro. Em caso de guerra, cabos, centros de dados e instalações de inteligência artificial também poderão ser alvos. Se o conflito voltar a eclodir, teremos um plano mais amplo. Mehdi Mohammadi, assessor do negociador iraniano Mohammad Ghalibaf, disse que Trump e Netanyahu concordaram, em princípio, com uma nova ofensiva. "Vemos o próximo conflito como uma ameaça existencial", afirmou. Segundo o Guardian, assessores militares dos EUA prepararam uma lista de alvos para a ofensiva. O que muda no preço dos combustíveis no Brasil? O Brent opera em alta nesta sexta, a US$ 114,50 por barril, maior valor em cinco meses, projetando a terceira semana seguida de ganhos. A cotação aproxima o diesel da Petrobras do teto do subsídio que hoje segura o preço na bomba. Segundo a Abicom (Associação Brasileira dos Importadores de Combustíveis), com o Brent a US$ 111 no fechamento de segunda (19), a defasagem do diesel das refinarias da Petrobras já estava em R$ 3,50 por litro ante o preço de importação. O valor fica a dois centavos do teto de R$ 3,52 que o subsídio cobre. A gasolina tinha diferença de 20%, R$ 0,43 por litro, abaixo do preço externo. Publicidade O diesel da Petrobras já quase batia o teto do subsídio antes da nova alta desta sexta, e o espaço para a estatal segurar o preço encolhe a cada dólar que o Brent sobe. Cada dólar a mais no Brent reduz o espaço da Petrobras para segurar o preço sem repassar a alta ao consumidor. A estatal encerrou em 2023 a paridade automática com o preço internacional. Mas o Goldman Sachs projeta que o diesel pode subir até 50% após o 2º turno das eleições brasileiras. O que acontece agora A lista de alvos preparada pelos assessores dos EUA só deve ser usada depois da eleição legislativa americana de 3 de novembro, segundo o Guardian. No Irã, a Guarda Revolucionária informou que quatro embarcações pegaram fogo no Golfo Pérsico. Outras três bateram em minas no Estreito de Ormuz, sem autoria assumida. No Brasil, a decisão de reajustar ou não o diesel e a gasolina é da Petrobras, que não antecipa calendário de revisão de preços.

artigo.texto: Siga o Times Brasil - Licenciado Exclusivo CNBC no Como a Bulgária se tornou uma potência europeia em armazenamento de energia? Publicado 23/10/2026 • 20:30 | Atualizado há 2 dias Lula vence eleição presidencial histórica no Brasil; Bolsonaro se recusa a reconhecer a derrota O que Democratas e Republicanos mais temem antes das eleições de meio de mandato nos EUA? Pesquisa da CNBC responde Lula e Bolsonaro mobilizam apoiadores na véspera do segundo turno das eleições presidenciais no Brasil Arábia Saudita diz ter interceptado mísseis e drones dos Houthis a caminho de Riad e outras cidades neste domingo (25) França vê protestos pressionarem mercados e investidores avaliam riscos para o déficit, o crescimento e setores expostos KEY POINTS Foto: Divulgação A Bulgária ampliou sua capacidade de armazenar eletricidade e ganhou espaço no mercado de energia da Europa. Com apoio financeiro da União Europeia e novas regras para atrair investimentos, o país dobrou sua capacidade de armazenamento em baterias no último ano e passou a aproveitar melhor a energia solar. Segundo a Reuters, em meio ao calor intenso e à alta demanda por eletricidade durante o verão europeu, o país aumentou suas exportações e ajudou países vizinhos a atender ao consumo. O resultado mostra como as baterias podem reforçar a segurança energética em uma região que busca reduzir os riscos de falta de energia. Leia também: IPCA-15 desacelera em outubro com recuo de passagens aéreas e energia elétrica; ficando abaixo das projeções De acordo com análises internacionais, a expansão contou com cerca de 700 milhões de euros (R$ 3,9 bilhões) em subsídios da União Europeia. Os recursos, junto com mudanças nas regras do setor, ajudaram a atrair empresas privadas para projetos de armazenamento de eletricidade. Segundo a associação responsável pela energia do país, a capacidade de armazenamento em baterias chegou a cerca de 6 gigawatts (GW), o dobro do nível registrado um ano antes. Esses sistemas guardam a energia solar produzida durante o dia e liberam eletricidade nos horários de maior consumo. Assim, o sistema ajuda a aproveitar melhor a geração renovável e reduz a necessidade de acionar outras fontes para atender aos picos de demanda. Siga o Times | CNBC no Google e receba as principais notícias do Brasil e do Mundo. Siga o Times | CNBC O aumento da capacidade de armazenamento contribuiu para elevar em 62% as exportações de eletricidade da Bulgária em relação ao ano anterior, chegando a 3,5 terawatts-hora (TWh). Durante alguns períodos analisados, o país chegou a exportar até 50 mil megawatts-hora (MWh) por dia. De acordo com as projeções do país, esse volume equivale a uma saída média de cerca de 2 mil megawatts de potência por hora. Leia também: França transforma antiga pedreira em usina solar com armazenamento de energia O crescimento do setor na Bulgária ajuda a mostrar como o armazenamento pode auxiliar as mudanças na produção de energia solar e eólica. Além disso, essas fontes de energia dependem das condições do tempo, e as baterias permitem guardar parte da eletricidade gerada. Entretanto, em diversos países da Europa, a expansão desses sistemas enfrenta obstáculos, como a demora para conseguir licenças e conectar novas instalações à rede elétrica.
