artigo.texto: Trump says tech companies should pay Georgians thousands to host data centers ATLANTA, Ga. (WRDW/WAGT) - President Donald Trump said local communities should have approval power over booming data center projects and receive significant financial benefits from tech companies to offset their impact. Trump said in an exclusive one-on-one interview Saturday backstage in Perry that developers have the resources to support host towns. The rapid spread of energy-intensive data centers has become a flashpoint across Georgia, sparking voter pushback over rising electric bills and straining regional power grids. Republican gubernatorial candidate Rick Jackson previously broke with Trump on the issue, insisting local city and county leaders must have veto power over where campuses are built. Trump said he agrees with Jackson on local approval, arguing the solution to neighborhood resistance is simple: tech companies need to open their checkbooks. “I agree with that. No, I agree with that. And I think locals should be paid a lot of money for data centers,” Trump said. “When a data center goes in, I’ve seen it, people are very unhappy. All of a sudden, a data center decides to pay a community in the form of taxes, in the form of whatever — and all of a sudden, the same people love what they’re doing.” Trump acknowledged the global race for artificial intelligence, noting China is aggressively building competing infrastructure. He insisted tech giants have the capital to compensate local families directly. “We have to have them because you know who likes them? China,” Trump said. “China wants data centers, and they’re building them rapidly, and we’re beating China. But the data centers, they have money. They can pay local communities a lot.” Speaking before thousands in Houston County, Trump urged Georgia communities to demand substantial cash payouts. “And as far as data centers, we don’t want to get controversial,” Trump told the crowd. “The community that they’re being built in, they’re great. They give you a lot of money and everything. Ask for a lot of money. Tell them to pay you $10,000, $15,000, $20,000 for everybody that lives in the community. They’ll do it. You just gotta ask.” Trump cited an example in Louisiana where he claimed developer payouts flipped neighborhood opposition into support. “I saw one case in Louisiana where they were really fighting ... and then the company, I think it was Meta, they agreed to pay everybody $10,000,” Trump said. “And they went from, ‘we will not have it,’ to ‘do you have any more you want to bring?’ I’m telling you, just pay. Pay the people. Give them the money. They have so much money.” Trump then turned to Jackson on stage to address their policy alignment. “Do you agree with that, Rick? They’ll be very happy,” Trump said as Jackson looked on. “Rick’s a little bit tentative on that one. But no, they’ll be very happy.” The rally also served as the backdrop for major economic news. Backstage, Trump revealed to Atlanta News First that Audi plans to build its first U.S. manufacturing facility roughly 20 minutes from Perry. Gov. Brian Kemp later confirmed the German automaker will invest $4 billion in the Middle Georgia Megasite in Peach County, creating an estimated 4,500 jobs. U.S. Rep. Mike Collins, R-Ga., who is running for U.S. Senate, added that federal funding will ensure the Port of Brunswick is fully dredged to handle automotive exports from the new plant. Trump also addressed the U.S. Department of Justice’s notification that it is sending federal election monitors to six Democratic-majority Georgia counties, including Fulton, DeKalb and Gwinnett. Facing criticism from local election boards that the federal presence could intimidate voters, Trump defended the deployment. “They want to watch. You know, in Fulton County, you know that disaster,” Trump said. “They’re not going to do anything other than watch ... we want to all have honest elections.” On stage, Trump repeatedly targeted Democratic opponents, calling U.S. Sen. Jon Ossoff a “radical-left extremist” and criticizing former Atlanta Mayor Keisha Lance Bottoms over crime rates. Jackson echoed the sentiment, telling voters that “bad mayors don’t make good governors.” Trump suggested that if Jackson and Collins win, he would respond to calls to send the National Guard into Atlanta, which he labeled a “dangerous hellhole.” The Perry stop marked Trump’s second Georgia rally in recent weeks, aimed at energizing rural voters as early voting continues across the state. artigo.texto: ENNA Solar, part of ENNA Group, has signed an agreement to acquire the Medgidia project, located in Constanța County, in Romania. The Medgidia project comprises 166 MWp solar plant with a 612 MWh battery energy storage system. The acquisition involves ENNA Solar acquiring a 100 per cent equity stake in CIC GREEN ENERGY MEDGIDIA S.R.L., holding the rights to develop the project. Furthermore, the project will be developed on approximately 204 hectares of land. Construction is scheduled to begin in the first quarter of 2027, while commercial operations are expected to start in the first quarter of 2028. Additionally, the project is expected to generate 265,932 MWh of electricity annually. The completion of the acquisition is subject to approval from the relevant Romanian foreign direct investment screening authority and competition authorities in the applicable jurisdictions. The Medgidia project will add to ENNA Group’s existing investments in Romania, including the 87.52 MWp Mihăilești solar project, which is under advanced construction.

artigo.texto: As rack densities climb toward 1 MW and beyond, traditional low-voltage alternating current (AC) architecture is being pushed into territory it wasn't originally designed to handle. A primary reason the industry is increasingly looking toward 800 VDC to support the next generation of high-density compute. But the bigger question isn't whether direct current (DC) can power these new racks. It's where the conversion to DC should happen and how much of the traditional power architecture is still necessary. Sidecars offer a bridge to 800 VDC One near-term answer is the sidecar, a power-conversion unit positioned next to the compute rack. Sidecars give operators a practical way to introduce 800 VDC racks into facilities built around existing low-voltage AC distribution. Rather than redesigning the facility, operators can convert AC power to DC beside the rack. That makes sidecars an important bridge between today's infrastructure and emerging DC compute. But much of the existing electrical architecture remains in place. Power still moves through transformers and low-voltage UPS infrastructure before another conversion takes place near the rack. Each stage introduces losses and nearly all of that lost energy ultimately turns into heat, putting more pressure on the cooling system to remove it. SMA's white paper models the difference. In the architecture studied, delivering 1 MW through a traditional AC system with rack-level conversion results in approximately 80 kW of power loss per megawatt delivered to the rack. Converting medium-voltage AC to 800 VDC outside the building and distributing DC directly reduces that loss to approximately 20 kW. At data center scale, the difference becomes more than significant. Moving power infrastructure outside Efficiency is only part of the equation. Data center operators are also under pressure to maximize one of their most valuable resources: white space. A native DC architecture takes a different approach. Instead of generating 800 VDC beside the rack, conversion from medium-voltage AC to DC happens once, outside the data center building. Native 800 VDC is then distributed throughout the facility. Much of the supporting electrical infrastructure can move outside as well, including power-conversion equipment, switchgear and energy storage. Inside, the architecture becomes more simplified: compute, cooling and DC busway. There are fewer conversion stages, fewer pieces of electrical equipment and more room for compute. Rethinking redundancy and energy storage Any new data center architecture still must meet demanding resilience requirements. DC creates new options. A rack can be supplied by two independent DC paths, each capable of carrying the full load. During normal operation, both can remain active and share the load. Unlike AC sources, DC sources don't have phases that must be synchronized. With the appropriate protection architecture, both sources can continuously supply the rack, potentially eliminating the need for a traditional transfer event. Sharing the load between two paths also reduces current on each path, helping lower electrical losses without sacrificing redundancy. Moving energy storage outside the building can expand its role. Instead of primarily waiting to provide backup power, storage integrated into an external DC power system can help smooth large power swings from AI workloads, provide ride-through during grid disturbances and control how quickly a facility returns to full power following an event. Depending on the system and market, storage could also support other grid services. Designing power around compute Sidecars have an important role as data centers begin adopting 800 VDC. They provide a practical way to deploy new compute infrastructure without rebuilding existing electrical systems. But the longer-term opportunity is bigger than changing the voltage delivered to the rack. Moving conversion outside the building and distributing native DC can reduce conversion stages and electrical losses, free up valuable space for compute, simplify redundancy and give energy storage a more active role. For an industry racing to add enormous amounts of computing capacity, those aren't incremental changes. They represent an opportunity to rethink data center power architecture from the grid to the rack.

artigo.texto: Srinagar, Oct 23 (KNS): Solar energy, battery technology and improved integration of renewable energy into existing electricity networks emerged as key areas of discussion at an international conference on sustainable energy and power systems that began at the National Institute of Technology (NIT) Srinagar on Friday. The three-day IEEE 2nd International Conference on Sustainable Technology for Energy and Power Systems (STEPS 2026), organised by the Department of Electrical Engineering, has brought together researchers, academicians and power-sector professionals to examine technological developments and challenges facing the energy sector. Speaking at the inaugural session, Prof Roohie Naaz Mir, Dean Research and Consultancy, NIT Srinagar, highlighted the growing importance of solar energy and battery technology in reducing dependence on conventional energy sources and strengthening sustainable power systems. Prof Bhim Singh, who delivered the keynote address, discussed the role of power electronics in integrating renewable energy into electricity networks. He explained how advances in power electronic technologies are changing the way renewable energy is generated, managed and utilised.Click Here To Follow Our WhatsApp Channel Officials from the Jammu and Kashmir Power Development Department (JKPDD), including Secretary Technical Shurjeel Ghani Lalla and KPTCL Chief Engineer Aaquib Waheed Deva, discussed developments in the power sector, particularly solar energy schemes and their implications for Jammu and Kashmir. Their interaction with students and researchers also focused on connecting academic research with practical requirements of the electricity sector. NIT Srinagar Director Prof Anurag Misra stressed the need for technological innovation and research to develop reliable and sustainable energy systems. Conference Chair Prof Shameem Ahmad Lone and Head of Electrical Engineering Department Prof Mairaj ud Din Mufti also highlighted the importance of research collaboration in addressing emerging energy challenges. The conference, themed "A Step Towards Green, Clean and Reliable Energy", will continue until October 25, with technical sessions and research presentations on renewable energy integration, power electronics and modern electricity systems. (KNS)

artigo.texto: O Banco Nacional de Desenvolvimento Econômico e Social (BNDES) credenciou o primeiro sistema de armazenamento de energia em baterias (SAE) que atende às exigências de conteúdo local do leilão de reserva de capacidade (LRCap) previsto para 2 de dezembro. A solução é da brasileira You.On, primeira empresa a concluir o processo de análise de um equipamento completo e obter o código Finame para o certame. O equipamento aprovado é o You.On MOD A 7MW, com potência de 7 MW e capacidade de armazenamento de 25 megawatts-hora (MWh). Segundo a descrição apresentada ao BNDES, a solução utiliza baterias de fosfato de ferro-lítio (LFP), conversores de potência e sistema de gerenciamento de energia (EMS), além de contar com tecnologia grid-forming, exigida para os equipamentos do leilão. O credenciamento é feito pelo Sistema de Credenciamento de Fornecedores Informatizado (CFI), plataforma do BNDES utilizada para cadastrar fornecedores e produtos submetidos às regras do Finame. O banco analisa separadamente a empresa e o equipamento: primeiro verifica se a companhia atende aos requisitos para atuar como fabricante ou empresa de engenharia e, depois, se o sistema cumpre as regras de nacionalização. Para o leilão com conteúdo local, o BNDES estabeleceu um índice mínimo inicial de nacionalização de 15%, que considera o valor agregado de componentes nacionais, mão de obra e serviços de engenharia e integração realizados no Brasil. O código Finame comprova que o sistema foi credenciado, mas não equivale à habilitação de um empreendimento para participar do leilão, que cabe à Empresa de Pesquisa Energética (EPE) aprovar ou não, e considera outros critérios, incluindo potência mínima de 30 MW e capacidade de operação durante quatro horas consecutivas. A comprovação do BNDES será obrigatória para os vencedores do primeiro leilão, mesmo que utilizem recursos próprios ou financiamento de outros bancos. Pelo cronograma divulgado, os empreendedores terão até 7 de maio de 2027 para apresentar o certificado de conformidade de credenciamento, exigido para a contratação. No início de outubro, a You.On anunciou um acordo vinculante com a chinesa HyperStrong para atuar conjuntamente nos leilões de baterias previstos para 2 e 4 de dezembro. Na ocasião, a empresa informou que já havia sido credenciada como fornecedora pelo BNDES e avançava no processo para obter o código CFI de seus equipamentos. A parceria reúne a tecnologia de armazenamento da HyperStrong e a atuação da You.On em engenharia, integração de sistemas, conteúdo local e prestação de serviços no Brasil. Financiamento pelo Fundo Clima Mesmo com o credenciamento, um eventual financiamento do investimento pelo BNDES, por meio de recursos do Fundo Clima, dependerá de comprovações adicionais sobre o cumprimento das regras de conteúdo local. O banco de fomento prevê financiamento para sistemas de armazenamento, packs de baterias, inversores e sistemas de gerenciamento de energia. A participação do BNDES pode chegar a 100% dos itens financiáveis para operações enquadradas nas rotas 2, 3 ou 4 do regulamento de credenciamento, que preveem diferentes níveis de nacionalização das próprias baterias. Para a rota 1, que permite cumprir as exigências de conteúdo local com outros componentes do sistema, como inversores e equipamentos de controle, o limite é de 80%, com complementação por outra operação de crédito. Nas operações diretas com empresas privadas, o custo financeiro do Fundo Clima é de 6,5% ao ano, acrescido da remuneração do BNDES, a partir de 1,3% ao ano. O financiamento tem prazo de até 16 anos, incluindo carência de até seis anos. O valor mínimo é de R$ 20 milhões, com limite de R$ 1 bilhão por grupo econômico a cada período de 12 meses. Em setembro, o BNDES estimou que o financiamento dos projetos dos leilões de baterias poderia demandar até R$ 34 bilhões em recursos de linhas incentivadas, volume ainda condicionado à definição do orçamento de 2027. O Fundo Clima é a principal fonte de crédito incentivado para os empreendimentos, em conjunto com o BNDES Mais Inovação, mas os investidores vão precisar combinar diferentes fontes de financiamento. Lista de fornecedoras cresce Além do primeiro sistema completo credenciado, a lista de fornecedoras reconhecidas pelo BNDES aumentou de sete para nove empresas desde setembro. As novas integrantes são a Canadian, classificada pelo banco como empresa de engenharia, e a SecPower, cadastrada como fabricante. Elas se juntam a BYD, Gotion, Moura, TBEA, Trina, WEG e You.On. O credenciamento como fornecedor é a primeira etapa do processo e permite que a empresa apresente seus equipamentos à análise do BNDES. Segundo o banco, essa fase representa aproximadamente 15% do percurso necessário para a obtenção do código Finame de um sistema completo. Para as empresas de engenharia, como You.On, Canadian, Gotion e TBEA, o BNDES exige a participação de um parceiro com capacidade industrial para comprovar o atendimento aos requisitos de fabricação. Outra atualização é a inclusão da Reivax na relação de empresas que tiveram validado pelo BNDES o desenvolvimento de software e firmware de sistemas de gerenciamento de energia (EMS). A companhia se junta à Moura e à Automa, que já constavam da lista em setembro. O EMS funciona como o centro de comando do sistema de armazenamento, coordenando quando as baterias devem carregar ou descarregar, em qual potência e como a operação será executada pelos demais equipamentos. O BNDES separa duas partes do EMS: o hardware, que corresponde aos equipamentos físicos de controle, e o desenvolvimento do software e do firmware, programa instalado nos controladores para executar as funções necessárias à operação.

artigo.texto: O diretor de Finanças e Relações com Investidores da Weg, Andre Salgueiro, disse, durante a teleconferência de resultados do terceiro trimestre deste ano, que a companhia estima o início da produção da fábrica de sistemas de armazenamento de energia (BESS, na sigla em inglês) para o segundo semestre do próximo ano. Entrando em operação neste período, a unidade poderá atender os projetos que devem ser contratados no primeiro leilão de baterias na modalidade reserva de capacidade de potência que será realizado em dezembro. Segundo ele, a companhia vê o leilão como o impulsionador do mercado e por isso, aumentou os investimentos na unidade e elevou a estimativa de capacidade instalada de 2 gigaswatt/hora (GWh) para 4GWh. A companhia vai aplicar R$ 330 milhões na nova unidade produtiva. “A decisão de construção da nova fábrica é pensando nas oportunidades nesse negócio no Brasil”, disse o executivo. “Olhando o médio e o longo prazos, acreditamos muito que esse é um negócio muito importante para trazer uma estabilização, uma equalização dos problemas que vemos no grid atualmente.” Já o vice-presidente Administrativo Financeiro da Weg, André Rodrigues, disse que a companhia vem aumentando o volume de investimentos a cada ano, mas ainda entrega um Retorno sobre o Capital Investido (ROIC) saudável. No terceiro trimestre, de acordo com o balanço da companhia, o indicador 33,2%, 0,8 pontos porcentuais acima do apurado no mesmo período de 2025. Segundo o executivo, no entanto, não há no mercado um novo negócio que demandará um investimento significativo. “Temos encontrado excelentes oportunidades em nossos produtos maduros. Temos investido para aumentar em alguns casos o nosso portfólio”, disse Rodrigues. “Aumentamos a capacidade de transformadores, e também na complementação do portfólio. Então, a companhia não vê um valor de investimento significativo para novos negócios.”

artigo.texto: Manejo adequado recupera pastagens e amplia estoque de carbono Experimentos de longa duração no interior paulista mostram que a intensificação moderada do pasto recupera a produtividade da terra e maximiza o sequestro de CO₂ Transformar pastos degradados em áreas férteis é um caminho prático para unir a produção pecuária à sustentabilidade ambiental. Experimentos de longa duração realizados no interior paulista revelam que ajustes simples no cuidado com o solo e na quantidade de animais não só recuperam a produtividade da terra, mas a convertem em um eficiente reservatório de carbono. Além de beneficiar o produtor, essa linha de pesquisa desenvolveu métodos mais simples e baratos para medir o carbono retido no solo, facilitando o futuro acesso de fazendeiros ao mercado de créditos de carbono. Os estudos fazem parte do Projeto Temático “Entendendo sistemas intensificados e integrados de produção: do mundo quântico à agricultura de baixa emissão de carbono”, apoiado pela Fapesp por meio do Programa Fapesp de Pesquisa sobre Mudanças Climáticas Globais, e coordenado pelo físico Ladislau Martin Neto, pesquisador da Embrapa Instrumentação, unidade de pesquisa da Empresa Brasileira de Pesquisa Agropecuária focada em unir a física, a química, a ciência dos materiais e as engenharias ao setor agropecuário. Para entender o impacto prático do manejo na retenção de carbono no solo, os pesquisadores compararam diferentes cenários de produção. As áreas avaliadas variaram desde pastagens degradadas –caracterizadas pela ausência de adubação e pelo pastejo contínuo do gado– até sistemas com diferentes níveis de tecnologia e intervenção. Esses modelos recuperados incluíram a chamada “intensificação moderada”, que combina a correção da acidez do solo, uso de fertilizantes e uma quantidade equilibrada de animais no pasto, e sistemas de alta intensificação, submetidos a irrigação artificial, doses elevadas de nitrogênio e uma grande densidade de gado. “Em uma das áreas estudadas, caracterizada como de moderada intensificação, o estoque de carbono no 1º metro do solo [a partir da superfície] aumentou de 102 para 162 toneladas por hectare entre 2011 e 2020 –um acréscimo médio de aproximadamente duas toneladas de carbono por hectare ao ano [em relação ao estoque da pastagem degradada]. Análises permitiram demonstrar que parte importante desse carbono adicional veio da própria forrageira [capim destinado à alimentação animal] cultivada na pastagem”, conta Martin Neto. A pesquisadora Patrícia Perondi Anchão Oliveira, que lidera o experimento, explica que o modelo vencedor em acúmulo de carbono (com doses moderadas de adubo e lotação equilibrada) não exige tecnologias inacessíveis. Pelo contrário, ele comprova a eficiência de uma fórmula familiar ao produtor brasileiro: a união de capins adaptados ao nosso clima com o gado de origem indiana, como o nelore. “Esse já é um caso de sucesso na pecuária brasileira, um sistema amplamente adotado pelos pecuaristas”, comenta a pesquisadora, ressaltando o potencial ambiental dessa base produtiva quando aliada ao manejo correto do solo. O objetivo dos pesquisadores foi descobrir não apenas quanto carbono havia sido acumulado no solo, mas como ele estava armazenado. Depois de mais de duas décadas de manejo, a pastagem apresentou 148 toneladas de carbono por hectare na forma de matéria orgânica associada aos minerais do solo, contra 92 toneladas na pastagem degradada. O resultado mostra o grande potencial de recuperação de áreas já convertidas para a pecuária. A relevância do achado está justamente em mostrar que é possível recuperar a qualidade de solos já degradados e aumentar sua capacidade de armazenar carbono sem que isso implique avançar sobre áreas de vegetação nativa. O título do projeto reúne duas vertentes que parecem, à 1ª vista, muito distantes. De um lado está o “mundo quântico”, no qual técnicas derivadas da física permitem investigar átomos, moléculas e interações entre a matéria orgânica e os minerais. Do outro, estão as extensas áreas de pastagens e o desafio de produzir com maior eficiência e menor emissão de gases de efeito estufa. É justamente a ligação entre essas escalas que orienta uma parte importante do projeto. “Trata-se de usar técnicas avançadas, como espectroscopias e outras, para pensar em uma situação real que beneficie simultaneamente o sistema produtivo e o planeta e motive a adoção pelo produtor”, diz Martin Neto. Segundo o pesquisador, os resultados –publicados na revista científica Geoderma– oferecem a perspectiva de remunerar produtores rurais pelo carbono adicional armazenado no solo de pastagens bem manejadas, por meio da geração e venda de créditos de carbono. Para isso, porém, é preciso demonstrar de forma confiável quanto carbono foi efetivamente incorporado ao solo e permanece ali. Onde o carbono se esconde Como explica Martin Neto, o solo é um ambiente extraordinariamente complexo. A matéria orgânica representa só uma pequena fração de sua massa, distribuída de forma extremamente heterogênea. “Saber que o teor de carbono aumentou, portanto, não responde a uma questão central para a mitigação climática. Esse carbono permanecerá ali por longo tempo ou será logo emitido para a atmosfera na forma de CO2?”, questiona o pesquisador. É preciso levar em conta que a matéria orgânica do solo se encontra em diferentes estágios de decomposição. Uma parte pode ser rapidamente metabolizada pelos microrganismos e devolver o carbono à atmosfera. Outra pode estabelecer interações com partículas minerais, especialmente argilas e óxidos de ferro e alumínio. Formam-se então associações organominerais que dificultam a decomposição e favorecem uma permanência mais longa do carbono no solo. “Hoje, sabemos pela ciência que um dos mecanismos mais importantes é justamente a associação da matéria orgânica com o componente mineral. Por meio de ligações e interações químicas, esse carbono pode ser retido por longo tempo. É isso que estamos procurando demonstrar”

artigo.texto: CCC chairs carbon markets panel The CCC’s chairmanship of the IACCM builds on its existing leadership functions in national climate policy and reporting. The Climate Change Commission (CCC) welcomes its designation as chair of the Inter-Agency Committee on Carbon Markets (IACCM) under Executive Order (EO) 127, which establishes a governance framework for the Philippines’ participation in international carbon markets under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement and in the Voluntary Carbon Market. Signed by President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr., EO 127 institutionalizes the country’s climate change mitigation efforts and seeks to unlock international climate finance. As IACCM chair, the CCC will guide inter-agency coordination and help ensure that carbon market policies support the Philippines’ Nationally Determined Contribution (NDC), national greenhouse gas inventory, and climate transparency reporting obligations under the Paris Agreement. The Commission will also serve as the committee’s Secretariat and provide technical and administrative support. This move supports the direction set by the Philippine Development Plan 20230-2028, particularly Chapter 15 on accelerating climate action and strengthening disaster resilience. The chapter calls for stronger collaboration with the private sector and the international community to scale up sustainable and green investments. It also advances the transition to a low-carbon economy while promoting economic growth and resilience. “Carbon markets can help advance these goals by providing an additional channel for private capital and international climate finance. Credible carbon projects can support emissions reduction and other climate solutions. Clear rules and reliable accounting will help protect environmental integrity and give investors greater certainty,” said CCC vice chairperson and executive director Robert E.A. Borje. The CCC’s chairmanship builds on its existing leadership functions in national climate policy and reporting. As Secretariat of the NDC Technical Working Group, the Commission supports the assessment of sectoral policies and measures against the country’s NDC. It also supports the monitoring, reporting, and verification of NDC implementation and the fulfillment of national and international reporting requirements. Under Executive Order 174, s. 2014, the CCC serves as the overall lead agency for the Philippine National Greenhouse Gas Inventory. It coordinates and consolidates emissions data from sector lead agencies. This information provides an important evidence base for national climate policy and emissions accounting.

artigo.texto: How data centers became a bipartisan political issue in Wisconsin Data centers are a big issue across the country. As midterms approach, many look to the swing state of Wisconsin for lessons for how that issue could play out nationally. SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST: In the center of the world... (CHEERING) PFEIFFER: ...That's where all sorts of Wisconsinites told me we were yesterday as they watched the Brewers win game one of the World Series. One of those people was Kristi Draver (ph). KRISTI DRAVER: Everybody knows it. Driving around Milwaukee, driving in from out of Milwaukee - everybody knows this is it, the center of the world, right here in Milwaukee. PFEIFFER: And I'm in Milwaukee today, hosting this program from NPR member station WUWM. Wisconsin, along with its Brewers fame, is known for its pivotal role in U.S. politics because of its rust belt geography and its urban rural divides. The midterms are 10 days from now, and Wisconsin is front and center on a contentious national issue, data centers. Many voters on the left and right dislike them, and midterm candidates are having to adapt. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) TOM TIFFANY: I have been consistent over the last year that we are not going to pay those subsidies to these companies. He just came around in the last week when he figured out, that's where the public is. I will not put my finger to the wind when making decisions like... PFEIFFER: That was the Republican contender for Wisconsin governor Tom Tiffany in this week's gubernatorial debate here. Just last week, the city of Milwaukee enacted a one-year moratorium on new data center construction. WUWM's Eddie Morales has been covering this, and he's with me in his station's studios right here in Milwaukee. Hi, Eddie. EDDIE MORALES, BYLINE: Hi, Sacha. PFEIFFER: What prompted this moratorium? MORALES: So there was a proposal to turn a vacant Walmart into a data center, and local community organizers - they rallied to stop that developer. Then residents mobilized in favor of a moratorium, with dozens coming to speak at city meetings. It's just one of several cities in Wisconsin to actually pause new data center construction. There are more than 50 different kinds of data centers already in Wisconsin, and the businesses who want to develop more say their projects will help stimulate the economy. PFEIFFER: This is definitely not the first time there's been backlash in Wisconsin to big tech companies coming in. Some of our listeners might remember the name Foxconn. Tell us about that history. MORALES: Yeah, so part of the reason why the anti-tech sentiment has been so quick and so strong here is because of that Foxconn deal. It was during President Trump's first term when he championed a massive project by the tech manufacturer Foxconn. The deal was supposed to bring more than 10,000 jobs to Wisconsin, and the state offered this substantial incentives package. But the company then dramatically shifted their plans. There was this public outcry, and it became a political mess for the governor's office, and it created this legacy of mistrust for Big Tech in Wisconsin. PFEIFFER: And, Eddie, as you know, the data center issue has even reached the governor's race. I've heard this week this ad with one candidate calling the other Data Center Dave - not a compliment. What's going on there? MORALES: Democrat David Crowley and Republican Tom Tiffany have accused each other of being too supportive of the data center industry, as we heard in that clip in your intro. Now, both candidates are trying to position each other as flip-floppers. PFEIFFER: There are different kinds of data centers. The new ones are the big hyper-scale ones people are concerned about, but I understand you've been on a tour of a different, more traditional one. What did you see? MORALES: Right, it was Potawatomi's Data Holdings. So that's on land that's owned by the Potawatomi tribe. And the building is really interesting. It has this design of a brick facade and fake windows that match the neighborhood's aesthetic. It's a 46,000-square-foot data center. It's small compared to the much bigger sites that are being built around the country for AI processing and that have been a little bit more in the public eye. The manager, Ryan Brooks - he took me on a tour, and while we were there, he told me that he's actually for the moratorium. PFEIFFER: The manager? - the management told you they're for the moratorium. MORALES: Mm-hmm. Well, he strongly supports data center regulations because he doesn't want more of the huge - what they call - hyperscale AI data centers versus his smaller data center, which has been operating for years. He's kind of worried about his business. RYAN BROOKS: The number of these large hyperscalers that are coming into town, the amount of power that they require - or coming into the state, even - the amount of power that they require is more than is planned by all the energy providers in your state. So someone's not going to make it. MORALES: So he thinks some of the other companies building the huge new sites don't have the community in mind, and he says his company is built on tribal land, so it's there to stay. But of course, his company does have its own incentives to take a position in this moment. PFEIFFER: Eddie, for communities who have been going through this, what have they learned? Any lessons here? MORALES: Well, Milwaukee, like in many places - it doesn't have the regulatory structures and the zoning laws in place to really manage the goals of huge new - of these huge companies who really want things done fast. And data centers, they can provide a lot of jobs, mostly construction jobs needed to build them, but then often it's just a very small number of jobs to maintain them. So different communities can offer a range of incentives to keep generating revenue like property taxes. But these centers can also create a lot of strain on a municipality's resources, and the public has been worried

artigo.texto: India’s efforts to strengthen its electric vehicle (EV) industry will require progress in battery manufacturing, critical mineral supplies, energy storage and advanced manufacturing, alongside the expansion of vehicle assembly. These priorities were highlighted during discussions at the Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo and The Battery Show India (TBSI) 2026 on October 23, Auto India Daily reported. Industry leaders explored opportunities to combine India’s manufacturing capabilities with international technology expertise and access to mineral resources. Stronger battery supply chains are increasingly important for EV production, technology development and the long-term competitiveness of the automotive sector. Australia’s mineral resources offer scope for cooperation Australia highlighted battery manufacturing and electric mobility as key areas for cooperation with India. Philip Green, Australia’s High Commissioner to India, said the two countries could combine Australia’s engineering expertise and mineral resources with India’s manufacturing strengths and integration into global supply chains. Green said Australia accounts for more than 50% of global lithium production and holds the world’s second-largest cobalt reserves. He also highlighted the country’s strong position in global rare earth resources. Lithium, cobalt and rare earth materials have applications across battery technologies and the wider clean energy sector. Cooperation between Australia’s resource base and India’s manufacturing ecosystem could create opportunities to develop battery-related supply chains. Twenty Australian companies and 32 exhibitors participated in the expo, showcasing technologies related to energy storage, grid infrastructure, green hydrogen and renewable energy integration. However, access to mineral resources alone does not guarantee lower battery costs or more affordable electric vehicles. The benefits will depend on the development of partnerships, processing capabilities, investment and effective commercial execution. India-Germany cooperation focuses on battery research India-Germany technology cooperation also featured in the discussions, with Anandi Iyer, director of the Fraunhofer Office in India, highlighting opportunities in battery research, power electronics, advanced engineering and industrial automation. Iyer cited global renewable energy and battery storage deployment figures, stating that renewable energy capacity additions worldwide would reach approximately 800 GW in 2025, while battery storage deployment would reach 108 GW, representing a 40% increase from the previous year. The growth of renewable energy and battery storage highlights the expanding role of technologies that are relevant to both electric mobility and energy systems. Battery research, power electronics and advanced engineering can support the development of these interconnected sectors. Iyer also emphasised that technological self-reliance can be pursued alongside international cooperation. Trusted partnerships and resilient supply chains can help translate research into commercially viable solutions. For India, the challenge will be to use international expertise while strengthening domestic manufacturing and technology development. Such cooperation could support future automotive innovation and improve supply chain resilience. Domestic manufacturing remains a key priority India is seeking to expand its domestic EV manufacturing capabilities, but access to raw materials, technology development and investment in manufacturing infrastructure remain important challenges. Discussions at the REI Expo and TBSI highlighted the potential role of international partnerships in strengthening India’s clean energy and EV supply chains. However, no new investments or agreements with individual EV manufacturers were announced at the event. The long-term impact on the automotive sector will depend on how effectively India converts access to mineral resources and international technological expertise into stronger domestic battery manufacturing, processing and research capabilities.

artigo.texto: Researchers have synthesized strontium divanadate (SrV2O6) nanoparticles through a sol–gel method and reported that the material performs well in two demanding roles at once: storing electrical charge in supercapacitors and breaking down organic dye pollutants under light irradiation. The study, published in the journal Ionics, describes a pure crystalline structure with a uniform elemental distribution across the nanoparticles, a combination the authors identify as the foundation for the material's dual functionality. According to the study, the sol–gel preparation yielded nanoparticles with this uniform elemental distribution, giving the team a well-defined material to test in both electrochemical and photocatalytic measurements. On the energy storage side, the nanoparticles delivered high specific capacitance together with good rate capability, meaning the material retained its charge-storage performance as the operating conditions became more demanding. The authors characterize the overall energy and power densities as moderate, positioning the compound as a candidate rather than a finished electrode material. Two headline figures stand out from the electrochemical testing. The measured energy density reached a maximum of 3.14 Wh/kg, while the power density reached 1046 W/kg. The authors highlight the power figure in particular as evidence of the material's potential for high-power energy storage devices. The optical and electronic properties underpin the second application. SrV2O6 exhibited a band gap of 2.16 eV, which the study links to good light absorption and semiconducting behaviour. When illuminated, the material generated reactive oxygen species efficiently, and these reactive species, combined with favourable surface interactions, drove the photocatalytic degradation of two common organic dyes. Efficient charge separation within the semiconductor is cited as the mechanism that keeps the reactive species production going. The degradation results were substantial in the laboratory tests. The nanoparticles degraded 90 percent of methylene blue and 94 percent of brilliant green under light irradiation, performance the authors attribute to the reactive oxygen species generation and the favourable surface interactions between the dye molecules and the nanoparticle surfaces. The findings are measured observations from a laboratory study of the synthesized nanoparticles, not demonstrations in operating devices or field-scale water treatment. The abstract itself flags two practical limitations: relatively poor electrical conductivity and particle agglomeration. To push the electrochemical performance further, the authors point to controlling the particle morphology and minimizing agglomeration as promising strategies. Within the scope of the reported results, SrV2O6 emerges as a promising multifunctional material for both energy storage and environmental remediation applications, with the caveat that overcoming its conductivity and aggregation limits will determine whether that promise survives outside the synthesis laboratory. artigo.texto: Missouri PSC approves Ameren Missouri battery storage, solar projects The Missouri Public Service Commission (PSC) on Oct. 21 approved Ameren Missouri’s plans to build three battery energy storage facilities, acquire two solar developments, and construct a new switching station to connect a battery storage project to the transmission system. The projects are intended to support electric grid reliability and provide energy during periods of high demand, including extreme heat and cold. The PSC’s approval includes an agreement among Ameren Missouri, PSC Staff, and Renew Missouri. The Office of the Public Counsel (OPC), which represents the public in cases before the commission, was not a signatory but did not object to the agreement. “Deploying these projects now helps prepare the grid for how our customers will use energy in the years ahead,” said Ajay Arora, executive vice president and chief growth and generation development officer for Ameren Missouri. “Battery storage can respond within moments to changing grid conditions and provide additional energy when demand is highest.” The approved projects include three battery energy storage systems (BESS): - Castle Bluff: A 95-megawatt (MW) battery storage facility in St. Louis County at the retired Meramec coal-fired facility, co-located at the Castle Bluff Energy Center, which is under construction. The project has a targeted in-service date of 2028. - Huck Finn: A 200-MW battery storage facility at Ameren Missouri’s Audrain Energy Center in Audrain County, with a targeted in-service date of 2028. - Millcreek: A 250-MW battery storage facility in Lincoln County, targeted to enter service in 2028. The PSC’s approval also includes the Quinn Switching Station, a new 161-kilovolt switching station in Lincoln County that will connect the Millcreek battery storage facility to the existing transmission system. Two solar developments are also part of the agreement: - Ringer: A 225-MW solar facility in Stoddard County that Ameren Missouri will acquire from Invenergy. Targeted to enter service in 2029, the facility is expected to produce enough energy to power more than 40,000 homes annually. - Tom Sawyer: A 175-MW solar facility in Audrain County that Ameren Missouri will acquire from EDF power solutions. It has a targeted in-service date of 2028 and is expected to produce enough energy to power more than 31,500 homes annually. The PSC said its decision considered safety and cost protections for Ameren Missouri customers while balancing the interests of landowners near the projects. Under the agreement, Ameren Missouri must address safety, environmental protection, construction oversight and cost reporting for the battery storage facilities. The company said it will work to expand information addressing community concerns about the Millcreek project, including fire safety, battery testing and nearby infrastructure. Ameren Missouri also must submit site-specific hazard mitigation analyses or plans for each battery facility after it enters service, along with information on emergency response procedures, environmental mitigation and containment practices related to fire response, according to the commission. The company must provide documentation of state, federal, and local permits obtained for each battery project and address safety testing before battery installation, including compliance with National Fire Protection Association (NFPA) 855 standards for stationary energy storage systems. The agreement also requires Ameren Missouri to notify the commission if a project’s total costs change by more than 15 percent of the applicable base or risk-adjusted project costs, explain the reasons for the increase, and describe efforts to mitigate the cost, the PSC said. Additionally, the company must submit quarterly progress reports covering construction milestones, permitting, costs, delays, and potential impacts from legislative or executive actions. For the Millcreek project, Ameren Missouri must meet with OPC and PSC Staff to discuss the results of Tesla Megapack 3 safety testing and steps taken by the supplier to ensure compliance with NFPA 855. At least 90 days before batteries are installed at the Millcreek site, Ameren Missouri must file a public pleading confirming completion of the testing, identifying the results and attaching the supplier’s confidential safety testing report for Staff and OPC review. The PSC review included input from residents, local officials, and other stakeholders. “We appreciate the participation of community members and stakeholders throughout the review process, and we’re focused on delivering projects that support safe and reliable service for our customers,” said Rob Dixon, vice president of regulatory, legislative and external affairs for Ameren Missouri.

artigo.texto: The Receipts: Air quality and representation fears rise with Taylor's data center AUSTIN, Texas — The Taylor City Council has approved a development agreement that could pave the way for a 664-acre data center campus just outside city limits, raising questions for neighbors who say they may feel the impact but have no voice in the process. CBS Austin has been investigating the proposed Taylor Technology Campus after residents reached out with concerns about noise, air quality and representation. Families living near the site say the project could alter the quiet, rural setting they have known for generations. "We wanted the fresh air, openness. We wanted a quiet life," said Connie Zycha, who lives directly across from the proposed campus. Zycha said her family has lived on their land for more than 140 years. "I won’t be able to sit in my front yard and watch the sunset. I won’t be able to watch the storms roll in or hear the train go by," she said. Neighbors near the site may attend council meetings and voice their opinions, but because the area is outside the city, they cannot vote in city elections. "We don't have a vote. We can't impact what they do," Zycha said. She added, "We don’t have a voice. We can’t yell at them and say, hey, we’re gonna vote you out. Because we can’t." Taylor officials said the agreement would allow the city to annex the land and apply specific regulations for the project. Daniel Seguin, executive director of community services for the City of Taylor, said the goal has been to deliver protections for people living nearby, even though they are outside city limits. "What our Taylor council has said is that their goal is to protect surrounding neighbors and the way that they were gonna do that is to negotiate for protections and ensure that this development is in city limits where regulations will apply," Seguin said. Seguin said the council worked to ensure the agreement included environmental protections and requirements for monitoring and enforcement. He explained that water for the data center would not be pulled from wells, addressing a concern raised by some nearby residents. "They will not be drilling wells. They're not gonna be accessing the aquifer beneath Taylor or impacting anyone's well water," he said. Air quality is also a major concern. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality said it has received Big Watt Digital’s application for an air permit for the campus’ natural gas electric generators but has not yet begun a technical review. Seguin said each natural gas generator will have its own air quality monitoring of the exhaust and the city is required to submit monthly reports to TCEQ. "Natural gas is unique in that it's one of the cleanest burning fossil fuels that is available, that exists," Seguin said. In an emailed statement, Big Watt Digital and PowerHouse Data Centers said the campus is being designed with dedicated on-site power generation and reclaimed-water cooling. They also pointed to noise limits, testing and property-line setbacks, and said they take neighbors’ concerns seriously. Carrie D’Anna, a community organizer with Halt Taylor Centers, said many questions still need answers. "People can’t make informed decisions without having information," D’Anna said. She added, "It’s not so much as control as responsibility. Because it impacts me, it impacts my family, it impacts the communities around me." The agreement also sets rules for water use and wastewater and limits noise at the property line to 65 decibels or the predevelopment baseline, whichever is higher. Seguin said the city will monitor compliance at the property line and that landscaping buffers are planned to lessen visible and audible impacts. "They're gonna be constructing berms along the property on the south side where the residents are. They're also going to covering those berms with multiple layers of planting," he said. Some residents remain frustrated that, despite the regulations, major decisions are being made without their ability to participate in city elections. Zycha said, "We have it less than a thousand feet from our home...The county commissioners are our voice. Not one has come to my property and asked me what I thought. Or sent a letter. What do you expect? We haven’t heard from them." Terry Pierce, a retired priest who lives nearby, said, "The problem here is that we need to regulate data centers and any other development in the city to build what is best for the neighbors, what is the best for children in this city." He continued, "If the air quality is such that kids can’t play outside. That is not a trade-off that is what we need here. It’s not a fair trade." D’Anna echoed concerns about the pace and transparency of the project. "Right now we have the intention that we are going to put, you know, regulations on it, but the ordinances and the agreements that we have made precede the amendments that they’re creating on behalf of us," she said. According to the city, the council posted the draft agreement online for public review ahead of the vote. Seguin said they work to reflect community input. "When community members have come and expressed concerns at a council meeting, then it came to the presentation, council members would directly parrot the community's questions back to the developers and back to city staff," he said. The council approved the development agreement on Oct. 8. Annexation remains a future step. Seguin said new zoning rules that specifically cover data centers are in development, but they would not apply retroactively to this project. The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality will review air permit applications and monitor compliance for the on-site generators. Williamson County stated it cannot zone or prohibit data centers and has no authority over Taylor's annexation of the area. artigo.texto: Neighbors frustrated over notice of proposed Cass County battery storage facility Cass County Planning Board to take up $240 million proposal Tuesday CASS COUNTY, Mo. (KCTV) - Neighbors near Pleasant Hill say they were given little notice about a proposed battery storage facility planned in their area. The Cass County Planning Board is scheduled to consider the proposal Tuesday at 6 p.m. at the Cass County Courthouse in Harrisonville. Sofos Power is seeking a special use permit to build a 280-megawatt battery energy storage facility along East 175th Street near Pleasant Hill. The company says the project represents a $240 million investment and would connect to an existing Evergy substation. Neighbors are concerned Lorretta Rowan, who lives near the proposed site, said she received a certified letter from Cass County Planning and Zoning about two weeks ago. “A little over two weeks ago I received a certified letter from the Cass County Planning and Zoning,” Rowan said. “And they informed us that there is a public meeting on the proposal to give them a special permit to put in a BESS system, a very large BESS system over here.” Rowan said the proposed site is less than 1,000 feet from her neighborhood. And a big worry she and other neighbors have is the potential thermal fire risk with a plant that size next door. “They’re going to put it right here, less than a thousand feet from a whole neighborhood,” Rowan said. Dave Kobie, another nearby resident, said his main concern is safety. “This Sofos special use permit request, a 280 megawatt BESS system, a battery energy storage system within Cass County, is absolutely not within the best interest of the county,” Kobie said. “Our main concern, obviously, is safety.” What’s next The Cass County Planning Board’s role Tuesday is limited to making a recommendation. Final approval authority rests with the Cass County Commission. Neighbors have organized a petition drive Saturday at 175th Street and Rock Island Road. Sofos Power provided the following statement: “Dogwood Resilient Power is following Cass County’s public review process, and the project as proposed is designed to be in full compliance with the siting and technology requirements addressed by the County’s battery storage code. artigo.texto: Press Releases New dashboard offers dynamic view of rated data center universe across Project Finance, Corporates, and Structured Finance Asset Backed Securities - Covers 32 digital infrastructure transactions totaling $105.3 billion in debt issuance - Includes market overview, issuer tear sheets and comparatives, and state-level capacity insights NEW YORK, Oct. 23, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- S&P Global Ratings, the world's leading provider of independent credit ratings, today launched a new interactive dashboard providing a dynamic view of its rated North American data center universe across Project Finance, and Corporates, and Structured Finance asset-backed securities (SF ABS). The dashboard brings together information across these three areas, providing an overview of the market, issuer tear sheets and comparatives, and insights into states where capacity is being leased. It accompanies S&P Global Ratings' fourth-quarter roundup, "North America Data Center Roundup: Fourth-Quarter 2026," published Oct. 16, 2026. "Our rated North American data center universe now spans 32 digital infrastructure transactions and $105.3 billion in debt issuance across project finance, structured finance ABS, and corporates," said Vishal Merani, Managing Director and Global Digital Infrastructure Team Leader, S&P Global Ratings. "Bringing this information together in an interactive format provides a more comprehensive view of our rated data center universe as demand continues to grow." said Dhaval Shah, Director, S&P Global Ratings. Key takeaways from the fourth-quarter roundup: - S&P Global Ratings currently rates 32 digital infrastructure transactions in North America across Project Finance (PF), Corporates, and Structured Finance asset-backed securities (SF ABS). The majority are SF ABS issuers (50%), followed by PF issuers (28%) and Corporates (22%), based on the number of issuers. - Total debt issuance across rated issuers reaches $105.3 billion, with PF accounting for 58.3%, SF ABS for 26.4%, and Corporates for 15.3%. - The rated transactions are backed by 143 properties with approximately 8.7 gigawatts of capacity available to tenants in North America. - S&P Global Ratings expects data center demand to remain strong in the foreseeable future, driven by exponential data growth, cloud migration, and the ongoing digitization of the global economy. - S&P Global Ratings believes power constraints, permitting challenges, public pushback and regulatory responses could delay or constrain new data center development. artigo.texto: Após quase uma década respeitando os limites de eficiência energética, a Samsung está se preparando para uma reestruturação significativa da duração da bateria em sua linha de celulares de ponta. Resultados de testes técnicos recentes mostram que a próxima série Galaxy S27 apresentará um grande avanço na capacidade de armazenamento de energia, resolvendo o problema da duração da bateria que tem sido uma das principais preocupações dos usuários de smartphones topo de linha. Vazaram as especificações da bateria de 5.700 mAh do Galaxy S27 Ultra: um salto histórico após 7 anos. Os dados de certificação confirmam que o Galaxy S27 Ultra e o S27 Pro terão capacidades de bateria aprimoradas de 5.700 mAh e 5.200 mAh, respectivamente, combinadas com a tecnologia de carregamento rápido de 60 W. Dados técnicos da agência de certificação Safety Korea e do sistema de padrões 3C obrigatório na China confirmaram oficialmente as especificações das novas baterias para a próxima geração de smartphones topo de linha. De acordo com essas informações, espera-se que o Galaxy S27 Ultra, o modelo mais sofisticado da linha, apresente uma bateria com capacidade nominal de até 5.700 mAh. Isso representa um aumento de aproximadamente 14% em comparação com os 5.000 mAh que permaneceram constantes por várias gerações. Não apenas a versão Ultra, mas também a nova variante chamada Galaxy S27 Pro possui uma bateria de 5.200 mAh. A fabricação e a produção dessas duas baterias são de responsabilidade da subsidiária Zhuhai CosMX Power Jinwan. Pressão competitiva e mudanças nas estratégias de segurança. Desde os problemas de superaquecimento da série Galaxy Note 7, a Samsung tem aplicado consistentemente uma filosofia de segurança rigorosa aos sistemas de bateria de seus dispositivos móveis. Por sete anos consecutivos, a empresa manteve uma capacidade de bateria padrão de 5.000 mAh para os modelos Galaxy S Ultra, visando otimizar a dissipação de calor e garantir a estabilidade mecânica. No entanto, o mercado de celulares entrou em uma fase de intensa competição, com outras marcas elevando os limites de armazenamento de energia a níveis sem precedentes, como exemplificado pelo Honor X80 Pro Max com sua bateria de 11.000 mAh. Para reduzir essa diferença, mantendo a segurança, a Samsung integrou gradualmente materiais de silício-carbono ao sistema de armazenamento do Galaxy Z Fold 8, Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra e Galaxy Z Flip 8. Embora a quantidade desse material em modelos dobráveis anteriores fosse cautelosa e pertencesse ao grupo tradicional de íon-lítio, essa plataforma abriu caminho para uma maior densidade de energia no Galaxy S27 Ultra. A potência do hardware incluída na nova geração. Além da capacidade de bateria aprimorada, o Galaxy S27 Pro promete oferecer especificações poderosas para otimizar a duração da bateria. O dispositivo possui uma tela de 6,47 polegadas, um sensor de câmera principal de 200 MP e duas opções de processador de última geração: Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 6 ou Exynos 2700, dependendo do mercado. Ambos os modelos suportam carregamento rápido com fio de 60 W, mantendo um desempenho de carregamento comparável ao do Galaxy S26 Ultra. No geral, a atualização simultânea de uma bateria de 5.700 mAh para um processador de última geração ajudará a série Galaxy S27 a estabelecer um padrão mais elevado de desempenho duradouro no segmento de dispositivos premium.

artigo.texto: Publicidade Por Luciana Magalhaes 23 Out (Reuters) – A fabricante chinesa de carros elétricos BYD deu início aos pedidos de licenças para dobrar a capacidade anual de produção de sua fábrica brasileira para 600.000 veículos, ao mesmo tempo em que entra na fase final de obras e testes de seus galpões de estamparia, soldagem e pintura, disse à Reuters o principal executivo da empresa no país. A unidade da BYD no Brasil deve iniciar 2027 ultrapassando o mínimo exigido de 50% de nacionalização de componentes, o que atenderá às exigências regulatórias e ajudará a empresa a iniciar as exportações regionais, afirmou o vice-presidente sênior Alexandre Baldy em entrevista. A empresa enfrentou reclamações de grupos da indústria local de que dependia muito de importações e de tarifas temporariamente baixas. ‘A gente trabalha para inaugurar 2027 já ultrapassando essa posição e termos essas etapas em operação para sermos considerados um fabricante local’, disse Baldy. Leia também: Volkswagen pode enfrentar greve histórica na Alemanha em janeiro Continua depois da publicidade A BYD tem como meta se tornar a maior montadora do Brasil em volume de vendas até 2030 e já vê a demanda superar sua capacidade atual de produção, disse Baldy. Embora a BYD esteja acelerando suas operações e planeje atingir uma produção mensal de 25.000 veículos até o final de 2026, a tendência é de que a demanda continue superando a oferta. ‘Nossa demanda tem ficado em uma média de cerca de 30.000 carros por mês, o que significa que estamos deixando de faturar cerca de 5.000 a 6.000 vendas adicionais’, disse Baldy. Continua depois da publicidade O investimento na nova fábrica da empresa no Brasil já ultrapassou os R$5,5 bilhões e as vendas faturadas da unidade brasileira atingirão esta semana a marca de 200.000 carros no acumulado de 2026, afirmou Baldy. Leia também: Diesel em alta no EUA favorece transporte ferroviário e ações do setor sobem Em setembro, a empresa teve um total de 22.209 veículos emplacados no Brasil, o equivalente a uma fatia de mercado de 8,5%, segundo dados da empresa. Continua depois da publicidade A BYD já é líder de mercado no Uruguai e suas vendas ocupam posições de destaque na Colômbia e na Argentina, disse o executivo. A montadora no Brasil também recebeu pedidos de 50.000 unidades do México e da Argentina cada, e estará apta a atendê-los a partir do ano que vem graças ao aumento do índice de componentes locais. A BYD inaugurou sua fábrica em Camaçari, Bahia, em 9 de outubro de 2025, em um complexo industrial que pertenceu à Ford Motor Co. Continua depois da publicidade A fábrica emprega atualmente cerca de 9.000 pessoas e espera expandir sua força de trabalho para cerca de 10.000 trabalhadores até o final deste ano. (Reportagem Luciana MagalhaesEdição Michael Susin)

artigo.texto: As word spread about NAVWAR being considered as a potential site for a data center, the community immediately responded. A group rallied last week calling for those plans to be scrapped. Stream San Diego News for free, 24/7, wherever you are with NBC 7. Others, like Francisco Martinez, are open to the idea of data centers coming to San Diego. “People don’t want the things too close to the neighborhood, but on the other hand, it’s the present and the future and we need all of that to develop the next step forward in many things,” Martinez said. District 9 Councilmember Sean Elo-Rivera, has been a vocal critic of the possibility of the U.S. Navy’s cybersecurity hub becoming what would be the largest data center in California. “The conversation that is happening in NAVWAR is a flashing red light, and we need to think about this as a threat and it can happen in San Diego and one that we need to get ahead of,” Councilmember Elo-Rivera said. Local He worries the project would impact San Diegans' energy costs and plans for affordable housing. Martinez thinks if the land is available, developers should be able to move forward. “If it’s a land that is open and has no use for anything else, they can put a bid. It’s fair,” Martinez said. The redevelopment plans extend beyond a data center. Ted Elridge, the project’s CEO, told NBC 7 that they are also exploring a medical center, a university and defense campus, along with a life sciences facility. Elridge also confirmed there have been early talks with energy providers but said there have been no negotiations or agreements. Since NAVWAR is federal property, Elo-Rivera is calling on congress to take the project off the table. This week, San Diego City Council is set to vote on a temporary moratorium on new data centers and the expansion of existing ones. “What we don’t want is a rush to submit permits and get projects going before rules are in place,” Elo-Rivera said. If approved, the initial moratorium would last 45 days, and the city council could vote to extend it once it expires. The moratorium would buy city leaders time while they work to establish regulations with clear guardrails for developers wishing to bring data centers to San Diego. Elo-Rivera said they have submitted a policy proposal and need to start drafting the law. He said they want to ensure the draft has no loopholes before it becomes permanent. Martinez hopes they’re able to reach an agreement that satisfies everyone while moving San Diego forward. “It’s a balance between new technology and new needs, and what people want around their neighborhoods,” Martinez said. Mayor Todd Gloria has signed an executive order to freeze any data center construction, marking what advocates described as a first step addressing concerns about the project. Poway was the first city in the county to ban data centers, earlier this month, citing air quality, noise and water-use concerns, as well as a lack of local long-term job creation because much of a data center is automated.

artigo.texto: The National Aeronautics and Space Administration (NASA) has announced the development of a groundbreaking battery technology that may play a crucial role in the United States’ plans for lunar exploration and could also transform the landscape of electric vehicle (EV) power sources on Earth. This innovative battery is designed to function efficiently at extremely low temperatures, which could enhance the operation of lunar rovers and other equipment under NASA’s Artemis program. According to reports, the newly developed “freeze-proof” solid-state battery has undergone successful thermal vacuum testing and has withstood temperatures as frigid as 274 degrees Fahrenheit below zero (minus 170 degrees Celsius). The testing revealed that while the prototype batteries showed reduced performance at temperatures down to 112 degrees Fahrenheit below zero (minus 80 degrees Celsius), they performed optimally in a range from negative 76 to positive 176 degrees Fahrenheit (minus 60 to 80 degrees Celsius). Such performance is vital for the moon’s South Pole, where temperatures can plummet to 328 degrees Fahrenheit below zero (minus 200 degrees Celsius)—conditions that conventional lithium-ion batteries simply cannot endure. Traditional lithium-ion batteries operate by transferring lithium ions through liquid electrolytes, which can freeze in harsh conditions and pose significant fire risks due to their flammable nature. In contrast, solid-state batteries utilize solid electrolytes, providing a safer and more stable environment for lithium ion movement, enabling faster charging and reduced risk of failure in extreme temperatures. While the EV industry may not currently require batteries that can survive extreme cold, advancements in solid-state technology from NASA’s endeavors could significantly impact terrestrial applications. The research suggests that these battery innovations could lead to enhanced safety, temperature tolerance, and efficiency for various electronic devices, including electric vehicles, commercial drones, and grid-scale energy storage systems operating in tough climates. Specifically, these breakthroughs might allow for longer ranges in colder regions and during winter months for electric vehicles. In addition to battery technology, NASA is exploring collaboration with the United States Department of Energy to develop next-generation nuclear energy solutions that could propel a new era for deep space exploration. This initiative is perceived as a transformative approach for space missions, as nuclear power is expected to extend the range and operational capabilities of spacecraft and instruments. As NASA forges ahead with these ambitious projects, the implications for both space exploration and energy technology may define the future of both fields, paving the way for innovative discoveries and advancements.

artigo.texto: Table of Contents Chinese billionaire Robin Zeng, the founder and chairman of Contemporary Amperex Technology Co., has seen $14.9 billion wiped off his fortune since March after shares of the world's largest electric-vehicle battery maker fell sharply on weaker-than-expected earnings. Zeng, 57, is now worth about $38.3 billion, down from $53.2 billion in March. Nearly all of his wealth comes from his stake in CATL, the company he founded in 2011 in Ningde, in China's southeastern Fujian province. CATL shares have dropped 33% in Shenzhen and 25% in Hong Kong over that period. The decline deepened on Wednesday, when the stock fell more than 12% in both markets, its worst one-day selloff in more than a year. The Hong Kong shares traded as low as HK$368 ($47.30), their weakest level since July 2025. The company's market value has nearly halved since peaking in May. Profit growth slows The selloff followed third-quarter results released on Tuesday. Net profit attributable to shareholders rose 14.5% from a year earlier to 21.25 billion yuan ($3.16 billion), well short of the 41.2% increase analysts had expected and down from growth of 36.5% in the second quarter. Profit also fell 5.8% from the previous three months. Revenue rose 58.6% to 165.2 billion yuan ($24.6 billion), slightly below forecasts. Gross margin narrowed to 20.69%, the second straight quarterly decline. In the first nine months of the year, CATL earned 64.53 billion yuan ($9.6 billion), up 31.6%, on revenue of 442.14 billion yuan ($65.8 billion). Management blamed new tax costs. China reinstated a consumption tax on lithium-ion batteries on Sept. 1 at a transitional rate of 2%, which is set to rise to 4% in September 2027. Separately, the export tax rebate on battery products was cut to 6% from 9% in April and will be scrapped on Jan. 1. Chief Financial Officer Zheng Shu said the consumption tax is built into product prices, so passing it on to carmakers means renegotiating contracts, and those talks are still under way. CATL said it hopes to "shoulder the costs together" with customers and is developing new products to protect margins. "Based on the significant fall in profit growth, it seems that the company itself has shouldered the bulk of them," said Kenny Ng, an analyst at Everbright Securities International. JPMorgan Chase & Co. cut its rating on the Hong Kong-listed shares to neutral and lowered its earnings forecasts, while keeping an overweight rating on the Shenzhen stock. Carmakers look for other suppliers Investors are also watching what Chinese commentators have called "de-CATLization," a push by carmakers to reduce their reliance on a single battery supplier. Li Auto and Xiaomi have started developing their own EV batteries, and Tesla added Sunwoda Electronic as a supplier this year. Industry data show CATL's share of China's battery market fell to 40.9% in September from 49.8% in January, while rival BYD's rose to 21.1% from 17.4%. Globally, CATL still supplied about 40% of EV batteries installed in the first half of the year, according to SNE Research, and counts almost every major carmaker as a customer. The company said growth of 20% to 30% in global demand for power and energy-storage batteries is achievable in 2027. Zeng, who holds a doctorate in physics, co-founded Amperex Technology Ltd. in 1999, making batteries for consumer electronics, before spinning off CATL to supply car batteries. artigo.texto: Russian ministry recommends underground data centers following Ukrainian drone strikes Russia's Digital Development Ministry has proposed building data centers underground, camouflaged from the air, and fitted with drone defenses, Russian state-controlled media Kommersant said on Oct. 25, following several Ukrainian drone attacks on data centers. Guidelines for existing, planned, and under-construction facilities outline the protection standards for three tiers of data centers, including whether sites are placed above ground or underground, according to Kommersant. The top tier includes strategic sites whose loss could disrupt key state functions for an hour or more; the second tier includes sites supporting regionally or economically important systems, where outages could last four hours or more; and the final tier covers corporate data centers whose damage would not have wider consequences for the state, Kommersant said. Existing data centers should be protected by reducing their visibility from the air and by deploying layered defenses, including reinforced structures, electronic warfare measures, and drone defense systems. The announcement came after Ukrainian drones struck three Yandex data centers, a Sberbank facility under construction, and a data center belonging to social media giant VK between Oct. 8 and Oct. 18. Russia's centralized digital infrastructure leaves Moscow facing two challenges: inflicting comparable damage on Ukraine and protecting its own data centers from further strikes. Serhiy Petrenko, former head of Yandex Ukraine, estimated that around 80% of Russia's data centers are concentrated in Moscow and the surrounding region — within reach of Ukrainian long-range drones. The consequences of Ukraine's strikes on Russian data centers could extend far beyond disrupted banking and online services, potentially setting back the country's AI development and affecting military technology. On Oct. 16, Kemerovo Oblast governor Ilya Seredyuk proposed housing data centers inside depleted open-pit mines and quarries, given their natural protection from aerial bombardment.
