artigo.texto: A data center is often discussed as a digital asset. Itâs also a physical one: a major site that depends on power, electrical equipment, and a connection to the grid. That matters as UK Chancellor John Healey prepares to deliver his first budget on Oct. 28, with the government planning to give mayors a larger share of business rates from April 2027. The case for devolution is clear. Places that attract investment should share in its benefits. But the way that investment is taxed will shape where projects go, what infrastructure gets built, and whether promised capacity can be delivered. Business rates are a recurring property tax, calculated by applying a multiplier to a propertyâs rateable value. For data centers, valuation can include plant and machinery as well as the building. Most pay the higher multiplier for the most valuable properties. This yearâs revaluation increased rateable values at prime sites in London and Slough by between a quarter and a half. If local mayors retain more of the resulting revenue, a data center can become a substantial continuing addition to a regionâs tax base. That creates a direct incentive to attract projects and potentially offer rate relief to win them. Devolving business rates therefore can become a form of tax competition: regions forgoing revenue today in the hope of collecting more tomorrow. The danger is that while tax policy can influence a developerâs choice of location, it canât create the power needed to operate the site. A tax break can bring a project to the table but not deliver a grid connection. The US offers a stark warning. States spent a decade using sales-tax exemptions to attract data centers and, this year, lawmakers in two dozen states tried to repeal or reduce them after costs exceeded forecasts. In Virginia, the cost reached about 16 times the original estimate. Tax relief can lower a developerâs bill, but if a site canât get power, the public bears the cost without securing the investment or capacity the incentive was meant to support. The UK budget should set a clear test for business-rate relief. Whether offered by local councils or mayors, it should be conditional on grid readiness â a firm connection date or capacity reserved in an AI growth zone. Relief should be linked to delivery milestones, with a review or clawback if a project fails to proceed on time. The tax benefit should follow progress on the ground, not simply a developerâs choice of location. A national framework would help avoid regions competing through increasingly generous packages. It should define connection readiness and delivery milestones, and require government to publish the expected and actual cost of relief. Business-rate discounts and capital allowances need to be assessed separately. A rate discount reduces local receipts while it applies; a capital allowance changes when a company can deduct qualifying investment from taxable profits. The budget should use capital allowances to support the grid infrastructure developers are starting to fund themselves. In AI growth zones, developers may be able to build their own substations and high-voltage lines where that gets them connected sooner. These assets can add capacity the network would otherwise need to fund and help ease constraints beyond a single data center site. Qualifying special-rate expenditure generally can now receive a 50% first-year allowance, with the remaining balance written down at 6% on a declining balance basis. A qualifying main-rate plant can receive a 100% first-year allowance. Electrical equipment around data centers may fall into either category, depending on its classification and use. The chancellor should consider extending a 100% first-year allowance to qualifying private substations and connection assets. Bringing tax relief forward would improve project cash flow and reduce the tax penalty on developers who invest in infrastructure that adds network capacity. It wouldnât be a cash grant; its fiscal cost would depend on the qualifying investment and the timing of deductions. Eligibility should depend on an assetâs contribution to connection, not simply its location inside a data center site. Power equipment is another constraint. Switchgear, transformers, and protection equipment can take months or years to arrive because manufacturers are fully booked. A targeted allowance or credit for investment in UK production capacity could support data centers, housing, transport, and other electrification projects. It should reward additional capacity, with clear eligibility and a measurable fiscal cost. These proposals should be judged on whether they change the location, timing, or scale of investment enough to justify the revenue forgone. Relief that only changes the timing of a project that was already proceeding may have little additional effect. Fiscal discipline and infrastructure delivery should be considered together. A data centerâs value is measured in megawatts. Tax policy should follow the power, not the location. Get the balance wrong, and regions may compete for projects the grid canât serve. Get it right, and tax relief can steer investment to available power, encourage developers to add capacity and help build the supply chain that Britainâs wider electrification depends on. artigo.texto: Publicidade A Finlândia estima que um quarto de milhão de árvores que ocupavam os 330 hectares de floresta perto da cidade de Muhos, na zona rural do norte da Finlândia, foram derrubadas pelo Google (GOGL34). Segundo reportagem do The Guardian, a empresa de tecnologia devastou ilegalmente toda a área para construir um centro de dados – levando consigo até mesmo a camada superficial do solo. Com 145 novos centros de dados em diferentes fases de planejamento, a Finlândia se encontra na vanguarda da mais recente investida das empresas de tecnologia. Além de sua relativa estabilidade geopolítica e geológica e da abundância de terras, o clima frio a torna especialmente atraente para a economia de custos de energia. Ainda de acordo com o jornal britânico, no início deste mês, a Autoridade Finlandesa de Licenciamento e Supervisão (LVV) ordenou ao Google que interrompesse temporariamente as obras em Muhos e em outro local a cerca de 100 km a sudeste, na vila de Otanmäki, após a empresa não ter concluído as avaliações de impacto ambiental necessárias antes do desmatamento da área. A notícia provocou indignação generalizada e um debate nacional sobre qual papel, se houver, o país deve desempenhar na corrida global para construir data centers e acompanhar o rápido desenvolvimento da inteligência artificial. Leia mais: Continua depois da publicidade - Brasil vira paraíso dos data centers; veja quais ações lucram - Data centers abrem nova fronteira para fundos imobiliários; veja oportunidades Na semana passada, o diretor da Google na Finlândia, Antti Järvinen, pediu desculpas pelo desmatamento, mas afirmou que a empresa agiu “com base no melhor entendimento que tínhamos da legislação na época”. Muhos e Otanmäki fazem parte de um projeto de infraestrutura de IA de € 13 bilhões do Google, que atraiu críticas de Donald Trump, que preferiria que os centros fossem construídos nos EUA e pediu publicamente que a empresa reconsiderasse. É o maior projeto desse tipo já realizado no país nórdico. O governo finlandês, que implementou profundos cortes de gastos, incentivou o investimento. No mês passado, quando os planos do Google foram anunciados, o primeiro-ministro do país, Petteri Orpo, afirmou que atrair investimentos era uma “prioridade máxima” e que “o valor da economia de dados vai muito além do investimento direto”. Ele disse que o acordo com o Google “traria benefícios duradouros para ambas as partes”. Continua depois da publicidade Além das 250.000 árvores derrubadas em Muhos, Annala estima que outras 150.000 árvores foram derrubadas em Otanmäki. Como as árvores foram derrubadas ilegalmente, a madeira dos dois locais não pode ser vendida para fábricas de processamento de madeira. A medida também gerou questionamentos sobre o motivo pelo qual as fontes de energia renováveis ??da Finlândia estão sendo usadas para abastecer corporações internacionais. Mais de 93 mil pessoas assinaram uma petição exigindo maior regulamentação dos centros de dados e uma taxa para compensar as comunidades locais pelos danos ambientais. Continua depois da publicidade Hanna Halmeenpää, presidente do conselho da SLL, disse ter ficado incrédula ao descobrir a violação da lei cometida pelo Google. “A princípio, não consegui acreditar”, disse ela ao The Guardian. “Nunca ouvi falar de nenhuma empresa que tenha feito algo assim na Finlândia.” Ela afirmou que o sistema depende muito da confiança, da qual acredita que o Google se aproveitou. “Eles compraram uma vasta área de terra e simplesmente começaram a desmatá-la, assim, sem mais nem menos”, disse ela. “É pura arrogância e é inacreditável.” Continua depois da publicidade A rapidez dos acontecimentos chocou o país, disse ela. “Muitas pessoas estão assistindo ao noticiário e se perguntando: ‘O que está acontecendo agora? O que podemos fazer a respeito? E precisamos mesmo aceitar todos esses projetos de data centers na Finlândia?'” Leia também: Nokia vê demanda forte de IA, com alta de 17% nas vendas de infraestrutura de redes ‘Para a Finlândia, não há benefícios’ Jussi Kangasharju, chefe do departamento de ciência da computação da Universidade de Helsinque, afirmou que, embora os centros de dados gerem um número limitado de empregos, potencialmente impulsionando a economia local, os benefícios em nível nacional são mínimos. “Na verdade, para a Finlândia, não há benefícios”, disse ele. “São empresas internacionais que atendem clientes internacionais. A Finlândia arrecada muito pouco imposto corporativo. Os centros de dados, em última análise, trazem muito pouco benefício para outros, exceto para o próprio operador do centro de dados.” Com a legislação ainda em processo de atualização, há uma corrida para iniciar os projetos o mais rápido possível. Alguns defendem a criação de um órgão centralizado para coordenar os projetos de centros de dados, em vez de deixar grande parte da tomada de decisões a cargo dos municípios, que provavelmente priorizarão as necessidades imediatas da área local. Leia também: Anthropic desafia turbulência do mercado e mantém plano de IPO bilionário Alteração na fauna e flora Em Otanmäki, o impacto na natureza e na vida cotidiana dos moradores é sentido de forma intensa. Quando as árvores foram derrubadas, os lobos que ali viviam vieram para a vila, disse Anni Ranta, de 53 anos, cuja família mora ali há gerações. Antiga vila mineira, a região é conhecida por seus elementos de terras raras. A família de Ranta mora no centro da vila, ao lado da torre triangular de uma igreja e de um antigo bar que está vazio há anos. A floresta tranquila costumava se estender por quilômetros a partir da vila. artigo.texto: Google vai pagar quem usar menos energia elétrica para alimentar data centers de IA Iniciativa nos Estados Unidos acontece em parceria com a empresa Voltus, e tem como base o modelo de “usina elétrica virtual” A empresa americana de energia Voltus anunciou nesta quarta-feira, 23, uma parceria com o Google para a exploração do sistema de energia elétrica americano. O Google pagará aos moradores e empresas dos Estados Unidos pela diminuição do consumo de sua energia, para que a sobra seja utilizada para alimentar seus data centers (centros de dados) de Inteligência Artificial (IA). A parceria com a empresa de energia Voltus serve para gerenciar essa redistribuição de energia elétrica. O modelo de negócios é conhecido como “usina elétrica virtual” (VPP), em que um sistema de gerenciamento de energia coordena os recursos espalhados por diversos locais, para reduzir o consumo geral da rede. Os benefícios financeiros para os participantes dos sistemas incluem economia nas contas de eletricidade e pagamentos diretos pela redução no consumo. De acordo com o jornal americano New York Times, a empresa de tecnologia receberá até 1.70 megawatts de capacidade elétrica, capacidade equivalente à de um reator nuclear. As empresas não divulgaram qualquer média de valores. Em comunicado, o Google e a Voltus explicaram que, com o financiamento da gigante de tecnologia, os sistemas da Voltus para a usina elétrica virtual irão identificar quando a rede de energia estiver sobrecarregada, e enviará de forma automática alertas para os locais que podem economizar ao acionarem termostatos inteligentes, ajustes internos e outras ações para reduzir o uso de energia.

artigo.texto: Conectividade por cabo submarino vai atrair investimentos para data centers no RN O Rio Grande do Norte tem dado passos importantes para investimentos em data center com a regulamentação do setor e deve seguir avançando nesse ambiente. No entanto, ainda há a necessidade de conectividade via cabo submarino para a instalação de grandes empreendimentos. O RN ainda aguarda definições do Governo Federal quanto à instalação de ao menos um cabo. O tema também integra as discussões da Data Center Conference, que ocorre nesta sexta-feira (23), na Federação das Indústrias do Estado do Rio Grande do Norte (Fiern), em Natal. De acordo com Gladson Mortoza, um dos palestrantes do evento, a expectativa é de que a tecnologia chegue ao RN no curto e médio prazos para que o estado seja capaz de instalar grandes estruturas que possam atender às demandas regionais e globais. “O estado já possui oferta de energia. Com a expectativa da chegada de conectividade via cabo submarino, o Rio Grande do Norte abre a porta para atender às demandas daqui, de todo país e até mesmo internacionais”, frisa o palestrante, que é gerente comercial da Mendes Holler, empresa especialista em data center. O presidente da Fiern, Roberto Serquiz, afirma que é preciso avançar no diálogo para que a conectividade chegue o quanto antes por aqui. “É uma etapa que nós precisamos trabalhar. Os cabos já existem no Ceará, então, a ligação com o RN se torna apenas um ponto de diálogo. Com essa conectividade, fechamos mais um ciclo para que, definitivamente, os investimentos cheguem ao RN”, comentou Roberto Serquiz. De acordo com Emília Casanova, secretária-adjunta de Desenvolvimento Econômico do Estado (Sedec), o Rio Grande do Norte ainda aguarda definição do Governo Federal para a instalação de, ao menos um cabo. “Nós temos um estudo de atracação em áreas de interesse, porém, não houve ainda uma decisão do Ministério de Telecomunicações, a qual inclui uma definição sobre os locais de instalação. A gente não sabe se será somente em Natal ou se haverá uma conexão também na região da Costa Branca”, explicou a secretária durante a Data Center Conference. O encontro conta com palestras de importantes nomes da área e também com representantes do setor energético no RN, a exemplo de Fabíola Almeida, diretora-presidente da Neoenergia Cosern, e Dennis Falcon, diretor técnico e comercial da Potigás. A programação também conta com Roberto Wagner Costa, presidente do Conselho Regional de Engenharia e Agronomia do Rio Grande do Norte (Crea-RN), e Larissa Dantas, diretora institucional da entidade. A lista de convidados inclui ainda Hugo Fonseca, diretor administrativo e financeiro da Codern; Olavo Bueno, diretor-presidente do PAX RN; Ângela Paiva, presidente do Conselho do PAX; Mayara Leal, do Idema; e Kepler Brito, representante da OAB/RN no Conema. O evento tem apoio da Fiern, WCA, ABDC, Crea-RN, Potigás, Neoenergia Cosern e Banco do Nordeste. artigo.texto: India Discusses Battery Manufacturing and Critical Minerals Partnerships at REI Expo Speakers cited lithium, cobalt and rare earth supply and research cooperation for India’s battery sector. The discussions did not specify new investments or agreements involving individual EV manufacturers. Industry leaders and officials from Australia, Germany and Scotland discussed cooperation with India on battery manufacturing, critical minerals and technology at the Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo & The Battery Show India (TBSI) on October 23, as India works to strengthen domestic battery manufacturing and the supply chain that could support its electric vehicle (EV) industry. Australia identified battery manufacturing and EVs as key areas for cooperation with India. Australia has significant lithium, cobalt and rare earth resources. Philip Green, Australia’s High Commissioner to India, said “The two countries could combine Australia’s engineering expertise and mineral resources with India’s manufacturing strength and integration into global supply chains.” “Australia produces more than 50 percent of the world’s lithium, according to Green, and holds the world’s second-largest cobalt reserves. It also ranks second or third globally in rare earth resources.” he said. Australia has 20 companies and 32 exhibitors at the expo, showing technologies in energy storage, grid infrastructure, green hydrogen and renewable energy integration. Anandi Iyer, Director of Fraunhofer Office in India, said “India and Germany had opportunities to collaborate in battery research, power electronics, advanced engineering and industrial automation.” Iyer stated, “Approximately 800 GW of renewable energy capacity additions globally in 2025, while global battery storage deployment reached 108 GW, an increase of 40 per cent from the previous year.” She said, “Technological self-reliance did not mean working in isolation, highlighting the importance of trusted partnerships and supply chains that can translate research into commercially viable solutions.” Scotland’s First Minister John Swinney also spoke of combining Scottish technological expertise with India’s manufacturing scale, talent and market potential. Yogesh Mudras, Managing Director of Informa Markets in India, said “Renewable energy generation and grid storage needed to expand together as the country advanced its energy transition.” According to Mudras, “India’s renewable energy market is projected to reach 486 GW by 2030, growing at a compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 15 percent. The country’s battery storage sector is projected to exceed USD 8.5 billion by 2031, with a CAGR of 33 percent.” These projections relate to the broader renewable energy and storage markets. The release said battery-related manufacturing and technology capabilities are also relevant to the wider EV ecosystem. Manu Srivastav, Additional Chief Secretary in Madhya Pradesh’s Power & Renewable Energy Department, said “Renewable energy was becoming increasingly competitive with conventional power as costs declined. He pointed to opportunities for wider adoption over the next two to five years.” Jai Asundi, Executive Director of the Centre for Study of Science, Technology & Policy (CSTEP), said “India would need continued investment in manufacturing, energy storage, grid infrastructure, research and skilled talent to build a resilient clean energy ecosystem.” The three-day event, organised by Informa Markets in India, has more than 1,080 exhibitors, 1,400 brands and over 54,000 professionals. The co-located expos bring together renewable energy developers, battery manufacturers, investors and policymakers. The cooperation in battery research and manufacturing technologies could contribute to domestic capabilities in India’s automotive sector. The discussions did not specify new investments or agreements involving individual EV manufacturers. The expo is run by Informa Markets in India. This year's three-day edition runs October 22-24 at India Expo Mart, Greater Noida. It is the 19th edition of Renewable Energy India (REI) Expo, held with The Battery Show India and Energy Storage Summit India. Australia sent a 32-member delegation representing 21 clean energy companies. The 18th REI Expo theme was achieving net zero, and it covered the clean energy chain from generation to storage and mobility. The opening focused on solar and national targets. TERI's Director General said India had reached 127 GW of installed solar capacity and was moving towards its 500 GW non-fossil target for 2030. The battery side was smaller, with over 350 exhibitors and 400 brands expected. The discussion at this year's expo has moved to what supports it: grid storage, domestic battery manufacturing, critical mineral access and international technology partnerships. Last year's stated focus was net zero targets. The 2026 speakers, including Australia's High Commissioner, talked about securing lithium, cobalt and rare earths and building domestic manufacturing. The addition of a separate Energy Storage Summit also points to storage getting more weight. artigo.texto: Publicidade 23 Out (Reuters) – Os investimentos globais em centrais de processamento de dados devem atingir US$1 trilhão em 2026 e mais que dobrar a US$2,1 trilhões até 2028, segundo estimativa da BofA Global Research divulgada nesta sexta-feira. O mercado de data centers, avaliado em US$275 bilhões em 2022, poderá atingir US$2,93 trilhões até 2030, afirmou o BofA. A inteligência artificial é vista como o motor dessa expansão, que, segundo a corretora, impulsionará uma taxa composta de crescimento anual (CAGR) de 37% em todo o mercado de 2025 a 2030. Fabricantes de chips e desenvolvedores de servidores têm estado entre os maiores beneficiários da expansão dos data centers impulsionada pela IA, particularmente nos Estados Unidos. Leia mais: Data centers abrem nova fronteira para fundos imobiliários; veja oportunidades O BofA estimou os custos de construção de centrais de processamento de dados em US$49 milhões por megawatt, com as despesas relacionadas à TI representando 78% do investimento total. Continua depois da publicidade As “neoclouds”, ou data centers focados em IA, custam cerca de US$57 milhões por megawatt, mas se beneficiam de menores requisitos de espaço em comparação com seus equivalentes tradicionais. A corretora estima que os servidores sejam o componente mais caro, custando US$31,4 milhões por megawatt, e que a rede seja o segundo maior item de investimento, com US$4,8 milhões por megawatt. A maioria das outras funções, quadros de comando, distribuição de energia, geradores, energia de reserva, resfriadores e refrigeração, custa entre US$100 mil e US$1,1 milhão por megawatt, segundo o levantamento do BofA. artigo.texto: An inside look of the massive data center tearing a Wisconsin community apart In Port Washington, Wisconsin, there's a data center being built that's as big as 500 football fields. Residents aren't sure if it could save their community or destroy it. SACHA PFEIFFER, HOST: Back here in Wisconsin, I've been driving through the state this week. And just north of Milwaukee, you quickly enter farm country - cornfields, rolling hills, barns and grain silos. Then suddenly, next to a highway, you get a visual shock. And - oh, Henry, is this the data center on the left? HENRY LARSON, BYLINE: It's huge. PFEIFFER: There's something massive under construction over there. It's a hyper-scale data center in Port Washington, Wisconsin. I went there with NPR producer Henry Larson, and we could barely find words for how colossal this project is. This skyline of cranes and... It stretches along 2 miles of highway. It covers 2 1/2 million square feet of former farmland. LARSON: It goes literally to the horizon. PFEIFFER: This emerging data center complex has torn up the land and torn up this community. It's a local story playing out nationally as artificial intelligence companies race to build data centers to power their AI and many people increasingly say we don't want these here. (SOUNDBITE OF ARCHIVED RECORDING) UNIDENTIFIED PERSON #1: Will you acknowledge the mental health impacts of the residents living closest to the data center? Will you offer support to people who have endured the most? PFEIFFER: Port Washington's gargantuan project has led to angry protests, multiple lawsuits and opponents arrested for civil disobedience. Supporters say data centers will keep the United States competitive and could bring great wealth to places where they're built. But many residents feel frightened and helpless as they watch this rapid change, like 67-year-old Amanda Mueller. She relocated to Port Washington five years ago. AMANDA MUELLER: This was my last move. I feel like an elephant looking for a place to die in life, and I found utopia. It was so perfect. PFEIFFER: She bought a four-bedroom ranch house within walking distance of a beautiful, undeveloped stretch of beach on Lake Michigan. (SOUNDBITE OF FOOTSTEPS ON GRASS) PFEIFFER: Is this all your yard you see here, all this? MUELLER: Yeah. I own... PFEIFFER: Wow. MUELLER: ...Three acres. PFEIFFER: All the way to that fringe of... MUELLER: Yeah. PFEIFFER: ...Pine trees. MUELLER: Oh, all the way through there. PFEIFFER: Wow. MUELLER: This is the perfect retirement home. I mean... PFEIFFER: Look at this view you have. But her view is different this year. You can glimpse cranes in the distance. Port Washington's data center is being built about a half mile from her house. When did you get a hint that something was about to dramatically change in your neighborhood? MUELLER: I'm going to say two years ago. The farmer right next to me just sold a lot of his farmland. Tom Barrett is pushing legislation to increase transparency around data center projects and protect local control over their development, alongside health insurance reforms and limits on presidential war powers as he seeks a second term. The Livingston Post and its partner, Michigan Firsthand, caught up with the Republican congressman as he went door-to-door in the Potterville neighborhood near the first home he bought after returning from an Iraq deployment. In the wide-ranging interview, Barrett — who faces Democratic challenger William Lawrence in the Nov. 3 election for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District — also discussed inflation, artificial intelligence, Israel, education and public safety. (You can watch the full discussions with Barrett and Lawrence on YouTube, and read our companion interview with Lawrence here.) Acknowledging the high stakes – the race is the nation’s costliest House race for advertising according to WKAR and AdImpact – Barrett said he is feeling “optimistic.” “I’ve been in tough political campaigns before, and I know what it feels like to be in a close race,” he said. Local control of data centers Barrett said data center decisions should rest with local townships, villages and cities, and that residents should have the right to examine proposals before agreements are signed. On Aug. 20, Barrett introduced legislation to protect state and local authority over data center siting. On Sept. 24, he joined Maryland Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin in co-sponsoring Ohio Democratic Rep. Greg Landsman’s No Secrets for Data Centers Act, which would make covered nondisclosure agreements unenforceable. “I don’t want to do a ban on the development of AI or a ban on data centers entirely,” Barrett said, saying he was concerned about rising electricity costs, water consumption, noise and what communities would do with large facilities if technological changes ever made them obsolete. “What I want to make sure is that any data center project is done with the consent of the residents who live there.” Barrett said some communities may conclude a proposal meets their needs, while others may reject it. He argued that transparency requirements would not undermine the United States’ ability to compete in artificial intelligence, saying “if we’re going to do this, we’re going to do it with transparency and in the right way that addresses the concerns that people have.” Keeping humans in control of AI The 22-year Army veteran, who served in Iraq, Guantanamo Bay and South Korea, also supports pursuing an international agreement governing artificial intelligence and autonomous weapons. “I think every country should agree that having fully autonomous lethal weapons is dangerous in so many different ways,” he said. Barrett joined Democratic Reps. Don Beyer of Virginia and Sara Jacobs of California in introducing the Human Authority over Autonomous Weapons Act, which would require meaningful human oversight of intentionally lethal strikes by autonomous or AI-enabled weapons used by the U.S. military. He said the possibility that terrorist groups could obtain such weapons should give countries a common interest in negotiating limits. “I can’t say with certainty that they would, but I can say that I believe that it’s the appropriate thing to do,” he said. Health care reform and private insurance On health care, Barrett called for substantial changes to the healthcare system, including requiring insurers to spend more of their premium revenue on patient care, and expanding access to tax-exempt health savings accounts. “So I agree that the healthcare system in the country is broken, and we need substantial, radical reform,” he said. “I’ve actually introduced legislation that would increase what’s called the medical loss ratio.” His Care Over Profits Act would require insurers to spend at least 85% of premium revenue on medical care and quality improvement. Barrett said he also wants broader access to health savings accounts and expanded eligible expenses, including healthy food, gym memberships and fitness equipment. He argued that allowing workers and employers to contribute to accounts that follow people between jobs would give families more control over their coverage and encourage preventive care. “These big health insurance companies have gotten by on raising premiums and not increasing quality of care,” he said. Barrett rejected the Medicare for All approach, arguing that eliminating the commercial insurance market could undermine medical innovation and reduce the revenue hospitals and physicians rely on. “Today, the Medicare system works because we have a robust commercial insurance program as well,” he said. He said providers depend on a mix of patients with commercial insurance, Medicare and Medicaid, and warned that moving everyone to government payment rates could affect services. Iran, affordability and congressional authority In between conversations with voters, Barrett said people frequently have concerns about gasoline and diesel prices, and the effects on groceries, deliveries and agriculture. He blamed today’s inflationary environment on spending during the Biden administration, and acknowledged the Iran war is helping drive fuel-price increases. Ending the conflict, he said, would help stabilize costs. In April, Barrett introduced the bipartisan Prevent Endless Wars Act with Democratic Rep. Jared Golden of Maine, a measure that would deny expedited congressional consideration to military-force authorizations lasting more than five years or lacking an expiration date. “Our Constitution makes it clear that only Congress can decide to send our men and women into combat or not,” he said. artigo.texto: Regulating data centers in San Antonio has boiled down to one choice. Should data centers be approved on a case-by-case basis or can they be built by-right, whenever they meet a set of pre-determined city standards? On Tuesday, the City of San Antonio’s Zoning Commission recommended a plan for regulating data centers. It gives San Antonio City Council, which will make a final decision next week, a fourth option for regulations after three were presented last week. All four use by-right, case-by-case or a combination of those approval processes. There are some clear starting points for any data center land-use policy in San Antonio. Data centers will only be built in industrial, commercial or manufacturing zones. They will also not be allowed over the Edwards Aquifer Recharge Zone. These rules are only for land use — regulations regarding power or water use would fall under CPS Energy and the San Antonio Water System’s authority. The city’s Development Services Department presented two initial options for data center rules. The by-right option allows data centers to be approved automatically once they meet a list of city requirements. The case-by-case policy would require each data center project in the city to be plead its own case in front of City Council. Mayor Gina Ortiz Jones presented a third option last week, giving developers a list of citywide standards that developers could meet before they earn approval from City Council on a case-by-case basis. On Tuesday, the city’s Zoning Commission put forward its own recommendation. The committee of council member-appointed residents, which makes recommendations on land-use to City Council, outlined a policy that allows by-right data centers in some parts of the city , but not in others. San Antonio City Council will decide what the new rules will be at an Oct. 29 A session. The newest proposal On Tuesday, the Zoning Commission put forward its proposal for regulations. The commission’s policy proposal would allow by-right development in industrial areas, specifically the general, heavy, mixed and mixed heavy industrial districts, while there would be specific use authorization in business park, light industrial and general commercial zones. To build data centers by-right, developers would have to leave 350 feet of separation between data centers and residential or neighborhood buildings and have a 100-foot setback from their own property line. The rules also require downward-facing lighting, to prevent light pollution. The Zoning Commission also considered data centers that were already built; San Antonio currently has at least 19 data centers, according to the Texas Tribune. Sparrow said many previously built data centers would be non-conforming with new rules. They would be allowed to keep operating, he said, but they would not be able to expand or conduct extensive repairs unless they come into line with new policies. Commissioner John Bustamante recommended including an exemption for older data centers under the new rules, allowing them to finish expansions or phased construction. It was approved as part of the Zoning Commission’s recommendation. The Zoning Commission does not enact policies. Its recommendation will go to City Council members, who will consider it when making their decision. The first two options Councilman Ric Galvan (D6) got the ball rolling on data center regulations almost a year ago, when he submitted a request in October 2025 to start the policymaking process. Data centers have multiplied across Texas as larger facilities look to serve artificial intelligence needs. Galvan’s district has been a hotspot for their development within city limits. Staff from the city’s Development Services Department had four public meetings between May and September, where they discussed potential policies with stakeholders. “If you wanted to participate, you were invited,” said Logan Sparrow, assistant director at the DSD. “Not going to lie, a lot of those folks were from the [data center development] industry, but we certainly tried our best to include as many people as we could.” Developers have pushed for a set of clear requirements for construction. They see those rules as more stable, making investment and construction more dependable. That’s why they want by-right development, one of the first policies proposed by DSD. Developers could build a data center if they own the land and meet city requirements, which would include being 500 feet away from residential, school, hospital, day care and assisted living properties and a landscape buffer onsite. City officials are referring to this as Option 1. “Anytime we want to attract investment, there has to be consistency and predictability. They want to know the rules of the game,” said Stephanie Reyes, president of the Real Estate Council of San Antonio, who spoke in favor of by-right development on Tuesday. DSD staff also proposed case-by-case evaluations of data centers. That would require what’s known as a specific use authorization for each proposed data center. That means every data center would go in front of the Zoning Commission and City Council, which would lay out specific requirements for each data center. City officials are referring to this as Option 2. “It’s so important for you all to recommend to City Council this specific use authorization because it would give the public the opportunity to ask these questions and to give feedback and to share their concerns,” said Deedee Belmares, Clean Energy advocate for advocacy group Public Citizen. Public Citizen monitors data centers and informs residents about their development in San Antonio and across the state. On Wednesday, Belmares advocated for case-by-case evaluations of data centers, speaking out against DSD’s by-right proposal and the Zoning Commission’s latest recommendation. artigo.texto: EUROMETAL, 19 European industry associations and the IndustriALL European Trade Union have called for a wide extension of the carbon adjustment mechanism at the EU border (CBAM) to products of subsequent processing. The joint statement was published on the EUROMETAL website on October 19, on the eve of the trilateral negotiations between the European Parliament, the Council of the EU and the European Commission scheduled for October 20. The signatories called on European politicians to agree on large-scale measures to protect industrial supply chains, investment and employment in Europe. "Products subject to CBAM are subject to more equal competition conditions, which will allow them to continue to be produced in Europe," the statement said. — It will become increasingly difficult for goods that remain outside the framework of the mechanism to compete with imports: they may be forced out of the market or their production transferred to third countries where producers do not bear comparable carbon costs. As free quotas are gradually eliminated under the EU Emissions Trading System, this threat will increase." CBAM now applies primarily to products with a high carbon footprint, including steel and aluminum. At the same time, free quotas are being gradually abolished within the framework of the EU Emissions Trading System. According to industry associations, manufacturers using these materials may face increased emissions costs, while imports of finished and semi-finished products from outside the EU will not bear a comparable burden. This could put European manufacturers at a disadvantage and increase the risk that imports will displace their products and production will shift to countries with less stringent carbon emissions requirements. Such a scenario, the organizations note, may also weaken the incentives to invest in cleaner production in Europe. Among the vulnerable industries, the signatories of the statement included construction, transport and automotive, mechanical engineering, energy, packaging and household appliances, environmentally friendly technologies, as well as other industries with high metal consumption. EUROMETAL represents European companies engaged in the trade of steel, pipes and metals. The association believes that the competitiveness of the processing industries depends on the sustainability of the entire European steel supply chain. Previously, the organization has also repeatedly stressed the need to extend CBAM to products of subsequent conversions. According to the association, the joint initiative is designed to ensure a coordinated approach in which European goods will not lose out due to carbon costs stipulated by legislation.

artigo.texto: A specific kind of development has been assigned new Washington County zoning requirements: battery energy storage facilities. The county’s board of supervisors voted unanimously last week to put special permits in place for projects involving large industrial installations that store and distribute power to the electric grid. The regulations apply to storage facilities that have a capacity greater than 600 kilowatts per hour and, with the approval of a permit, they can be built only in light and heavy industrial zones. With the ordinance in place, the supervisors will have to vote to approve any battery energy storage projects. Lightshift Energy, an Arlington-based energy storage developer, has expressed interest in building one in Washington County, according to county officials. The projects would likely only be built in places near electrical substations, said Stephen Richardson, the county’s planning commission coordinator. “They don’t want to be very far away because you lose all your efficiency,” Richardson said. “You lose your current the longer the line is.” Combined with the new zoning restrictions, the only viable places would likely be in industrial parks, he said. There are three Appalachian Power substations around Abingdon: the Hillman Highway Substation, South Abingdon Substation and Arrowhead Substation. The power company also operates a major facility at Highlands Business Park near Glade Spring. Data centers have begun using energy storage systems to act as a buffer for voltage spikes and reduce reliance on diesel generators, and utility companies have begun to install them too. Earlier this spring, the Salem-based Blue Ridge Power Agency announced it was pairing with Lightshift to deploy energy storage installments across five sites in the region. In addition to the projects in Salem, Lightshift is also seeking federal approval for an energy storage installation at Highlands Business Park. The company is leasing a parcel there for $10,000 annually until it gets the proper permits, and then it plans to buy the property, County Administrator Jason Berry said by phone. It should be beneficial for anyone using the grid, Berry said, since the facility would be able to stabilize it and prevent blackouts. Appalachian Power uses the lines the facility would attach to, and its parent company, American Electric Power, also feeds power through those lines to multiple other states, he said. Lightshift declined to comment on the Washington County project. Once the company buys the property, the board of supervisors would have to vote to approve the development plans now that the stricter zoning regulations are in place. Though battery energy storage facilities require no onsite jobs, it would bring in more business property tax revenue for the county, Berry said. “For us, it’s more of a tax generator than a job generator,” he said. Other than Lightshift, there has been no other interest in battery energy storage projects in Washington County, Berry said.

artigo.texto: BYD FCB Ti 9 full-size SUV to launch post-Nov 15, Shark pickup enters China in December BYD’s Fang Cheng Bao brand will launch the Ti 9 full-size plug-in hybrid SUV in China after November 15, 2026, followed by the domestic debut of its Shark plug-in hybrid pickup in late November or early December. General Manager Xiong Tianbo announced the schedule, with Ti 9 display and test-drive vehicles expected at dealerships in late October ahead of launch. Fang Cheng Bao’s Ti 9 offers a six-seat layout and a 310 km electric range. The Ti 9 will become the flagship of Fang Cheng Bao’s Ti series, which targets the urban family segment with unibody SUVs. It measures 5,270 mm long, 1,999 mm wide and 1,880 mm tall, with a 3,130 mm wheelbase. Unlike the Bao 5 and Bao 8, which use body-on-frame construction, the Ti 9 adopts a monocoque structure and BYD’s DMS hybrid platform. The cabin has a six-seat, 2+2+2 layout with independent second-row seats. Equipment includes heating, ventilation, and massage functions across all three rows, a 30-inch panoramic front display, and a 21.4-inch ceiling-mounted, fold-down rear entertainment screen. The plug-in hybrid powertrain combines a 1.5-litre turbocharged gasoline engine rated at 115 kW (154 hp) with two electric motors producing up to 200 kW each. Together, they produce 400 kW (536 hp) and drive both axles. A 66.48 kWh lithium iron phosphate (LFP) battery from BYD’s FinDreams Battery delivers a claimed 310 km of electric-only range under the WLTC test cycle. BYD also claims a total range exceeding 1,600 km with a full tank and fully charged battery. The Ti 9 comes standard across all trims with BYD’s DiSus-A air suspension with road-preview capability and the iATS (Intelligent All-Terrain System). It also features flash-charging technology and second-generation Blade batteries. Exterior options include six finishes: Flowing Light Gold, Universal Silver, Starburst Gold, Crimson Cloud Red, Deep Space Blue and Meteorite Black, with solid and two-tone options. BYD Shark pickup prepares for domestic launch in China Fang Cheng Bao plans to introduce the Shark plug-in hybrid pickup in China in late November or early December 2026. The model debuted in Mexico in May 2024 and has since entered international markets. China’s Ministry of Industry and Information Technology (MIIT) lists the domestic version as a light-duty multipurpose truck. It measures 5,457 mm long, 1,971 mm wide and 1,925 mm tall, with a 3,260 mm wheelbase. The cargo bed measures 1,520 × 1,530 × 515 mm. The filing lists a curb weight of 2,710 kg, a gross vehicle weight rating of 3,495 kg and a rated payload of 460 kg. The domestic Shark uses a 1.5-litre turbocharged gasoline engine, designated BYD476ZQF, with a net output of 135 kW (181 hp). Its all-wheel-drive system pairs a 170 kW front electric motor with a 150 kW rear motor, delivering a combined peak electric-motor output of 320 kW (429 hp). The listed maximum speed is 180 km/h. An LFP battery supplied by Xi’an FinDreams Battery powers the plug-in hybrid system. Available domestic regulatory specifications do not list battery capacity or electric-only range, so overseas figures should not be treated as confirmed specifications for the Chinese version. Pricing remains unannounced Fang Cheng Bao has not yet announced domestic prices or trim levels for either model. The Ti 9 targets family buyers seeking a large, six-seat plug-in hybrid SUV, while the Shark extends the brand into the pickup segment. Fang Cheng Bao is a premium BYD brand that sold around 126,000 cars in the third quarter of 2026, up 131% from the same period last year.

artigo.texto: Found an error? Report now Marcel Aumer, CEO and majority shareholder of Flexbase, is having a large battery storage facility built in Laufenburg, Aargau. Keystone FlexBase is building a technology center in Laufenburg, Aargau. At its heart is a battery that will one day help stabilize the power grid. But from the perspective of FlexBase CEO Marcel Aumer, this can only be the beginning. When the Keystone-SDA news agency visited FlexBase in mid-September, the large construction site in Laufenburg was characterized above all by a massive excavation pit and numerous cranes. In the future, a building 218 meters long, 80 meters wide, 25 meters deep, and 30 meters high will stand there, as Aumer explained. To blend into the landscape, the concrete structure will be clad with a blue photovoltaic system, as Aumer explained. This complements the often-blue skies of the Fricktal region. The system will be one of the largest PV facade installations in Europe and will have “a capacity of at least two megawatts.” However, according to Aumer, the PV system is out of proportion to the battery storage system being installed. Plans at the time called for 108 vanadium redox flow batteries (VRFB) with a maximum capacity of 1.2 gigawatts by 2029—equivalent to that of the Leibstadt nuclear power plant. According to FlexBase, the planned storage capacity of 2.1 gigawatt-hours corresponds to the electricity needs of 170,000 households over a 24-hour period. Unlike a lithium-ion battery, the VRFB model planned for Laufenburg is neither flammable nor explosive, as Aumer noted. The tanks are mostly filled with water, which also simplifies disposal. Furthermore, the vanadium dissolved in the water—which is used as an electrolyte—is reusable. There is virtually no degradation, and the service life of redox flow batteries is longer than that of lithium-ion storage systems, for which the disposal problem remains unresolved. The largest facility of its kind to date is located in China and began operations at the start of the year, as Rongke Power announced at the time. According to the company’s figures, its capacity and output amount to one gigawatt-hour and 200 megawatts—significantly less than what is planned for Laufenburg. From Aumer’s perspective, this is the technology for a sustainable future, and it is gaining ground worldwide. “I have clear goals in mind,” said Aumer. “The peaks caused by renewable energy need to be smoothed out.” This refers both to short-term fluctuations and to storing excess capacity during the day and releasing it at night when capacity is insufficient. “But we still have a long, long way to go before we can ensure a 24-hour, 356-day power supply from renewable energy sources,” Aumer said. He cited Europe as an example. In its Electrification Action Plan published in July, the European Commission cited a need for 200 gigawatts of storage capacity by 2030 and as much as 500 gigawatts by 2040. According to Aumer, the demand for power and capacity is enormous. “Our project is large, but our 1.2 gigawatts of power and 2.1 gigawatt-hours of capacity are just a drop in the bucket,” Aumer noted. However, he added, batteries cannot simply be connected to the grid at will. The grids are aging, and there is a lack of connection capacity. Expansion is difficult—partly due to objections. “It’s the only place to build something on this scale. There’s no other place like it,” Aumer said of the site. That’s because the Laufenburg star connects the Swiss power grid to the European grid—here, more than 41 cross-border lines provide access to the European electricity market. “I don’t have that anywhere else,” said Aumer. Aumer knows the location very well. Over the past ten years, he has been coming and going from the Stern in Laufenburg for work. He developed the idea for the project over the course of several years, drawing on his experience. When the property in Laufenburg went up for sale in 2023, he “knew within a second: This is it.” When it comes to finances, Aumer is keeping a low profile. He said the total costs would range from 2.5 to 5 billion Swiss francs. The money comes from private funds—but he does not want to publicly disclose his investors. The CEO revealed that he is the majority shareholder of FlexBase. However, he isn't doing it for the money—his passion project can only be realized in this location and in this way, as a campus that covers a wide range of subject areas. These include, for example, an AI data center above the Batterie and space for startups.

artigo.texto: Wall Street's fastest traders are building data centers and backing chip startups to stay ahead in AI High-frequency traders like Jane Street and Hudson River Trading are now racing each other for AI computing power. The biggest firms are spending billions on cloud contracts, startups, and their own data centers, Bloomberg reports. Part of the reason is that they increasingly rely on machine learning to predict market moves. One executive estimates that compute spending is now ten to twenty times higher than it was before ChatGPT launched. XTX Markets is building a data center in Finland, and Jane Street runs one in Texas with more than 4,000 Nvidia GPUs. Hudson River spends $1 billion a year on AI, according to AI chief Iain Dunning, and signed a multiyear deal with CoreWeave. Jane Street went a different route. It invested $1 billion directly in CoreWeave and committed $6 billion to its computing services. Jane Street also led a funding round for chip startup Etched and became the first customer for its AI chip, which is supposed to deliver more performance by running at a lower voltage. According to Bloomberg, the industry sees rising costs and fast-aging chips as real risks. Executives like Jan Boomaars, CEO of Amsterdam-based high-frequency trader Optiver, still think doing nothing is more dangerous. artigo.texto: Every weekday, the CNBC Investing Club with Jim Cramer holds a "Morning Meeting" livestream at 10:20 a.m. ET. Here's a recap of Friday's key moments. 1. Stocks are mostly lower Friday, with the Dow leading the declines as the selling broadens out beyond just the AI trade. The 30-stock average is down about 1%. The S & P 500 and the Nasdaq are little changed after Thursday's brutal tech plunge. Pockets of tech are stronger Friday, with Palo Alto Networks and CrowdStrike our best portfolio stocks on the session. Both are up more than 6%. We trimmed some of our CrowdStrike into strength. We exited Broadcom . Rising bond yields and West Texas Intermediate crude up over $103 per barrel, due to fears of renewed tensions between the U.S. and Iran, are not helping stocks. Portfolio director Jeff Marks pointed out that despite yesterday's broader weakness, it wasn't all bad news for our Club names, with Eli Lilly , Johnson & Johnson , and Kimberly-Clark seeing notable gains. While all three are down Friday, Jeff said the moves are a reminder of why it is "always good to have some of these in a portfolio to be diversified for months like this." All three still have nice gains week to date. 2. Meta Platforms shares fell again Friday, extending Thursday's nearly 7% decline. It's one of our worst performers for the week. Jeff said that Meta is at the center of a growing concern among investors — "how is the AI buildout going to get funded?" Wall Street is increasingly worried about how the social media giant will finance its AI ambitions, which include expansion of its hit new AI agent Muse, as free cash flow turned negative for the first time since the company's 2012 initial public offering. Meta raised the low end of its full-year capital expenditure outlook. In an SEC filing, the company mentioned needing to raise "hundreds of billions of dollars over a period of several years beginning as early as fall 2026." As for the Club, we're sticking with Meta given its strong fundamentals and promising Muse roadmap, which were on display during the just-reported quarter. However, the bright spots have been overshadowed by all this other stuff. 3. We picked up a few shares of GE Vernova during yesterday's sell-off. Jim Cramer felt that it was a good time to make the move after watching and waiting. "Why don't we pick up a little bit, play for a little bit of a bounce, because remember the data center demand story is still quite strong," he said. When GE Vernova reports earnings next week, Jeff said we want to hear about continued strong orders for the company's heavy-duty gas turbines and strong pricing. We will also want to see that their electrical business is doing well, too. Looking ahead, 10 other Club names are on next week's earnings docket: Boeing , Alphabet , Microsoft , Linde , Eli Lilly , Starbucks , Amazon , Intel , FedEx , and FedEx Freight . artigo.texto: Democratic congressional nominee William Lawrence is calling for a federal moratorium on new data centers until regulations give communities greater control over development, saying opposition to the projects is bringing together voters across party lines. In a wide-ranging interview with Michigan Firsthand for The Livingston Post, Lawrence also outlined a gradual expansion of Medicare that could retain a role for private insurance, proposed a national infrastructure bank to finance housing, and endorsed legislation restricting transfers of offensive weapons to Israel. He also discussed his association with political streamer Hasan Piker, and his relationship with U.S. Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed. Lawrence faces Republican incumbent U.S. Rep. Tom Barrett in the Nov. 3 election for Michigan’s 7th Congressional District, which includes all of Livingston County. Advertising spending in the district has exceeded $61 million this election cycle, making it the nation’s costliest House race for advertising, according to WKAR and AdImpact data, as Democrats hope to wrest control of the U.S. House and Senate away from Republicans. Watch the full discussion with Lawrence on Michigan Firsthand, the YouTube podcast produced in partnership with The Livingston Post, by clicking here. Read our companion interview with Barrett in The Livingston Post and watch the full discussion on Michigan Firsthand here. A pause on data centers The Lansing resident and community organizer who defeated the former U.S. Ambassador Bridget Brink and former Navy SEAL Matt Maasdam for the Democratic nomination argues that communities should not have to accept the projects to secure a prosperous future, particularly when the technology they support could displace workers. “We need to slow this down,” Lawrence said, calling for federal rules that would help communities “determine their own future rather than having it pushed onto us from above.” He described concerns over data centers as a bipartisan issue that surfaced in his meetings in Howell Township, Lyon Township, Mason and elsewhere with residents who shared concerns about electricity bills, water use and property values. “Unfortunately, there’s also been a lot of bipartisan support from the top down for supporting the interests of the big tech companies and data center developers,” he said. “I think people deserve to have a good future and a prosperous economy without just having to accept this deal that’s being pushed to us from Silicon Valley with no opportunity for local communities to determine their own futures.” Lawrence also acknowledged the state’s role in attracting data center developers through incentives such as tax breaks, and he criticized Gov. Gretchen Whitmer and state lawmakers for their handling of data center development. “I’ve been clear that I disagree with how the governor and the Michigan legislature has handled this issue,” he said. “And I think it really demonstrates that, again, this is an area where people from the grassroots have a lot in common: Democrat, independent and Republican.” Earlier this year, Attorney General Dana Nessel, in a previous interview with Michigan Firsthand for The Livingston Post, said that she thinks the Governor sold the legislature a “bill of goods.” A gradual expansion of Medicare On health care, Lawrence described Medicare for All as a goal reached through successive changes rather than an immediate replacement of the existing system. “It’s gonna be a step-by-step process,” he said. His proposed steps include lowering Medicare’s eligibility age to 55 or 50, adding dental, vision and hearing benefits and expanding coverage for long-term care. He also said reversing Medicaid cuts would be an immediate priority. Asked whether he still sees a role for private insurance, Lawrence said a public plan could provide baseline coverage while people purchase additional benefits. “I think that we can continue to have private insurance in some form,” he said. But he did not give a firm guarantee that people could keep their current insurance. Asked directly, he began with “most likely” before saying the answer would depend on the plan’s details and the transition. “What I’m clear on is that we need to have universal guaranteed coverage,” he said. Housing and tenant protections On housing, Lawrence proposed stronger tenant protections, including legal representation in eviction proceedings, alongside efforts to make construction and financing less expensive. He said he would co-sponsor existing legislation to establish a “national infrastructure bank,” with lending directed toward housing, water systems and transportation. “Now we can have a national infrastructure bank that still delivers profit to its investors and has a public purpose and can be targeted towards investments like housing,” he said. Lawrence said the goal should include housing affordable to middle-income residents as well as people with lower incomes, with opportunities for both renters and prospective homeowners. Tariffs and rising costs Lawrence also criticized President Donald Trump’s tariff policies, arguing that unpredictable changes make it harder for businesses to invest and families to plan. “You know, tariffs can be okay if it’s part of a consistent trade and industrial strategy,” he said. “But what the president is doing is he’s seemingly waking up in the morning and then just deciding what he wants the tariff rate to be – 55% or 40% or 25% or 5%, depending on his mood, or depending on the last of his advisors who happen to have his ear. That creates completely erratic business conditions.” Lawrence said Michigan families were paying an average of $5,000 more over the past year because of tariffs. The National Taxpayers Union Foundation estimated $23 billion in executive tariff costs on imports into Michigan from January 2025 through June 2026. That’s equivalent to $5,619 per household when divided by the state’s household count. Foreign policy

artigo.texto: Australian installers will get a closer look at Solis’ expanding battery storage range at All Energy Australia 2026. The company will showcase three SolisStorage products: EverCore C&I ESS, FlexCore-OD, and FlexAIO. Together, they cover integrated commercial storage, modular outdoor batteries, and all-in-one home energy storage. Visitors can explore the range at Stand JJ143, Melbourne Convention and Exhibition Centre, on 28 and 29 October. For retailers, installers, and engineering, procurement, and construction (EPC) providers, the display offers an opportunity to discuss practical project requirements. These include system configuration, installation planning, inverter compatibility, and matching storage to customer needs. Solis will also host an on-site product launch during the exhibition, giving visitors another reason to stop by. Quick summary - Commercial storage: EverCore integrates battery storage, power conversion, and energy management, while FlexCore-OD offers modular outdoor battery storage. - Residential storage: FlexAIO combines an all-in-one approach with a modular, stackable design and plug-and-play connections. - Visit Solis: Explore the products and discuss upcoming installations at Stand JJ143 on 28 and 29 October. EverCore brings an integrated approach to commercial storage Commercial battery projects can involve very different operating requirements. A business managing daytime demand may need a different configuration from one with substantial evening consumption. The SolisStorage EverCore C&I ESS brings battery storage, power conversion, and energy management functions together in an integrated solution. For installers and EPCs, that makes it a product to investigate when considering an integrated approach to commercial and industrial storage. At the exhibition, Solis will discuss how EverCore may support energy cost management and greater energy flexibility. The team will also address application requirements, system design, and project planning. These conversations can help installers assess whether the solution suits a customer’s operating needs. The useful starting point is the project itself: how the business consumes electricity, its storage objectives, and its installation constraints. Bringing those details to the stand can help move discussions beyond product features and towards a suitable system configuration. FlexCore-OD offers modular outdoor battery storage Solis will also showcase SolisStorage FlexCore-OD, an outdoor battery storage solution for commercial and industrial applications. Its modular, stackable architecture offers another approach for projects with different capacity and site requirements. FlexCore-OD features a plug-and-play design and IP66 protection, supporting its intended use in outdoor installations. For installers, the exhibition provides an opportunity to examine the product and discuss how its modular design works in practice. Visitors can also explore compatible inverter solutions and ask how different configurations accommodate site conditions and customer energy requirements. That compatibility discussion matters. Selecting a battery involves understanding how the complete system will operate, including its inverter and control arrangements. EverCore and FlexCore-OD give commercial installers two approaches to compare: integrated energy storage and modular outdoor battery storage. The right fit will depend on the application, configuration requirements, and conditions at the installation site. Visitors can examine FlexAIO at the stand and discuss configuration options, installation workflows, and home energy management. Visitors should also clarify product availability, applicable certifications, warranty terms, and technical documentation before progressing a customer proposal. Those details help turn an exhibition conversation into a practical next step. artigo.texto: The Next Cooling Challenge: Building Resilience Beyond Technology The conversation around data center cooling has changed dramatically over the past few years. Not long ago, discussions focused primarily on efficiency, airflow, and uptime. Today, the rise of AI has exponentially elevated the urgency behind efficient cooling. As operators race to deploy new capacity, the ability to effectively manage heat is becoming just as important as access to power. According to the International Energy Agency (IEA), data centers accounted for roughly half of U.S. electricity demand growth in 2025, reflecting the rapid expansion of digital infrastructure. At the same time, AI workloads are driving higher rack densities and accelerating the industry's adoption of new cooling approaches, including a mix of air and liquid cooling for the most demanding applications. What's emerging, however, is a broader market lesson. The industry's challenge is no longer just how to cool the next generation of infrastructure; it's how to build the resilience needed to support that growth over the long term. Over the past several years, data center operators have learned that supply chains can be just as critical as technology. Whether the disruption comes from global logistics bottlenecks, component shortages, geopolitical tensions, or changing trade policies, the impact is often the same: delayed projects, rising costs, and uncertainty around delivery timelines. Recent tariff activity has reinforced that reality. New duties affecting materials such as steel and aluminum, along with ongoing questions surrounding technology imports, have prompted many organizations to take a closer look at where critical infrastructure components come from and how vulnerable those supply chains may be. These various impacts have directly led to a growing focus on localization. Companies are increasingly looking for ways to shorten supply chains, diversify sourcing, and bring manufacturing closer to the markets they serve. This isn't a retreat from globalization. Rather, it reflects a practical recognition that resiliency often comes from having more options, not fewer. We've seen this lesson play out repeatedly in the data center industry. Operators don't rely on a single power source. They build redundancy into critical systems. Cooling infrastructure includes backup capacity. Network connectivity is designed with multiple paths. The objective is simple: reduce risk while maintaining flexibility. There is growing evidence that the same thinking is being applied to supply chains. Regional manufacturing investments across North America are helping create additional layers of stability for industries that depend on specialized equipment and long planning horizons. In many cases, closer proximity between manufacturers and customers can help organizations adapt more quickly when market conditions change. As AI adoption continues to accelerate, cooling will remain one of the defining topics shaping data center strategy. But the lessons emerging from the market suggest that the future conversation will be larger than cooling technology alone. The most successful organizations will likely be those that view resilience holistically, balancing innovation with operational flexibility, and technological advancement with supply chain preparedness. The data center industry has always excelled at planning for failures before they happen. As demand continues to grow, that mindset may become just as valuable beyond the walls of the data hall as it is inside them. About the Author Tom Carroll Tom Carroll serves as Director of Data Center within the ACV Strategic Business Field at ebm-papst Americas, a global leader in heating and air movement technology. With more than 15 years of experience in air moving, motor, and electronic systems— including 11 years with ebm-papst—he leverages deep technical expertise and leadership across the HVAC and data center ecosystem to drive innovation and growth in high efficiency cooling solutions. He works closely with OEM partners and ebm-papst’s R&D teams to develop advanced solutions for the evolving data center and HVAC markets. Tom holds a B.S. in Mechanical Engineering and an M.S. in Management of Technology from Fairfield University.

artigo.texto: 3 min leitura Mercado Voluntário de Carbono abre portas ao financiamento do restauro de pradarias marinhas Nova metodologia, em consulta pública até 22 de novembro, permite criar créditos de carbono associados à recuperação destes ecossistemas e prevê créditos adicionais para projetos com benefícios para a biodiversidade. 23 Out 2026 - 16:14 3 min leitura O Mercado Voluntário de Carbono (MVC) poderá passar a financiar projetos de restauro e conservação de pradarias marinhas em Portugal continental. A proposta de metodologia para o “Restauro e Conservação de Pradarias Marinhas em Portugal Continental” entrou nesta sexta-feira, 23 de outubro, em consulta pública, abrindo caminho ao desenvolvimento de projetos que conciliem ação climática, proteção da biodiversidade e restauro da natureza. A metodologia foi proposta pela ANA – Aeroportos de Portugal, S.A., com o apoio da NBI – Natural Business Intelligence, do Centro de Ciências do Mar da Universidade do Algarve e do Instituto Mediterráneo de Estudios Avanzados, tendo sido objeto de análise pela Comissão Técnica de Acompanhamento do Mercado Voluntário de Carbono. O parecer técnico desta Comissão reconhece o carácter inovador da proposta e considera que a criação desta metodologia constitui uma oportunidade para mobilizar financiamento privado para a recuperação destes ecossistemas, reforçar o conhecimento técnico e científico e diversificar a oferta de projetos no MVC, segundo informa o Ministério do Ambiente e da Energia (MAEn). A proposta prevê a possibilidade de atribuição de Créditos de Carbono + quando os projetos demonstrem benefícios adicionais para a biodiversidade e o capital natural, reforçando a ligação entre ação climática e restauro da natureza. A metodologia contribuirá igualmente para a concretização do Plano Nacional de Restauro da Natureza (PNRN), ao criar condições para mobilizar investimento privado para o restauro dos ecossistemas marinhos e a recuperação da biodiversidade. “Queremos que o Mercado Voluntário de Carbono seja também um instrumento para financiar a recuperação da natureza. Com esta nova metodologia, damos um passo concreto para valorizar o carbono azul e o papel dos ecossistemas marinhos na ação climática”, afirma a ministra do Ambiente e Energia, Maria da Graça Carvalho. O MVC encontra-se já em funcionamento, com três metodologias aprovadas, cinco projetos submetidos na plataforma, dos quais dois já aprovados, 10 verificadores qualificados, 30 utilizadores registados e 977 créditos de carbono futuros emitidos. Completado o primeiro ano de funcionamento, o MVC entra agora numa nova fase de desenvolvimento, orientada para o aumento do número de projetos, a diversificação das metodologias disponíveis e o reforço da procura de créditos de carbono nacionais. “Depois de um primeiro ano dedicado a criar as condições para o funcionamento do Mercado Voluntário de Carbono, queremos agora acelerar a sua dinamização, com mais projetos, novas metodologias e maior procura de créditos de carbono nacionais, para canalizar mais investimento privado para a descarbonização e para a valorização dos nossos recursos naturais”, assinala Maria da Graça Carvalho.

artigo.texto: Big Tech's Next Nuclear Bet: More Power From Reactors Already Running Key Highlights - Google and Amazon's agreements with Constellation Energy support approximately 1,080 MW of additional nuclear generation, while Meta is backing hundreds of megawatts in planned uprates through separate agreements. - The Nuclear Regulatory Commission anticipates 31 reactor uprate applications through 2032, representing approximately 2.4 GW of potential additional electrical generating capacity. - Long-term corporate power agreements, regulated utility investments and federal financing are creating new pathways for modernizing operating nuclear plants and expanding their output. - Nuclear uprates can increase generation without constructing new reactors, but equipment modifications, scheduled outages and regulatory approvals still impose multiyear delivery timelines. - FERC's October 9 rejection of key elements of PJM's large-load framework highlights the continuing gap between financing additional generation and securing deliverable power for individual AI data centers. The next wave of nuclear power for AI data centers may come not from new reactors, but from generating stations that have been operating for decades. In a pair of agreements announced just a week apart, Google and Amazon committed to long-term electricity purchases supporting approximately 1,080 MW of additional nuclear generating capacity from Constellation Energy's existing fleet. The transactions follow earlier commitments by Meta to support reactor upgrades at operating nuclear facilities in Ohio, Pennsylvania and Illinois, establishing a broader commercial model in which hyperscale technology companies help finance increases in nuclear output. Under its October 6 agreement with Google, Constellation plans to invest more than $4.3 billion in equipment and technology upgrades at 11 operating reactor units across Illinois, Pennsylvania and New Jersey. The 20-year power purchase agreement supports 890 MW of new generating capacity, with the first upgrades expected to begin delivering additional electricity in 2028. A separate 15-year agreement covers 2,700 MW of existing nuclear generation, underscoring the distinction between securing today's electricity supply and financing additional capacity. Amazon's September 30 agreement similarly supports 190 MW of new generation at Maryland's Calvert Cliffs nuclear station, alongside purchases of existing output. Together, the two arrangements underpin more than $7 billion in planned infrastructure investment. Unlike proposed advanced reactors, these facilities already have operating licenses, grid connections, established workforces and decades of operating experience. Increasing their output avoids some of the cost, permitting and construction challenges associated with building entirely new nuclear plants, although significant upgrades still require extensive engineering, equipment modifications and regulatory approval. The potential scale is substantial. According to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission's current application schedule, the agency anticipates 31 applications for reactor power uprates through 2032, representing approximately 2,421 MW of potential additional electrical generating capacity. That is roughly equivalent to the output of two large nuclear reactors without constructing new reactor units. However, these figures represent anticipated applications, not approved projects or guaranteed additions to the grid. For data center developers facing immediate power shortages, the strategy offers no quick fix. Many of the largest upgrades will not be completed until the early 2030s, and additional generation entering a regional transmission system does not necessarily resolve local power-delivery constraints. Nevertheless, the emergence of long-term, hyperscaler-backed financing for nuclear uprates marks an important shift: major technology companies are investing not only in securing existing electricity supplies, but also in expanding the generating capacity available to the grid. Google Brings Agentic AI to Nuclear Operations Interestingly, beyond financing additional generating capacity, Google's agreement with Constellation includes an expanded five-year technology partnership to deploy Google Cloud and Gemini Enterprise across the utility's operations. Constellation plans to use agentic AI workflows for engineering and permitting, power-flow modeling, interconnection planning, equipment monitoring and outage management. The companies also envision using Google Cloud technologies to strengthen security across operational technology networks supporting critical infrastructure. The arrangement illustrates how AI is beginning to influence both sides of the electricity equation: driving demand for additional generation while providing tools intended to accelerate infrastructure development and improve operating efficiency. Those benefits remain prospective, however. Constellation has not demonstrated measurable improvements from the new deployment, and AI-assisted planning does not eliminate the engineering, safety and regulatory requirements governing nuclear uprates. Inside a Nuclear Uprate: What Actually Changes? Increasing the output of an operating nuclear plant is not simply a matter of turning up the reactor. Depending on the scope of the project, a power uprate can require changes to instrumentation, control systems, turbines, generators, cooling equipment and other infrastructure, along with engineering analysis demonstrating that the plant can operate safely at higher power levels. The approach is well established. According to the Nuclear Regulatory Commission, uprates approved over the past 20 years have added approximately 6 GW of electrical generating capacity to the U.S. grid, equivalent to the output of roughly six large reactors.
